name: Hyperkalemia (Elevated Blood Potassium)
overview: Severe hyperkalemia (≥6.5 mEq/L) or any hyperkalemia with ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS) is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate myocardial stabilization with IV Calcium Gluconate (or Calcium Chloride). This must be followed by intracellular potassium-shifting agents (IV Insulin with Dextrose, Albuterol) and eventually potassium-removing agents (Loop diuretics, GI cation binders like Patiromer, or emergent Hemodialysis).
patient_plain_language: Hyperkalemia is dangerously high potassium in the blood, usually because the kidneys cannot filter it out. Because potassium controls the heart's electrical rhythm, high levels can cause the heart to suddenly stop.

symptoms.name: Peripheral and facial edema
symptoms.description: Fluid retention in periorbital tissue, pretibial, and ankles. Characteristically observed in Hyperkalemia (Elevated Blood Potassium).

symptoms.name: Urinary alterations (Frothy / Dark / Dysuria)
symptoms.description: Changes in urine color, foaminess, or frequency. Characteristically observed in Hyperkalemia (Elevated Blood Potassium).

symptoms.name: Fatigue and anemia-related weakness
symptoms.description: Due to reduced erythropoietin and uremic toxin buildup. Characteristically observed in Hyperkalemia (Elevated Blood Potassium).

symptoms.name: Hypertension
symptoms.description: Volume overload and hyperreninemia driving elevated blood pressure. Characteristically observed in Hyperkalemia (Elevated Blood Potassium).

symptoms.name: Pruritus and metallic taste
symptoms.description: Uremic symptoms in advanced renal compromise. Characteristically observed in Hyperkalemia (Elevated Blood Potassium).

red_flags: Muscle weakness, numbness, or tingling in the limbs
Heart palpitations, skipped beats, or severe shortness of breath (Medical Emergency)

name: Aortic Valve Stenosis
overview: In 1,000 low-risk patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis, transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (TAVR) with a balloon-expandable valve was superior to surgical replacement with respect to composite death, stroke, or rehospitalization at 1 year (8.5% vs 15.1%; difference -7.1 percentage points; 95% CI -10.8 to -3.5; p<0.001 for noninferiority, p=0.001 for superiority). Standard therapy requires echocardiographic surveillance and valve intervention once AVA <1.0 cm2 or mean gradient >=40 mmHg with symptoms.
patient_plain_language: Aortic stenosis is like a doorway in your heart's main valve that has become calcified, stiff, and narrow. When the door cannot open fully, your heart has to squeeze much harder to pump blood to the rest of your body.

name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM)
overview: In 251 patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the cardiac myosin inhibitor mavacamten significantly increased peak oxygen consumption (pVO2) and reduced LVOT gradient by 36 mmHg vs placebo (p<0.0001). 37% of mavacamten-treated patients met the primary composite endpoint vs 17% in placebo. First-line therapy includes non-vasodilating beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.
patient_plain_language: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a genetic condition where the heart muscle walls become abnormally thick and bulky, like an over-muscled pump. This extra thickness makes it harder for the heart chamber to relax and can partly block blood leaving the heart.

name: Infective Endocarditis
overview: AHA/ESC guidelines mandate modified Duke Criteria for diagnostic confirmation (positive blood cultures across multiple bottles and transesophageal echocardiographic demonstration of oscillating vegetation or abscess). Intravenous bactericidal antibiotic therapy tailored to organism (viridans streptococci, S. aureus, Enterococcus) for 4-6 weeks is required. name: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)
overview: ESVS and SVS guidelines recommend ultrasound screening for men aged 65-75 with any smoking history. Threshold for elective repair (EVAR or open surgical repair) is an aneurysm diameter >= 5.5 cm in men, >= 5.0 cm in women, or rapid expansion >= 1.0 cm/year. patient_plain_language: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a bulge or ballooning in the main blood vessel (the aorta) that carries blood through your belly. It happens when the artery wall weakens over time, often due to high blood pressure and smoking, much like a weak spot on a bicycle tire.

name: Neurogenic Orthostatic Hypotension (nOH)
overview: Diagnostic consensus defines orthostatic hypotension as a sustained reduction of systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing or head-up tilt. In neurogenic forms (Parkinson's, MSA, diabetic autonomic neuropathy), blunted reflex tachycardia (ratio of delta HR to delta SBP <0.5 bpm/mmHg) reflects sympathetic failure. Pharmacotherapy includes droxidopa, midodrine, or fludrocortisone titrated against supine hypertension.
patient_plain_language: Orthostatic hypotension means your blood pressure drops sharply when you stand up. Normally, nerve reflexes squeeze your leg blood vessels like elastic bands to keep blood flowing up to your brain; in this condition, those nerve reflexes are sluggish, leaving blood pooled in your legs.

name: Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS)
overview: HRS consensus criteria require a sustained heart rate increase of >= 30 bpm (or >= 40 bpm in individuals aged 12-19) within 10 minutes of standing or tilt-table testing, in the absence of orthostatic hypotension, accompanied by chronic orthostatic symptoms for >= 3 months. First-line therapy centers on non-pharmacological intravascular volume expansion: 2-3 L oral fluids daily, 8-10 g sodium daily, structured recumbent/rowing exercise training. Pharmacologic adjuncts include fludrocortisone, propranolol/bisoprolol, pyridostigmine, and midodrine.
patient_plain_language: POTS is a condition where your body has trouble balancing blood flow when you are upright. When you stand, blood pools in your legs and belly, and your heart races frantically trying to pump blood back up to your brain, making you feel lightheaded, exhausted, and shaky.

name: Raynaud's Phenomenon
overview: Primary Raynaud's (idiopathic vasospasm) is distinguished from secondary Raynaud's (underlying connective tissue disease such as systemic sclerosis, SLE) by normal nailfold capillaroscopy, symmetric attacks, absence of digital ulceration/necrosis, and negative antinuclear antibody (ANA) serology. First-line pharmacotherapy consists of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (nifedipine 30-60 mg daily or amlodipine 5-10 mg daily), reducing attack frequency by 33% and severity by 35% in meta-analyses. Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) are effective for refractory symptoms or digital ulcers.
patient_plain_language: Raynaud's phenomenon is an over-reaction of the tiny blood vessels in your fingers and toes to cold temperatures or stress. The vessels spasm shut temporarily, turning your fingers white, then blue, and finally red and throbbing as blood rushes back in.

name: Supraventricular Tachycardia (AVNRT / AVRT)
overview: Clinical guidelines recommend modified Valsalva maneuver (REVERT protocol: 15-second strain at 40 mmHg followed by immediate supine repositioning and 45-degree passive leg elevation for 15 seconds) as first-line bedside therapy, achieving 43% cardioversion vs 17% standard Valsalva (p<0.0001). name: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH)
overview: Hemodynamic definition updated to mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) > 20 mmHg with pulmonary capillary wedge pressure <= 15 mmHg and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) > 2 Wood units. Initial upfront oral dual combination therapy (ERA + PDE5i: macitentan/tadalafil or ambrisentan/tadalafil) demonstrated significant reduction in clinical failure events (AMBITION trial, HR 0.50, p<0.001). Parenteral prostacyclin analogues (epoprostenol) are mandatory for high-risk patients.
patient_plain_language: Pulmonary arterial hypertension means blood pressure inside the arteries of your lungs is dangerously high. It is different from regular arm blood pressure: the small blood vessels in your lungs become stiff and narrow, forcing the right side of your heart to work overtime to push blood through.

name: Bronchiectasis (Non-Cystic Fibrosis)
overview: Diagnostic confirmation requires high-resolution CT (HRCT) demonstrating bronchoarterial ratio > 1.0 (signet-ring sign) and lack of bronchial tapering. Airway clearance techniques (oscillating PEP devices, active cycle of breathing) twice daily significantly improve sputum clearance and quality of life. patient_plain_language: Bronchiectasis is a condition where the airways in your lungs have become abnormally widened, scarred, and flabby, like stretched-out elastic bands. Because they lose their shape, thick mucus pools inside, making it hard to clear bacteria and leading to repeat lung infections.

name: Pulmonary Sarcoidosis
overview: ATS guidelines require consistent clinical and radiographic presentation, noncaseating granulomas on histopathology (bronchoscopy with EBUS-TBNA preferred), and exclusion of alternate causes (fungal/mycobacterial infections, berylliosis). First-line therapy for organ-threatening disease (progressive pulmonary decline, cardiac or neurosarcoidosis, hypercalcemia) is oral prednisone (20-40 mg daily tapered over 6-12 months). patient_plain_language: Sarcoidosis is an immune system condition where your white blood cells cluster together to form microscopic inflammatory lumps called granulomas, most often in the lungs and lymph nodes. Think of your immune system setting off false fire alarms and leaving small clumps of inflammatory tissue behind.

overview: ATS/JRS/ALAT guidelines distinguish non-fibrotic vs fibrotic HP using high-resolution CT (three-density pattern / headcheese sign, mosaic attenuation, centrilobular ground glass) and bronchoalveolar lavage (lymphocytosis >20-30%). In progressive fibrotic HP, nintedanib slows FVC decline by 57% (INBUILD trial, p<0.001), while systemic steroids and mycophenolate mofetil target non-fibrotic inflammation.
patient_plain_language: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an allergic reaction deep inside the air sacs of your lungs caused by repeatedly breathing in microscopic organic dust, such as mold spores, bird droppings, or down feathers. Over time, this chronic allergy can cause stiff scar tissue to form in your lungs.

name: Pleural Effusion & Empyema
overview: Diagnostic thoracentesis with Light's criteria differentiates transudate (heart failure, cirrhosis) from exudate (infection, malignancy). Complicated parapneumonic effusion and empyema are defined by pleural fluid pH < 7.20, glucose < 60 mg/dL, elevated LDH (>1,000 U/L), or positive Gram stain/culture. Immediate intercostal chest tube drainage and parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics covering anaerobes and Gram-negative bacilli are mandatory. Intrapleural tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) plus DNase (MIST-2 trial) significantly improves fluid drainage and reduces surgical referral by 77% (p=0.005).
patient_plain_language: A pleural effusion is an abnormal buildup of fluid in the space between your lung and your chest wall, like water pooling around a sponge. When bacteria infect this fluid, it forms a pocket of pus called an empyema, which compresses the lung and makes breathing painful and difficult.

name: Acute Bronchitis
overview: Over 90% of acute bronchitis cases in immunocompetent adults are caused by respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, coronavirus, influenza, RSV, parainfluenza). Cochrane meta-analysis of 17 RCTs (n=5,099) established that routine antibiotic therapy provides no clinically meaningful benefit (reducing cough duration by only 0.5 days) while doubling adverse drug events (nausea, diarrhea, rash; OR 1.20) and driving antimicrobial resistance. Routine guidelines (CDC, NICE, ACP) recommend symptomatic therapy alone: honey, guaifenesin, short-acting beta-agonists only if wheezing present, and patient education on natural 2-3 week cough duration.
patient_plain_language: Acute bronchitis is a temporary viral infection of the large breathing tubes in your lungs, usually coming after a common cold. Because it is almost always caused by viruses, antibiotics will not cure it, but soothing remedies and rest allow the airway lining to heal over 2 to 3 weeks.

name: Chronic Refractory Cough
overview: Chronic cough is defined as daily cough lasting > 8 weeks. Systematic guideline evaluation rules out the 'triad' of upper airway cough syndrome, cough-variant asthma (bronchoprovocation test), and non-acid reflux before diagnosing cough hypersensitivity syndrome. In unexplained or refractory chronic cough, targeted neuromodulators (low-dose slow-release morphine 5-10 mg BID, gabapentin 300-900 mg daily, speech pathology cough suppression therapy) achieve significant reductions in cough frequency and Leicester Cough Questionnaire improvement.
patient_plain_language: Chronic cough is a cough that lingers for more than 8 weeks after any initial infection has cleared. Often, the nerves in your throat and airways become hyper-sensitive—like a car alarm that goes off when a gentle breeze blows—triggering sudden coughing fits from talking, laughing, or cold air.

name: Asbestosis & Occupational Pneumoconiosis
overview: Diagnostic attribution per Helsinki criteria requires documented occupational latency (typically >15-20 years from first exposure), high-resolution CT demonstration of bilateral basilar interstitial fibrosis, subpleural curvilinear lines, dot-like opacities, and pleural plaques. PFTs demonstrate a classic restrictive ventilatory defect with reduced DLCO. Tobacco smoking acts synergistically, increasing lung cancer risk by up to 50-fold in asbestos-exposed workers. Management focuses on rigorous smoking cessation, prompt treatment of respiratory infections, and screening for pleural mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma.
patient_plain_language: Asbestosis is scarring of the lung tissue caused by inhaling microscopic asbestos mineral fibers years ago at work. The body cannot dissolve the tiny needle-like fibers, so the lungs form stiff fibrous scar tissue around them, making the lungs less elastic and harder to inflate.

name: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
overview: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells results in absolute insulin deficiency, requiring lifelong exogenous insulin replacement. Multiple daily injections (MDI: basal long-acting degludec/glargine + rapid-acting prandial aspart/lispro) or automated insulin delivery (AID / hybrid closed-loop pump systems) are standard of care. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) is a Class 1 recommendation, targeting Time in Range (TIR 70-180 mg/dL) > 70% and Time Below Range (<70 mg/dL) < 4%, reducing severe hypoglycemia and microvascular complications (DCCT/EDIC cohorts).
patient_plain_language: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition where your body's immune system mistakenly attacks the insulin-producing factory cells in your pancreas. Because your body makes zero insulin, you must supply it daily through injections or a pump to allow sugar to enter your cells for energy.

name: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
overview: Diagnostic triad: Hyperglycemia (blood glucose > 250 mg/dL), ketosis (beta-hydroxybutyrate > 3.0 mmol/L or moderate/large urine ketones), and metabolic acidosis (arterial/venous pH < 7.30, serum bicarbonate < 18 mEq/L, anion gap > 12). Protocolized management mandates IV fluid resuscitation (0.9% NaCl 1,000 mL/hr initially), fixed-rate continuous IV insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/hr), and strict potassium replacement (adding 20-30 mEq K+ per liter of IV fluid once K+ < 5.2 mEq/L) to prevent lethal hypokalemic arrhythmias. Insulin is withheld only if serum potassium is < 3.3 mEq/L until repleted.
patient_plain_language: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening medical emergency where the body has so little insulin that it cannot burn sugar for fuel. Instead, it breaks down body fat at an extreme speed, flooding the bloodstream with toxic acids called ketones.

name: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's Disease)
overview: Primary adrenal insufficiency results from autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex (80-90% of cases in developed nations), leading to deficient glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, and adrenal androgen production. Standard confirmation requires cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH 250 mcg) stimulation test yielding peak serum cortisol < 18 mcg/dL (500 nmol/L) at 30 or 60 min with elevated plasma ACTH (>2x ULN). Maintenance therapy requires hydrocortisone (15-25 mg/day divided 2-3 doses) plus fludrocortisone (0.05-0.2 mg/day). Patient education on emergency 'sick-day rules' (doubling/tripling oral doses) and injectable hydrocortisone (100 mg IM) prevents fatal adrenal crises.
patient_plain_language: Addison's disease is like having an empty battery in your body's stress hormone factory. Your adrenal glands cannot make cortisol, the vital hormone that keeps your blood pressure stable, manages energy, and protects you during illness.

name: Cushing's Syndrome (Hypercortisolism)
overview: Endogenous hypercortisolism causes central obesity, proximal muscle weakness, wide violaceous striae (>1 cm), facial plethora, osteopenia, and severe neuropsychiatric symptoms. Diagnosis requires at least two concordant first-line screening tests: 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC >3x ULN), late-night salivary cortisol (>145 ng/dL on 2 separate evenings), or overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test (serum cortisol > 1.8 mcg/dL at 8 AM). Cushing disease (ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma, 70%) is treated with transsphenoidal adenomectomy; adrenal adenomas require laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Steroidogenesis inhibitors (ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat) serve as bridge or adjuvant medical therapy.
patient_plain_language: Cushing's syndrome is like your body's stress alarm getting permanently stuck in the 'ON' position. An excess of cortisol hormone leads to sudden weight gain around your waist and face, muscle weakness in your thighs, easy bruising, and high blood pressure.

name: Primary Hyperparathyroidism
overview: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) is characterized by hypercalcemia driven by autonomously elevated or inappropriately normal intact parathyroid hormone (PTH), primarily caused by a single benign parathyroid adenoma (85%). Classic clinical manifestations include nephrolithiasis, cortical bone resorption (osteoporosis at the distal 1/3 radius), constipation, and cognitive impairment. Parathyroidectomy provides definitive surgical cure with >95% success. Surgical criteria for asymptomatic patients include: serum calcium > 1.0 mg/dL above normal ULN, T-score ≤ -2.5 at lumbar spine, hip, or 1/3 radius, age < 50 years, eGFR < 60 mL/min, or 24-hour urinary calcium > 250 mg (women) / 300 mg (men).

name: Hypoparathyroidism
overview: Hypoparathyroidism results in hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypercalciuria due to absent or inadequate PTH secretion (most commonly iatrogenic after total thyroidectomy or neck dissection). Neuromuscular irritability manifests as perioral numbness, paresthesias, Chvostek's/Trousseau's signs, carpopedal spasms, and laryngospasm. Standard therapy relies on oral calcium carbonate/citrate (1,000-3,000 mg/day elemental) combined with active vitamin D metabolites (calcitriol 0.25-2.0 mcg/day). The therapeutic objective is maintaining serum albumin-adjusted calcium in the low-normal range (8.0-8.5 mg/dL) while avoiding hypercalciuria (24-hr urine calcium < 300 mg/day) to prevent nephrocalcinosis and renal failure.
patient_plain_language: Hypoparathyroidism is a shortage of parathyroid hormone, usually after neck or thyroid surgery. Without this hormone, calcium levels in your blood drop dangerously low, causing tingling in your fingertips and lips, painful muscle cramps, and tremors.

name: Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HeFH)
overview: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) is a dominant monogenic disorder (prevalence ~1:250) caused by mutations in LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9, leading to lifelong severe LDL-C elevation (>190 mg/dL in adults) and a >10-fold increased lifetime risk of premature coronary artery disease. Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria score clinical history, tendon xanthomas, and LDL-C levels. First-line therapy mandates high-intensity statin therapy (atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 40 mg) combined early with ezetimibe 10 mg (adds ~24% reduction), and PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies (evolocumab or alirocumab; adds ~50-60% reduction, FOURIER and ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trials) to achieve LDL-C targets (<55 mg/dL for secondary prevention; <70 mg/dL for primary prevention).
patient_plain_language: Familial hypercholesterolemia is an inherited gene mutation that prevents your liver from filtering 'bad' LDL cholesterol from your blood. Because cholesterol builds up from childhood, plaque forms in heart arteries decades earlier than normal unless treated with medication.

name: Male Hypogonadism (Testosterone Deficiency)
overview: Diagnosis of male hypogonadism requires persistent low morning fasting total testosterone (<300 ng/dL [10.4 nmol/L] on two separate occasions drawn between 8 AM and 10 AM) accompanied by unequivocal signs and symptoms: diminished libido, erectile dysfunction, decreased spontaneous erections, loss of axillary/pubic hair, and osteopenia. Serum LH and FSH differentiate primary (hypergonadotropic, testicular failure) from secondary (hypogonadotropic, hypothalamic-pituitary pathology). The TRAVERSE trial (NEJM 2023) demonstrated noninferiority of testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) regarding major adverse cardiac events in men with confirmed hypogonadism and pre-existing CVD. TRT is contraindicated in active prostate cancer, PSA > 4.0 ng/mL, severe untreated sleep apnea, or baseline hematocrit > 50%.
patient_plain_language: Male hypogonadism happens when a man's testicles or pituitary gland produce abnormally low levels of testosterone. This can cause persistent fatigue, loss of muscle mass, decreased sex drive, low mood, and thinning bones.

name: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
overview: Rotterdam diagnostic criteria require 2 out of 3 features: oligo- or anovulation, clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism (Ferriman-Gallwey hirsutism score ≥ 4-6, elevated free/total testosterone), and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (≥20 follicles per ovary or ovarian volume ≥10 mL), after excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, and non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Insulin resistance drives excess ovarian theca cell androgen production. Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) are first-line for irregular menses and hyperandrogenism; metformin improves insulin sensitivity and metabolic parameters; letrozole is first-line for ovulation induction in infertility (surpassing clomiphene in the PPCOS II trial; NEJM 2014).
patient_plain_language: PCOS is a hormonal and metabolic imbalance where ovaries make slightly higher levels of androgen hormones and eggs don't release predictably every month. This causes irregular periods, facial hair growth, acne, and difficulty getting pregnant.

name: Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)
overview: Peptic ulcer disease involves mucosal breaks ≥ 5 mm in the stomach or duodenum extending into the muscularis propria, primarily driven by Helicobacter pylori infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) provides definitive diagnosis and endoscopic Forrest classification for bleeding risk. H. pylori eradication with 14-day bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth subcitrate + metronidazole + tetracycline) achieves >85-90% cure rates despite clarithromycin resistance, reducing ulcer recurrence from >60% to <5%. Eradication must be confirmed via urea breath test or stool antigen ≥ 4 weeks post-treatment and ≥ 2 weeks off PPI therapy. NSAID ulcers require PPI therapy and switching to celecoxib or acetaminophen.
patient_plain_language: A peptic ulcer is an open sore on the lining of your stomach or upper intestine, most often caused by a stomach bacterium called H. pylori or frequent use of pain relievers like ibuprofen. When the stomach's protective mucus layer breaks down, stomach acid irritates the tissue.

name: Chronic Hepatitis B Infection
overview: Chronic hepatitis B (persistence of HBsAg > 6 months) causes immune-mediated necroinflammation, progressing to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Treatment indications depend on serum HBV DNA levels, ALT elevations, and stage of liver fibrosis (transient elastography / FibroScan). Nucleos(t)ide analogues with high genetic barrier to resistance (entecavir 0.5 mg daily, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate [TDF] 300 mg daily, or tenofovir alafenamide [TAF] 25 mg daily) suppress viral replication to undetectable levels in >95% of adherent patients, reversing fibrosis and dramatically reducing HCC incidence. HCC surveillance with abdominal ultrasound ± alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) every 6 months is mandatory for all cirrhotic patients, Asian men >40, Asian women >50, and African Americans >20.
patient_plain_language: Chronic hepatitis B is a persistent viral infection in your liver. While many people have zero symptoms for years, the virus can quietly damage liver cells over time. Daily antiviral pills can suppress the virus so low that it stops causing harm and prevents liver scarring.

name: Gastroparesis
overview: Gastroparesis is a chronic neuromuscular gastric disorder characterized by delayed gastric emptying without mechanical mechanical obstruction, most commonly idiopathic (50%) or diabetic (30%). Gold-standard diagnosis requires 4-hour solid-phase gastric emptying scintigraphy (GES) showing > 10% gastric retention at 4 hours or > 60% at 2 hours. Management begins with dietary modifications (small, frequent, low-fat, low-insoluble-fiber meals). In diabetes, strict glycemic control is paramount because acute hyperglycemia (>200 mg/dL) slows gastric peristalsis. Prokinetic therapy includes metoclopramide (FDA-approved, limited to <12 weeks when possible due to tardive dyskinesia risk) or erythromycin; oral dopamine antagonist domperidone is utilized under special programs. Refractory cases may benefit from gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy (G-POEM).
patient_plain_language: Gastroparesis, or 'stomach paralysis', means the stomach muscles take far too long to push food into the intestines, even though there is no physical blockage. Food sits in the stomach for hours, leading to early fullness, nausea, bloating, and vomiting.

name: Achalasia
overview: Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by loss of myenteric plexus inhibitory ganglion cells, causing incomplete lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation and absent peristalsis. Patients present with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, chest pain, and weight loss. High-resolution manometry (HRM) is the gold standard diagnostic tool, categorizing disease via Chicago Classification: Type I (classic), Type II (panesophageal pressurization; >90% treatment response), and Type III (spastic). Diagnosis requires Integrated Relaxation Pressure (IRP > 15 mmHg) and 100% aperistalsis. Definitive therapies disrupt LES smooth muscle: Pneumatic balloon dilation (PD), laparoscopic Heller myotomy (LHM with partial fundoplication), or peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM; European achalasia trial demonstrated >85-90% success rates at 2-5 years, Eckardt score ≤ 3).
patient_plain_language: Achalasia is a condition where the muscular valve at the bottom of your swallowing tube (the esophagus) cannot relax to let food drop into your stomach, and the esophagus loses its ability to squeeze food down. Food and liquids pool in your chest, causing regurgitation.

name: Microscopic Colitis
overview: Microscopic colitis encompasses lymphocytic colitis (≥20 intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 surface epithelial cells) and collagenous colitis (subepithelial collagen band thickness ≥ 10 µm), presenting with chronic, non-bloody, watery diarrhea (often 5-15 bowel movements/day), fecal urgency, nocturnal diarrhea, and fecal incontinence. Macroscopic colonoscopy appearance is typically normal, making systematic mucosal biopsies throughout the ascending, transverse, and descending colon mandatory. First-line medical therapy is oral budesonide (9 mg/day for 6-8 weeks; Cochrane Meta-analysis RR for clinical remission 3.18, 95% CI 2.04-4.97). Discontinuation of potential offending triggers (NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, statins) is recommended. Low-dose budesonide (3-6 mg/day) maintains remission in frequent relapsers.
patient_plain_language: Microscopic colitis is an inflammatory bowel condition where the large intestine looks completely normal to the naked eye during a colonoscopy, but shows inflammation when examined under a microscope. It causes frequent, sudden, watery diarrhea without blood.

name: Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH)
overview: Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic immune-mediated hepatic necroinflammation characterized by hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG), circulating autoantibodies (Type 1: ANA, ASMA; Type 2: anti-LKM1), and interface hepatitis with plasma cell infiltrates on liver biopsy. Untreated, 5-year survival is <50% in severe disease. Standard induction therapy consists of oral prednisone (30-60 mg/day tapered) or budesonide (9 mg/day in non-cirrhotic patients) combined with azathioprine (1-2 mg/kg/day). Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) and NUDT15 genotype/phenotype testing prior to azathioprine initiation prevents life-threatening myelosuppression. Treatment aims for complete biochemical remission (normalization of both serum transaminases and IgG levels), which must be maintained for ≥ 2 years before attempting cautiously supervised withdrawal.
patient_plain_language: Autoimmune hepatitis is a condition where your own immune defense system gets confused and attacks your liver cells as if they were invaders. If untreated, this causes chronic inflammation and scarring, but immunosuppressive medications can put the disease into remission.

name: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)
overview: Primary biliary cholangitis is a chronic autoimmune cholestatic liver disease predominantly affecting women (9:1 ratio), characterized by progressive immune destruction of intrahepatic interlobular bile ducts. Hallmark diagnosis requires ≥2 of 3 criteria: sustained elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP > 1.5x ULN), presence of antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA titer ≥ 1:40, found in >95% of patients), and compatible liver biopsy findings (florid duct lesions). First-line therapy is oral ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA 13-15 mg/kg/day), which delays disease progression, prolongs transplant-free survival, and normalizes life expectancy in complete biochemical responders (Paris II criteria: ALP and AST ≤ 1.5x ULN with normal bilirubin at 1 year). Incomplete responders are escalated to second-line obeticholic acid or PPAR agonists (bezafibrate/elafibranor).
patient_plain_language: Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks and damages the tiny drainage tubes (bile ducts) inside your liver. When bile gets trapped, it leaks into the bloodstream, causing deep itching, fatigue, and eventual liver scarring.

name: Acute Pancreatitis
overview: Diagnosis requires at least 2 of 3 Atlanta criteria: characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back, serum lipase or amylase > 3x the upper limit of normal, and characteristic cross-sectional imaging findings (contrast-enhanced CT or MRI). Gallstones (40-50%) and alcohol (30%) are leading etiologies. Landmark WATERFALL trial (NEJM 2022) demonstrated that aggressive fluid resuscitation significantly increased fluid overload (20.5% vs 6.3%) without improving clinical outcomes compared to moderate resuscitation (Lactated Ringer's 1.5 mL/kg/hr after 10 mL/kg bolus if hypovolemic). Prophylactic antibiotics are strictly not recommended. Early oral refeeding with a low-fat solid or liquid diet as soon as ileus has resolved and pain improves shortens hospital stay and reduces infectious complications.
patient_plain_language: Acute pancreatitis is sudden, severe inflammation of the pancreas gland behind your stomach. Digestive enzymes that the pancreas normally sends to your intestines become prematurely active inside the pancreas itself, irritating and digesting its own delicate tissues.

name: Hemorrhoidal Disease and Anal Fissure
overview: Hemorrhoids are vascular cushions in the anal canal; enlargement and distal displacement result in bleeding, prolapse, and thrombosis. Internal hemorrhoids present with painless bright red rectal bleeding on toilet paper or in bowl; external hemorrhoids cause hygiene issues or acute severe pain when thrombosed. Anal fissures are longitudinal mucosal tears distal to the dentate line causing sharp knife-like pain during defecation and bright rectal streaks. Cochrane meta-analysis confirms dietary fiber supplementation (25-35 g/day) and water intake reduce bleeding by 50%. First-line medical therapy for chronic fissures is topical calcium channel blockers (diltiazem 2% ointment) or topical nitroglycerin 0.4% ointment for 6-8 weeks (heals 65-75% by relaxing internal anal sphincter hypertonicity). Office procedures (rubber band ligation) treat persistent Grade I-III internal hemorrhoids.
patient_plain_language: Hemorrhoids are swollen, inflamed blood vessel cushions in your lower rectum, while an anal fissure is a small crack or tear in the delicate skin of the anus. Hard stools and straining stretch these tissues, causing bright red bleeding and sharp stinging pain with bowel movements.

name: Acute Diverticulitis
overview: Acute diverticulitis represents inflammation and micro-perforation of a colonic diverticulum, predominantly in the sigmoid and descending colon. Contrast-enhanced abdominal pelvic CT is the imaging gold standard (sensitivity/specificity >95%), differentiating uncomplicated (localized colonic wall thickening and pericolic fat stranding) from complicated disease (abscess, macroperforation/peritonitis, fistula, or stricture). Randomized clinical trials (AVOD and DIABOLO) demonstrated that systemic antibiotics do not improve recovery time, complication rates, or recurrence in immunocompetent patients with mild, uncomplicated diverticulitis, supporting conservative outpatient observation without antibiotics. Colonoscopy is recommended 6-8 weeks post-resolution of complicated or first-episode diverticulitis to rule out misdiagnosed colorectal carcinoma (present in 2-4%).
patient_plain_language: Diverticulitis occurs when small pouches in your colon wall become inflamed or irritated. This typically causes sharp aching pain in the lower left side of your belly, mild fever, and nausea.

name: Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO)
overview: SIBO is defined as excessive colonic-type bacterial colonization in the small intestine (≥ 10³ colony-forming units/mL on duodenal aspirate culture), or positive non-invasive breath testing (increase in breath hydrogen ≥ 20 ppm above baseline within 90 minutes or breath methane ≥ 10 ppm at any time [intestinal methanogen overgrowth, IMO] using glucose or lactulose substrate). Patients experience chronic postprandial bloating, flatulence, watery diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and in severe cases, fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption (A, D, E) and B12 deficiency from bacterial deconjugation of bile acids. Rifaximin (550 mg three times daily for 14 days) is the evidence-based first-line non-absorbable antibiotic, producing symptom response in >60-70% of hydrogen-predominant SIBO. Methane-positive IMO requires dual therapy (rifaximin + neomycin or metronidazole).
patient_plain_language: SIBO occurs when bacteria that normally belong in the large intestine migrate backwards and colonize the small intestine in high numbers. When you eat carbohydrates, these bacteria ferment the food prematurely, creating large amounts of hydrogen or methane gas that cause severe bloating, pain, and diarrhea.

name: Barrett's Esophagus
overview: Barrett's esophagus (BE) is the metaplastic replacement of normal squamous esophageal epithelium by specialized columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia), extending ≥ 1 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction, resulting from chronic GERD. BE is the sole established precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Screening with high-definition endoscopy is recommended in men with chronic GERD symptoms (>5 years) and ≥2 risk factors (age >50, Caucasian, central obesity, history of smoking, first-degree relative with BE/cancer). All patients require once-daily PPI maintenance therapy. Endoscopic surveillance follows the Seattle biopsy protocol (4-quadrant biopsies every 2 cm): non-dysplastic BE requires repeat EGD every 3-5 years; confirmed low-grade or high-grade dysplasia warrants endoscopic eradication therapy (radiofrequency ablation [RFA] ± endoscopic mucosal resection [EMR]).
patient_plain_language: Barrett's esophagus happens when years of acid reflux irritate the bottom of your swallowing tube. To protect itself from stomach acid, the lining transforms its delicate cells into tougher, intestinal-type cells. Because these changed cells carry a small risk of turning cancerous over time, doctors monitor them with regular cameras.

name: Clostridioides difficile Infection (CDI)
overview: C. difficile infection is toxin-mediated colitis typically precipitated by broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure (clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins) disrupting colon microbiota. Diagnosis requires ≥ 3 unformed liquid stools in 24 hours plus laboratory confirmation: multi-step testing with NAAT/PCR and toxin EIA or cell cytotoxicity assay. The 2021 IDSA guidelines designate fidaxomicin (200 mg orally twice daily for 10 days) as the preferred first-line agent over oral vancomycin (125 mg orally four times daily for 10 days), demonstrating sustained clinical cure and significantly lower recurrence rates (15% vs 25%, p=0.005). Metronidazole is no longer recommended for non-severe CDI. Recurrent CDI is treated with tapered vancomycin, fidaxomicin, or fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT / live biotherapeutic products, e.g., fecal microbiota spores, live-brpk / Rebyota / Vowst).
patient_plain_language: C. diff is a stubborn bacterial infection of the colon that takes over when strong antibiotics wipe out your bowel's normal 'friendly' bacteria. C. diff bacteria release toxins that cause severe diarrhea, fever, and intestinal inflammation.

name: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
overview: A TIA is defined neurobiologically as a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, without acute tissue infarction on diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI). ABCD2 score (Age ≥60, BP ≥140/90, Clinical features [unilateral weakness, speech impairment], Duration, Diabetes) stratifies 90-day stroke risk. Landmark POINT and CHANCE randomized trials demonstrated that high-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥ 4) or minor stroke requires dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT: aspirin 81 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg daily after loading doses) initiated within 24 hours and continued for 21 days (POINT trial: major ischemic events reduced by 25%, HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.59-0.95; CHANCE trial: HR 0.68), followed by single antiplatelet monotherapy long-term to minimize major bleeding risk.
patient_plain_language: A TIA (transient ischemic attack), sometimes called a 'warning stroke' or 'mini-stroke', occurs when blood flow to a part of your brain is briefly blocked. The symptoms disappear within minutes to hours, but it is a critical warning sign that a major, permanent stroke could happen soon unless treated immediately.

name: Myasthenia Gravis
overview: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder caused by pathogenic autoantibodies directed against acetylcholine receptors (AChR-Ab, 85%), muscle-specific kinase (MuSK), or LRP4, manifesting as fluctuating, fatigable skeletal muscle weakness with diurnal variation (worse in the evening or after exertion). Ptosis and diplopia occur in >85%; bulbar and respiratory involvement produce dysarthria, dysphagia, and dyspnea. First-line symptomatic treatment is oral pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, 30-60 mg every 4-6 hours). Corticosteroids (prednisone) combined with steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil) induce immunosuppression. Landmark MGTX trial (NEJM 2016) proved extended transsternal thymectomy provides long-term clinical benefit in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG under age 65.
patient_plain_language: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune condition where your body's antibodies block communication between your nerves and muscles. This causes muscles to tire out unusually fast with use, leading to drooping eyelids, double vision, and weakness when chewing or lifting your arms.

name: Trigeminal Neuralgia
overview: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by sudden, unilateral, brief, electric shock-like paroxysmal pain limited to the distribution of one or more branches of the fifth cranial nerve (most frequently V2 maxillary and V3 mandibular), triggered by innocuous sensory tactile stimuli (washing, shaving, talking, brushing teeth, light breeze). Classical trigeminal neuralgia is caused by neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root entry zone (most often by the superior cerebellar artery), detectable on high-resolution 3D constructive interference in steady state (CISS/FIESTA) MRI. Carbamazepine (200-1,200 mg/day; Cochrane review NNT=1.7) and oxcarbazepine (600-1,800 mg/day) are the gold-standard first-line pharmacotherapies. Microvascular decompression (MVD / Janetta procedure) provides long-term pain freedom in >70-80% of refractory classical cases.
patient_plain_language: Trigeminal neuralgia, sometimes referred to as 'tic douloureux', is a severe nerve pain disorder caused by an irritated nerve in your face. Simple daily actions like brushing your teeth, chewing, or feeling a gentle breeze against your cheek can trigger excruciating, lightning-bolt shocks across your jaw or cheek.

name: Essential Tremor
overview: Essential tremor is the most common movement disorder, characterized by an 8-12 Hz bilateral action or kinetic tremor prominently affecting the hands and forearms during voluntary movement (drinking from a cup, handwriting, using utensils), with or without head ('no-no' or 'yes-yes') or voice tremor, in the absence of other neurological signs (rigidity, bradykinesia, resting tremor). Family history is present in >50% (autosomal dominant transmission). Level A first-line therapies include propranolol (60-240 mg/day, reducing tremor amplitude by ~50%) and primidone (50-250 mg/day). Topiramate, gabapentin, and atenolol serve as Level B alternatives. For medically refractory disabling tremor, magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) thalamotomy or deep brain stimulation (DBS) targeting the ventral intermediate nucleus (VIM) of the thalamus produces >70% long-term tremor reduction.
patient_plain_language: Essential tremor is a nervous system disorder that causes rhythmic shaking of your hands when you try to use them for everyday tasks like holding a coffee cup, eating soup, or writing. It is an 'action tremor' (worse when moving) rather than a resting tremor.

name: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH)
overview: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus is characterized by the classic clinical triad of gait disturbance ('magnetic', shuffling, wide-based, apraxic gait; typically the earliest and most responsive symptom), cognitive decline (subcortical dementia, psychomotor slowing), and urinary urgency/incontinence ('wobbly, wacky, and wet'). Brain MRI demonstrates ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal enlargement (Evans' index > 0.30) with tight high-convexity sulci and enlarged Sylvian fissures (DESH pattern: disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid-space hydrocephalus). Diagnostic confirmation requires a high-volume lumbar puncture tap test (removal of 30-50 mL CSF) showing quantitative improvement in timed 10-meter walk velocity and step count. Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting provides dramatic and sustained functional improvement in >75% of carefully selected patients (SINPHONI trials).
patient_plain_language: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a treatable brain condition where excess spinal fluid slowly builds up in the fluid cavities (ventricles) of your brain. This extra fluid presses on nearby brain circuits, causing a classic trio of symptoms: a shuffling 'feet stuck to the floor' walk, mild memory confusion, and urinary urgency.

name: Cluster Headache
overview: Cluster headache is the most severe trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, characterized by strictly unilateral, excruciating, piercing, or boring retro-orbital/temporal pain lasting 15-180 minutes, occurring from once every other day up to 8 times daily during cluster periods (often lasting 6-12 weeks). Attacks are accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms (conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, forehead sweating, or miosis/ptosis) and severe motor agitation/restlessness (pacing). First-line acute abortive therapy mandates 100% normobaric oxygen via non-rebreather mask (12-15 L/min for 15-20 min; aborts >75% of attacks within 15 min; Cochrane review) or subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg. First-line preventive therapy is oral verapamil (high-dose: 240-960 mg/day), requiring baseline and serial ECG monitoring for PR prolongation and heart block. Galcanezumab (300 mg SQ monthly) is FDA-approved for episodic cluster prevention.
patient_plain_language: Cluster headaches are excruciating, one-sided headaches centered around or behind one eye that strike in clusters lasting weeks to months. Often nicknamed 'suicide headaches' due to their extreme intensity, they cause the eye to water and turn red, with intense restlessness that makes sitting still impossible.

name: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
overview: ALS is a progressive, fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by simultaneous degeneration of upper motor neurons (corticospinal: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) and lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells: muscle weakness, atrophy, fasciculations) across bulbar, cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral regions. Gold standard diagnosis follows the Awaji/Gold Coast criteria supported by electromyography (EMG). Multidisciplinary specialized care extends survival and improves quality of life. Riluzole (50 mg orally twice daily) extends median tracheostomy-free survival by 2-3 months by modulating glutamatergic neurotransmission. Edaravone (IV/oral free radical scavenger) slows functional decline in early disease. Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (NIV / BiPAP) significantly prolongs survival and slows respiratory decline when initiated once forced vital capacity (FVC) drops below 80% or sniff nasal inspiratory pressure (SNIP) < 40 cmH2O.
patient_plain_language: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a condition where the nerve cells in your brain and spinal cord that control voluntary muscles slowly break down. Over time, muscles become weak and thin, affecting walking, speaking, swallowing, and breathing.

name: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri)
overview: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) predominantly affects women of childbearing age with obesity (BMI > 30), characterized by elevated intracranial pressure (>250 mmH2O on lumbar puncture in adults) in the absence of ventriculomegaly, mass lesion, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Classic symptoms include daily throbbing headaches, transient visual obscurations (dimming of vision lasting seconds with postural changes), pulsatile tinnitus ('whooshing' sound in ears), and horizontal diplopia (cranial nerve VI palsy). The hallmark physical sign is bilateral papilledema, which risks permanent optic atrophy and blindness. The landmark IIHTT trial proved that weight reduction combined with acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, titrated up to 1-4 g/day) significantly improved Humphrey visual field mean deviation, reduced papilledema grade, and improved quality of life compared to placebo.
patient_plain_language: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, or pseudotumor cerebri, occurs when fluid pressure builds up inside your skull without an actual tumor. This high pressure squeezes your optic nerves, leading to daily headaches, a rhythmic whooshing heartbeat sound in your ears, and brief dimming or blurring of vision.

name: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS / Willis-Ekbom Disease)
overview: Diagnostic criteria (IRLSSG) require: (1) an irresistible urge to move the legs usually accompanied by uncomfortable paresthesias, (2) symptoms begin or worsen during periods of rest or inactivity, (3) symptoms are partially or totally relieved by movement (walking, stretching), and (4) symptoms occur exclusively or predominantly in the evening or night. Central nervous system iron deficiency in the substantia nigra impairs dopamine neurotransmission. Serum ferritin should be evaluated; oral iron supplementation is indicated if ferritin < 75 mcg/L or transferrin saturation < 20%, and IV ferric carboxymaltose is superior for refractory iron deficiency. First-line pharmacotherapy has shifted to alpha-2-delta calcium channel ligands (gabapentin enacarbil, pregabalin) over dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) because dopamine agonists cause severe clinical augmentation (earlier symptom onset, increased intensity, spread to arms) in up to 50-70% of long-term users.
patient_plain_language: Restless legs syndrome is a neurological sensory condition that causes an overwhelming, creepy-crawly urge to move your legs when you try to rest, sit still, or fall asleep. Moving or walking provides temporary relief, but the sensations return as soon as you lie down again.

name: Bell's Palsy (Idiopathic Facial Paralysis)
overview: Bell's palsy is an acute, unilateral peripheral lower motor neuron facial nerve (CN VII) paresis or paralysis, causing weakness of both upper and lower facial muscles (inability to furrow forehead, close eye, or smile), peaking within 72 hours, thought to result from HSV-1 reactivation causing nerve edema inside the fallopian canal. It is distinguished from central stroke where forehead movement is preserved due to bilateral cortical innervation. Cochrane systematic reviews and landmark RCTs confirm that oral corticosteroids (prednisone 60-80 mg/day for 7-10 days initiated within 72 hours of symptom onset) significantly increase complete recovery rates from ~70% to >85% (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.05-1.26; NNT=10). Adding antiviral therapy (valacyclovir 1 g TID) provides modest incremental benefit in severe complete paralysis (House-Brackmann grade V-VI). Aggressive corneal protection is paramount to prevent exposure keratitis.
patient_plain_language: Bell's palsy is a sudden, temporary weakness or paralysis of the muscles on one side of your face caused by inflammation of the main facial nerve. Unlike a stroke, Bell's palsy causes your entire half of the face to droop, including your eyebrow and forehead, making it difficult to close your eye or smile.

name: Nephrolithiasis (Kidney Stones)
overview: Nephrolithiasis affects ~10% of individuals, with calcium oxalate (75-80%) and uric acid (10%) being the most prevalent compositions. Acute presentation involves severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with microscopic or gross hematuria. Low-dose non-contrast abdominopelvic CT is the imaging gold standard. Stones < 5 mm have an ~75-80% spontaneous passage rate, while stones ≥ 7-10 mm frequently require urologic intervention (ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy or shock wave lithotripsy). Prevention requires 24-hour urine collection. High fluid intake to achieve > 2.5 L daily urine output halves recurrence risk (Cochrane RR 0.45). Normal dietary calcium (1,000-1,200 mg/day) reduces stone formation by binding dietary oxalate in the gut, whereas calcium restriction paradoxically increases stones. Thiazide diuretics reduce hypercalciuria; potassium citrate alkalinizes urine to dissolve uric acid stones and bind calcium.
patient_plain_language: Kidney stones are hard mineral crystal deposits that form inside your kidneys when your urine becomes overly concentrated. When a stone moves down the narrow drainage tube toward your bladder, it causes intense, cramping back and flank pain, nausea, and blood in your urine.

name: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)
overview: ADPKD is the most common hereditary kidney disorder (1:400 to 1:1,000 live births), caused by germline mutations in PKD1 (80%) or PKD2 (15%), resulting in progressive bilateral fluid-filled renal cyst expansion, destruction of renal parenchyma, and end-stage kidney disease in >50% by age 60. Hypertension develops early and requires aggressive control (target BP < 110/75 mmHg in young patients with preserved eGFR; HALT-PKD trial). Total kidney volume (TKV) measured by MRI and classified via the Mayo Imaging Classification (Classes 1C-1E) stratifies rapid progressors. The selective vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist tolvaptan (TEMPO 3:4 and REPRISE trials) significantly slowed TKV growth and reduced the rate of eGFR decline by ~1.0-1.2 mL/min/1.73m² per year, and is indicated for patients with rapidly progressive disease.
patient_plain_language: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is a genetic condition where thousands of fluid-filled sacs (cysts) slowly grow and multiply inside your kidneys over decades. As the cysts enlarge, your kidneys grow to several times their normal size, crowding out healthy kidney tissue and causing high blood pressure.

name: Nephrotic Syndrome
overview: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria (> 3.5 g/24 hr or spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio [uPCR] > 3.0 g/g), hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin < 3.0 g/dL), generalized peripheral and periorbital edema, and hyperlipidemia. Major primary adult etiologies include membranous nephropathy (anti-PLA2R positive in 70-80%), focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), and minimal change disease (MCD). Renal biopsy provides definitive histological confirmation. MCD responds dramatically to high-dose oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day, achieving remission in >80%). Membranous nephropathy risk stratification dictates therapy: rituximab (CD20-depleting B-cell therapy, MENTOR trial; NEJM 2019) is superior to cyclosporine for inducing sustained complete/partial remission with favorable safety profile. Severe hypoalbuminemia (<2.0-2.5 g/dL) carries high venous thromboembolism risk (DVT/PE/renal vein thrombosis), requiring prophylactic anticoagulation.
patient_plain_language: Nephrotic syndrome is a kidney condition where the tiny filtering units in your kidneys (glomeruli) become damaged and leaky. Instead of keeping essential proteins in your blood, they spill large amounts of protein into your urine, causing your body to retain fluid and swell, particularly around your eyes, ankles, and legs.

name: IgA Nephropathy (Berger's Disease)
overview: IgA nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, caused by galactose-deficient IgA1 deposition in the glomerular mesangium, inducing mesangial proliferation, matrix expansion, and glomerulosclerosis. Classic presentation is episodic synpharyngitic gross hematuria (coca-cola colored urine 24-48 hours after an upper respiratory infection) or asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with persistent proteinuria. Definitive diagnosis requires kidney biopsy scored via the Oxford Classification (MEST-C score). Foundational supportive therapy for all patients with proteinuria > 0.5 g/day mandates maximally tolerated ACE inhibitors or ARBs, combined with SGLT2 inhibitors (DAPA-CKD trial; 71% reduction in kidney failure composite). For persistent proteinuria ≥ 0.75-1.0 g/day despite supportive therapy, targeted-release enteric budesonide (Nefecon 16 mg daily) provides significant eGFR preservation and proteinuria reduction.

This triggers chronic inflammation and scarring, often noticed when your urine turns brown or tea-colored during or right after a throat infection.

name: Overactive Bladder (OAB)
overview: Overactive bladder is a clinical syndrome characterized by urinary urgency (compelling desire to pass urine which is difficult to defer), usually accompanied by frequency (≥8 micturitions/24 hr) and nocturia (≥2 voids/night), with or without urgency urinary incontinence (OAB wet vs OAB dry), in the absence of UTI or other pathology. Initial management focuses on behavioral therapies (bladder training, timed voiding, fluid management, pelvic floor muscle therapy). Second-line therapy consists of oral antimuscarinics (solifenacin, oxybutynin; cautioned in elderly due to anticholinergic cognitive burden and dementia risk) or beta-3 adrenergic agonists (mirabegron 25-50 mg daily, vibegron 75 mg daily; relax detrusor without anticholinergic side effects). Third-line modalities for refractory cases include intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (100 units), sacral neuromodulation (InterStim), or percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS).
patient_plain_language: Overactive bladder is a condition where your bladder muscles squeeze and spasm before your bladder is actually full, creating a sudden, urgent need to run to the bathroom that can be hard to hold back. It often causes frequent daytime trips and waking up multiple times each night.

name: Stress Urinary Incontinence
overview: Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is involuntary leakage of urine upon physical exertion, sneezing, coughing, laughing, or lifting, occurring when intra-abdominal pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure in the setting of pelvic floor muscle laxity or intrinsic sphincter deficiency. First-line therapy is supervised pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT / Kegels; Cochrane systematic review confirms PFMT yields >5-fold higher cure/improvement rates vs control, RR 5.34). Vaginal pessaries or urethral inserts provide non-surgical mechanical urethral support. For patients desiring definitive surgical correction, the synthetic midurethral sling (retropubic or transobturator tape) remains the gold standard procedure with >85-90% subjective cure rates at 5 years. Burch colposuspension or autologous fascial slings serve as non-mesh alternatives.
patient_plain_language: Stress urinary incontinence happens when the muscles and tissues supporting your bladder and urethra weaken. Sudden physical pressure on your abdomen—such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, jumping, or exercising—causes accidental urine leakage.

name: Interstitial Cystitis (Bladder Pain Syndrome)
overview: Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is defined as an unpleasant sensation (pain, pressure, discomfort) perceived to be related to the urinary bladder, associated with lower urinary tract symptoms of more than 6 weeks duration, in the absence of infection or other identifiable causes. Pain typically intensifies as the bladder fills and temporarily relieves following voiding. Cystoscopy may reveal glomerulations (petechial hemorrhages on hydrodistention) or Hunner lesions (circumscribed reddish mucosal lesions with radiating vessels; present in 10-15%). Stepwise management: Step 1 involves patient education, fluid regulation, and elimination of dietary triggers (caffeine, citrus, alcohol, artificial sweeteners). Step 2 incorporates specialized pelvic floor physical therapy (targeting muscle spasms and trigger points; strictly avoiding strengthening Kegels) and oral medications (amitriptyline 25-75 mg, cimetidine, hydroxyzine, or pentosan polysulfate sodium). Hunner lesions respond to endoscopic fulguration.
patient_plain_language: Interstitial cystitis, or bladder pain syndrome, is a chronic inflammatory condition where you feel aching, pressure, or burning pain in your bladder that worsens as your bladder fills with urine. People often feel the urge to urinate dozens of times a day to relieve the aching pressure.

name: Chronic Prostatitis / Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome (CP/CPPS)
alternative_names: Chronic Prostatitis / Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome (CP/CPPS)
overview: NIH Category III chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS) is characterized by chronic pelvic, perineal, scrotal, penile, or suprapubic pain persisting for at least 3 months within the previous 6 months, in the absence of uropathogenic bacteria on standard cultures. It is frequently accompanied by painful ejaculation, voiding dysfunction, and severe negative cognitive and emotional impact. Management utilizes the multi-modal UPOINT clinical phenotyping system (Urinary, Psychosocial, Organ-specific, Infection, Neurological/systemic, Tenderness of muscles), directing tailored therapy rather than empiric repeated antibiotic courses: alpha-blockers (tamsulosin 0.4 mg) for urinary obstruction; anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs); neuromodulating medications (pregabalin, duloxetine); specialized myofascial pelvic floor physical therapy for pelvic floor hypertonicity; and cognitive-behavioral therapy.
patient_plain_language: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men causes ongoing aching pain, pressure, or discomfort in the pelvic floor, groin, or testicles, often made worse by sitting or after ejaculation. It is usually not an active bacterial infection, but rather a combination of tense pelvic floor muscles and irritated pelvic nerves.

name: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) with LUTS
overview: Benign prostatic hyperplasia involves non-malignant adenomatous stromal and epithelial proliferation of the prostate transition zone, causing bladder outlet obstruction and lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS: weak stream, hesitancy, intermittency, straining, post-void dribbling, frequency, nocturia). patient_plain_language: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is an age-related, non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland in men. name: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
overview: KDIGO diagnostic criteria define AKI by any of: increase in serum creatinine by ≥ 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours; increase in serum creatinine to ≥ 1.5 times baseline within 7 days; or urine volume < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Etiologies are categorized into prerenal (hypovolemia, heart failure, sepsis, NSAIDs/ACEi causing decreased renal perfusion; fractional excretion of sodium FeNa < 1%, BUN:creatinine ratio > 20:1); intrinsic renal (acute tubular necrosis [ATN] from ischemia or nephrotoxins, acute interstitial nephritis [AIN], glomerulonephritis; FeNa > 2%, muddy brown granular casts); and postrenal obstructive (nephrolithiasis, BPH, neurogenic bladder; hydronephrosis on renal ultrasound). Core management mandates prompt hemodynamic resuscitation with balanced crystalloids (SMART trial; NEJM 2018), discontinuation of all nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV iodinated contrast), relief of obstruction, and dose-adjustment of all renally cleared drugs.
patient_plain_language: Acute kidney injury is a sudden, sharp decline in kidney function that occurs over hours or days. When the kidneys suddenly struggle to filter the blood—often due to severe dehydration, an infection, or certain medications—waste products and excess fluids rapidly build up in the body.

name: Ankylosing Spondylitis (Axial Spondyloarthritis)
overview: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is a chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease predominantly affecting the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints, strongly associated with HLA-B27 (>85%). It presents as chronic inflammatory back pain (onset <45 years, insidious onset, improvement with exercise but not with rest, morning stiffness >30 minutes, waking during the second half of the night). Sacroiliitis on MRI (active bone marrow edema) or pelvic radiographs (modified New York criteria) confirms diagnosis. First-line pharmacotherapy is continuous treatment with full-dose NSAIDs (naproxen, celecoxib). For patients with persistently high disease activity (ASDAS ≥ 2.1) despite ≥ 2 NSAIDs, biological DMARDs targeting TNF (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) or IL-17A (secukinumab, ixekizumab), or JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, tofacitinib) provide significant symptom relief, suppress spinal inflammation, and improve function.
patient_plain_language: Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic autoimmune form of arthritis that targets your spine and pelvic joints. Unlike ordinary mechanical back pain, the stiffness and ache feel worse after resting or sleeping and actually improve when you get up and move around. Over years, it can cause the spinal bones to fuse together.

name: Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA)
overview: Psoriatic arthritis affects ~20-30% of patients with cutaneous psoriasis, presenting across six clinical domains: peripheral arthritis (often asymmetric, involving DIP joints), enthesitis (inflammation at tendon insertions, e.g., Achilles, plantar fascia), dactylitis ('sausage digits'), axial disease, skin psoriasis, and nail dystrophy (pitting, onycholysis; strongly correlates with DIP arthritis). CASPAR criteria require inflammatory articular disease plus ≥ 3 points from personal/family psoriasis, nail dystrophy, negative RF, current/past dactylitis, and juxta-articular new bone formation. Conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate 15-25 mg/week) treat peripheral arthritis. GRAPPA guidelines recommend targeted biologics—TNF inhibitors, IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab), IL-23 inhibitors (guselkumab, risankizumab), or JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib)—to inhibit structural joint damage and clear skin lesions simultaneously.
patient_plain_language: Psoriatic arthritis is an autoimmune condition where your immune system attacks both your skin and your joints. Beyond red, scaly skin patches, it can cause swollen fingers or toes that look like little sausages, painful heels where tendons attach to bone, and stiff, aching joints.

name: Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma)
overview: Systemic sclerosis is a complex autoimmune disease characterized by microvascular obliteration, immune dysregulation, and progressive widespread fibrosis of skin and internal organs. Divided into limited cutaneous (lcSSc: CREST syndrome; anti-centromere positive in 60-80%) and diffuse cutaneous (dcSSc: anti-Scl-70/topoisomerase I or anti-RNA polymerase III positive; rapid proximal skin thickening and early visceral organ failure). Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) presents with acute malignant hypertension and oliguric renal failure, strongly linked to anti-RNA polymerase III and high-dose corticosteroid use (>15 mg/day prednisone is contraindicated); immediate ACE inhibitor therapy (captopril) is lifesaving. Interstitial lung disease (SSc-ILD) is the leading cause of death; mycophenolate mofetil (SLS II trial; Lancet Respir Med 2016) and nintedanib (SENSCIS trial; NEJM 2019) preserve FVC and slow lung fibrosis.
patient_plain_language: Systemic sclerosis, or scleroderma, is a rare autoimmune disorder where the body produces too much collagen protein, causing the skin to become tight, thick, and firm. In addition to fingers turning white and painful in the cold (Raynaud's), it can cause acid reflux and stiffen lung tissues.

name: Sjögren's Syndrome
overview: Sjögren's syndrome is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands, predominantly the lacrimal and salivary glands, resulting in severe keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) and xerostomia (dry mouth). ACR-EULAR criteria require a score ≥ 4 based on: labial salivary gland biopsy with focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (focus score ≥ 1/4 mm²), positive anti-SSA/Ro antibodies, ocular staining score ≥ 5, Schirmer's test ≤ 5 mm/5 min, and unstimulated whole saliva flow rate ≤ 0.1 mL/min. Symptomatic secretagogue therapy (pilocarpine 5 mg QID or cevimeline 30 mg TID) stimulates M3 muscarinic receptors to increase saliva and tear secretion. Topical ophthalmic cyclosporine (0.05%) or lifitegrast (5%) treats ocular surface inflammation. Hydroxychloroquine (200-400 mg/day) reduces inflammatory arthralgias and systemic fatigue. Patients have a ~15-20 fold increased lifetime risk of non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma (predominantly MALT lymphoma).
patient_plain_language: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune condition where your immune system attacks your body's moisture-producing glands. The primary symptoms are severely dry, gritty eyes and a dry mouth that makes chewing dry crackers, speaking for long periods, or swallowing difficult.

name: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR)
overview: Polymyalgia rheumatica is an inflammatory disorder occurring almost exclusively in individuals > 50 years (mean age 73), presenting with sudden-onset, severe bilateral aching and morning stiffness (>45 minutes) in the shoulder girdle, pelvic girdle, and neck, accompanied by elevated inflammatory markers (ESR > 40 mm/hr, CRP > 10 mg/L). Musculoskeletal ultrasound characteristically demonstrates bilateral subacromial/subdeltoid bursitis, trochanteric bursitis, or biceps tenosynovitis. Hallmark diagnostic feature is a rapid, dramatic clinical response (>70% improvement within 48-72 hours) to moderate-dose oral corticosteroids (prednisone 12.5-25 mg/day). Tapering is performed slowly over 12-24 months. For frequent relapsers or high steroid-toxicity risk, the IL-6 receptor antagonist sarilumab is FDA-approved (SAPHYR trial; NEJM 2023: 28% sustained remission on sarilumab vs 10% on placebo, p=0.02). Approximately 15-20% of PMR patients develop concurrent Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA).
patient_plain_language: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory condition affecting older adults that causes severe stiffness and aching across both shoulders, hips, thighs, and neck, particularly upon waking in the morning. Getting out of bed or lifting your arms to put on a jacket can feel almost impossible, but it responds quickly to low-dose steroid medication.

name: Dermatomyositis / Polymyositis
overview: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are characterized by symmetric, progressive proximal skeletal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, lifting objects overhead) and markedly elevated serum creatine kinase (CK, often 5-50x ULN). Dermatomyositis features pathognomonic cutaneous signs: heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital erythema and edema) and Gottron's papules (scaly violaceous plaques over MCP and PIP joints), plus shawl sign, V-sign, and mechanic's hands (anti-synthetase syndrome). Myositis-specific antibodies (anti-Mi-2, anti-Jo-1, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-NXP2, anti-MDA5) define clinical phenotypes and cancer risk. Anti-TIF1-gamma and anti-NXP2 carry high risk of age-associated underlying malignancy (ovarian, breast, lung, GI), mandating comprehensive cancer screening. First-line therapy is high-dose oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day) plus steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (methotrexate, azathioprine). The landmark ProDERM phase 3 trial established IVIG (2 g/kg monthly) as safe and significantly superior to placebo (79% response vs 44%, p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune condition where your immune system causes inflammation in both your muscles and skin. It causes progressive muscle weakness in your thighs and shoulders—making it hard to stand up from a low chair or brush your hair—along with distinct purple-red rashes over your eyelids and knuckles.

name: Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy and Tears
overview: Rotator cuff disorders encompass tendinopathy, partial-thickness tears, and full-thickness tears primarily involving the supraspinatus tendon. Patients present with anterolateral shoulder pain exacerbated by overhead activity, pain radiating to the deltoid insertion, and nocturnal pain when lying on the affected side. Physical exam reveals painful arc (60-120 degrees), positive Hawkins-Kennedy/Neer impingement signs, and weakness on empty-can (Jobe's) or external rotation tests. MRI of the shoulder is the imaging gold standard. Cochrane reviews and randomized clinical trials confirm that structured, supervised physical therapy focusing on rotator cuff strengthening and scapular stabilizing exercises is as effective as surgical acromioplasty or repair for non-traumatic, degenerative rotator cuff tears at 1, 2, and 5-year follow-up. Acute full-thickness traumatic tears in young, active patients benefit from prompt surgical repair within 3 months to prevent muscle retraction and fatty infiltration.
patient_plain_language: The rotator cuff is a team of four muscles and tendons that keep your shoulder ball centered in its socket. Wear-and-tear or injury can fray or tear these tendons, causing aching pain on the outside of your shoulder, especially when reaching up overhead or trying to sleep on that side.

name: Plantar Fasciitis
overview: Plantar fasciitis is a degenerative non-inflammatory fasciosis of the thick plantar aponeurosis origin at the medial calcaneal tuberosity. Pathognomonic clinical presentation is sharp, stabbing heel pain with the first steps in the morning upon getting out of bed, or after prolonged periods of sitting (post-static dyskinesia), which temporarily eases after walking a few minutes, but worsens by the end of the day. Risk factors include obesity (BMI > 30), limited ankle dorsiflexion (<0 degrees), pes planus or pes cavus, and prolonged occupational weight-bearing. Evidence-based first-line conservative management resolves >90% of cases within 6-12 months: plantar fascia-specific stretching exercises, gastrocnemius/soleus calf stretching, prefabricated or custom arch orthoses (NNT=5), night splints maintaining neutral dorsiflexion, and cushioned supportive footwear. Corticosteroid injections provide short-term relief (<4-6 weeks) but carry risks of plantar fascia rupture and calcaneal fat pad atrophy.
patient_plain_language: Plantar fasciitis is an irritation and thickening of the strong, shock-absorbing band of tissue that supports the arch of your foot. It causes sharp, stabbing heel pain during your very first morning steps out of bed, which feels like stepping on a nail before it gradually loosens up.

name: Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder)
overview: Adhesive capsulitis is characterized by progressive, painful loss of both active and passive glenohumeral range of motion in all planes, predominantly external rotation (>50% reduction or <30 degrees) and abduction, caused by capsular contracture and synovial inflammation. Strongly associated with diabetes mellitus (prevalence up to 20%), thyroid disorders, and periods of prolonged shoulder immobilization. Follows a three-phase continuum: Freezing (painful stage, 2-9 months), Frozen (stiff stage, 4-12 months), and Thawing (recovery stage, 12-42 months). Cochrane systematic reviews and randomized trials demonstrate that an early intra-articular glenohumeral corticosteroid injection (e.g., triamcinolone 40 mg with ultrasound guidance) combined with gentle, pain-free stretching physical therapy significantly accelerates pain relief and functional motion recovery compared to physical therapy alone (standardized mean difference -0.65). Aggressive forceful manipulation is contraindicated in the inflammatory freezing stage.

name: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis
overview: Lumbar spinal stenosis involves narrowing of the central spinal canal, lateral recess, or neural foramina by degenerative bone and soft tissue changes (facet arthropathy, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, disc bulging). Pathognomonic symptom is neurogenic claudication: bilateral or unilateral aching, heaviness, weakness, cramping, or numbness in the buttocks, thighs, or calves brought on by walking or prolonged standing, and characteristically relieved by sitting or lumbar flexion ('shopping cart sign'—forward leaning increases spinal canal cross-sectional area by up to 20%). It is distinguished from vascular claudication, which is provoked by bicycling (flexed posture) and relieved simply by standing still. Lumbosacral spine MRI confirms anatomical stenosis. Conservative management includes flexion-based physical therapy, NSAIDs, and epidural steroid injections. The landmark SPORT trial demonstrated that surgical decompression (laminectomy) produces significant and sustained improvement in pain and function in symptomatic patients failing conservative therapy.
patient_plain_language: Lumbar spinal stenosis is an age-related narrowing of the bone canal in your lower back that houses your nerves. Standing or walking upright pinches these nerves, causing aching heaviness, cramping, and fatigue in your legs and buttocks that goes away when you sit down or lean forward over a grocery cart.

name: Herpes Zoster (Shingles)
overview: Herpes zoster results from reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia. Classic presentation involves prodromal dermatomal pain, burning, or allodynia followed by a unilateral, dermatomal eruption of grouped, painful, erythematous maculopapules that rapidly evolve into clear vesicles. Antiviral therapy (valacyclovir 1,000 mg TID or famciclovir 500 mg TID for 7 days) initiated within 72 hours of rash onset accelerates lesion healing, reduces acute viral shedding, and decreases the severity and duration of postherpetic neuralgia (PHN: pain persisting > 90 days after rash onset). Landmark ZOE-50 and ZOE-70 randomized trials established that the 2-dose recombinant adjuvanted zoster vaccine (Shingrix) provides >97% protective efficacy against shingles and >91% protection against PHN in adults ≥ 50 years, with sustained immunity > 10 years. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (involving CN V1) risks permanent corneal blindness.
patient_plain_language: Shingles is a painful blistering rash caused by the chickenpox virus waking up after sleeping quietly in your nerve roots for decades. It typically forms a sensitive band of red blisters on just one side of your chest, back, or face, accompanied by burning nerve pain.

name: Infectious Mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr Virus)
overview: Infectious mononucleosis is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV / HHV-4), transmitted via infected saliva ('kissing disease'), peaking in adolescents and young adults aged 15-24 years. Classic clinical triad: fever, exudative pharyngitis, and prominent symmetric posterior cervical and generalized lymphadenopathy, frequently accompanied by marked fatigue, palatal petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, and transient periorbital edema (Hoagland sign). Laboratory confirmation relies on heterophile antibody testing (Monospot test; sensitivity ~85%, can be false-negative in first week) and peripheral blood smear showing lymphocytosis (>50%) with >10% atypical activated CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes. EBV-specific serologies (viral capsid antigen [VCA] IgM/IgG, EBNA) confirm atypical cases. Administration of aminopenicillins (amoxicillin, ampicillin) induces a characteristic pruritic maculopapular rash in >90% of patients. Splenic rupture occurs in 0.1-0.5% (typically between days 4 and 21 of illness).
patient_plain_language: Infectious mononucleosis ('mono') is a viral infection caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, spread through saliva. It causes severe sore throat with swollen neck glands, fever, and extreme fatigue that can last for weeks, along with temporary enlargement of your spleen.
