name: Influenza Infection (Flu)
overview: Influenza is an acute respiratory infection caused by influenza A and B orthomyxoviruses, presenting abruptly with high fever (38-40°C), rigors, myalgias, prominent headache, dry cough, sore throat, and profound prostration. Rapid molecular assays (RT-PCR) are the preferred diagnostic test with high sensitivity/specificity (>95%). Neuraminidase inhibitors (oral oseltamivir 75 mg BID for 5 days) or the cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor baloxavir marboxil (single oral dose) shorten symptom duration by ~1-1.5 days and reduce lower respiratory tract complications, otitis media, and hospitalizations when initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset. In hospitalized, severely ill, or high-risk patients (age ≥65, children <2, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, immunosuppressed, pregnant/postpartum), antiviral therapy is recommended as early as possible, regardless of duration of illness.
patient_plain_language: Influenza, or the flu, is a highly contagious viral lung infection that strikes suddenly like a freight train, knocking you off your feet with a high fever, shaking chills, severe body aches, headache, and intense fatigue.

name: Malaria (Plasmodium falciparum / vivax)
overview: Malaria is a mosquito-borne protozoan infection caused by Plasmodium species (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi), transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Classic presentation features paroxysmal fevers, rigors, diaphoresis, headache, hemolytic anemia, and splenomegaly. Gold standard diagnosis requires microscopic examination of Giemsa-stained thick (sensitivity) and thin (species identification and parasitemia quantification) blood smears, repeated every 12-24 hours if initially negative. Uncomplicated P. falciparum is treated with Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT: oral artemether-lumefantrine [Coartem] or atovaquone-proguanil [Malarone]). Severe malaria (parasitemia > 5%, cerebral malaria, severe anemia, acute kidney injury, ARDS, lactic acidosis) requires immediate IV artesunate (2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, and 24 hours), which reduced mortality by 35% in Asia (SEAQUAMAT) and 22% in Africa (AQUAMAT) compared to IV quinine. P. vivax and P. ovale require primaquine or tafenoquine to eradicate dormant liver hypnozoites, mandatory after G6PD deficiency screening.
patient_plain_language: Malaria is a serious, mosquito-transmitted blood infection caused by microscopic parasites that multiply inside your liver and then burst out into your red blood cells. It causes intense cycling waves of shaking chills followed by high, burning fevers and drenching sweats.

research_papers.key_findings: Malaria is a mosquito-borne protozoan infection caused by Plasmodium species (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi), transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Classic presentation features paroxysmal fevers, rigors, diaphoresis, headache, hemolytic anemia, and splenomegaly. Gold standard diagnosis requires microscopic examination of Giemsa-stained thick (sensitivity) and thin (species identification and parasitemia quantification) blood smears, repeated every 12-24 hours if initially negative. Uncomplicated P. falciparum is treated with Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT: oral artemether-lumefantrine [Coartem] or atovaquone-proguanil [Malarone]). Severe malaria (parasitemia > 5%, cerebral malaria, severe anemia, acute kidney injury, ARDS, lactic acidosis) requires immediate IV artesunate (2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, and 24 hours), which reduced mortality by 35% in Asia (SEAQUAMAT) and 22% in Africa (AQUAMAT) compared to IV quinine. P. vivax and P. ovale require primaquine or tafenoquine to eradicate dormant liver hypnozoites, mandatory after G6PD deficiency screening.

name: Dengue Fever
overview: Dengue is an arboviral infection caused by 4 distinct serotypes (DENV-1 to 4) transmitted by diurnal Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Classic 'breakbone fever' features sudden high fever (up to 40°C), severe retro-orbital headache, diffuse arthralgias/myalgias, and a transient macular rash. Diagnosis is confirmed by serum NS1 antigen or RT-PCR within days 1-5, or IgM serology after day 5. The disease progresses through 3 phases: Febrile (days 1-3), Critical (days 3-7, coinciding with defervescence when capillary permeability peaks), and Recovery. Severe dengue (dengue hemorrhagic fever / dengue shock syndrome) is characterized by severe plasma leakage (defined by hematocrit increase ≥ 20% alongside acute thrombocytopenia < 100,000 cells/µL, or narrow pulse pressure ≤ 20 mmHg), severe bleeding, or severe organ impairment. Management during the critical phase hinges on meticulous, protocolized isotonic IV fluid titration to match microvascular leakage without precipitating pulmonary edema. NSAIDs and aspirin are strictly contraindicated due to antiplatelet effects and bleeding risk.
patient_plain_language: Dengue fever, known as 'breakbone fever' due to the intense pain in your muscles and joints, is a mosquito-spread tropical virus. The most critical window happens right as the high fever breaks (days 3 to 7), when blood vessels can suddenly become leaky.

name: Community-Acquired MRSA Skin Infection
overview: Community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA) typically presents as a painful, erythematous, fluctuant skin abscess, furuncle, carbuncle, or purulent cellulitis, often carrying the Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL) cytotoxin gene. Landmark randomized trials establish that incision and drainage (I&D) is the primary and essential definitive therapy for cutaneous abscesses. The landmark DAWN trial proved that adding oral antibiotic therapy (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole [TMP-SMX 1-2 DS tablets BID] or clindamycin [300-450 mg TID] for 7-10 days) significantly increased cure rates (82-83% vs 69% placebo, p<0.001) and reduced recurrence rates in drainable abscesses. Oral doxycycline (100 mg BID) is an alternative. For recurrent CA-MRSA furunculosis, a 5-day decolonization protocol (intranasal mupirocin 2% ointment BID plus chlorhexidine 4% body washes daily) significantly reduces reinfection and household transmission.
patient_plain_language: A MRSA skin abscess is a bacterial infection of the skin that forms a tender, pus-filled boil, often mistaken for a spider bite. Because MRSA is resistant to ordinary penicillins, the boil must be cleanly drained by a clinician and treated with targeted antibiotics.

name: Giardiasis
overview: Giardiasis is an intestinal protozoan infection caused by Giardia duodenalis (lamblia/intestinalis), acquired via ingestion of fecally contaminated water (backcountry hikers drinking wilderness stream water, municipal water supplies, swimming pools) or food. Ingested cysts excyst in the duodenum into flagellated trophozoites that attach to the enterocyte brush border with a ventral sucking disk, causing blunting of microvilli and malabsorption. Incubation period is 1-2 weeks, presenting with foul-smelling, watery, greasy stools that float (steatorrhea), sulfurous burping/eructations, abdominal cramping, flatulence, and significant weight loss, characteristically without fever or blood/fecal leukocytes. Diagnosis is established via stool stool antigen enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or stool multiplex PCR (sensitivity >95%). First-line therapy is tinidazole (single oral dose of 2 g; cure rate >90-95%) or nitazoxanide (500 mg BID for 3 days), which have superseded 5-7 day metronidazole due to superior tolerability and single-dose compliance.
patient_plain_language: Giardiasis, sometimes called 'beaver fever', is a microscopic parasite infection in your intestines picked up by drinking untreated wilderness stream water or unpurified water. It causes foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea that floats, lots of gas, and characteristic 'rotten egg' burps.

name: Streptococcal Pharyngitis (Strep Throat)
overview: Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes, GAS) accounts for 20-30% of acute pharyngitis in children and 5-15% in adults. Clinical features are scored via Modified Centor / McIsaac criteria (tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fever > 38°C, absence of cough, age-based points). Patients meeting ≥ 2-3 points should undergo Rapid Antigen Detection Testing (RADT) or throat throat molecular NAAT; negative RADT in children/adolescents mandates backup throat culture. Antimicrobial therapy is indicated only for confirmed GAS to prevent acute rheumatic fever, reduce symptom duration by ~1-2 days, and prevent suppurative complications (peritonsillar abscess). Penicillin V (500 mg orally BID/TID for 10 days) or amoxicillin (50 mg/kg once daily, max 1,000 mg for 10 days) remains first-line, as GAS remains 100% susceptible to beta-lactams globally. Cephalosporins, clindamycin, or azithromycin serve as penicillin-allergic options.
patient_plain_language: Strep throat is a contagious bacterial throat infection caused by Group A Streptococcus bacteria. It typically causes sudden severe throat pain when swallowing, swollen red tonsils with white patches of pus, and fever, noticeably without cold symptoms like a runny nose or cough.

name: Lyme Disease (Borrelia burgdorferi)
overview: Lyme disease is a tick-borne spirochetal infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto (in North America), transmitted by Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes pacificus blacklegged ticks attached for ≥ 36-48 hours. Stage 1 (Early localized): Erythema migrans (EM) rash (expanding annular erythematous patch ≥ 5 cm, often with central clearing / 'bull's-eye') appears 7-14 days post-bite. Diagnosis of EM in an endemic area is purely clinical; serology is insensitive (<40%) in early localized disease and should not be ordered. Stage 2 (Early disseminated): Multiple EM lesions, cranial neuropathy (unilateral or bilateral Bell's palsy), lymphocytic meningitis, or Lyme carditis (AV heart block). Stage 3 (Late): Asymmetric, migratory mono/oligoarthritis (prominently knee). Standard two-tier serologic testing (EIA screen followed by Western blot or second EIA) confirms disseminated/late disease. Oral doxycycline (100 mg BID for 10-14 days) is first-line; amoxicillin (500 mg TID for 14 days) or cefuroxime are alternatives.
patient_plain_language: Lyme disease is a bacterial infection spread by the bite of an infected blacklegged deer tick. The classic first sign is an expanding red rash that often resembles a target or 'bull's-eye', accompanied by flu-like fatigue, headaches, fever, and achy joints.

name: Sepsis and Septic Shock
overview: Sepsis-3 consensus defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, clinically quantified by an acute increase in SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score ≥ 2 points. Septic shock is a subset characterized by profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities, defined by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg and serum lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation, carrying mortality > 40%. The 1-Hour Sepsis Bundle mandates: (1) measure serum lactate level (remeasure if initial > 2 mmol/L), (2) obtain blood cultures prior to antibiotics, (3) administer broad-spectrum IV antimicrobials within 1 hour, (4) rapidly infuse 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloids (e.g., Plasmalyte or Lactated Ringer's) for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L, and (5) initiate norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor if MAP remains < 65 mmHg during or after fluid loading.
patient_plain_language: Sepsis is a medical emergency that happens when your body's immune system has an extreme, overwhelming response to an infection. Instead of just fighting the germs, the immune system triggers widespread inflammation that can drop your blood pressure dangerously low and damage vital organs.

red_flags: Systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg, mottled cold extremities, confusion or inability to stay awake, breathing rate > 25 breaths/min, or no urine output

name: Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA)
overview: Iron deficiency anemia is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide, defined by microcytic hypochromic red cell indices (MCV < 80 fL) with low body iron stores: serum ferritin < 30-45 ng/mL (in non-inflammatory states; ferritin < 100 ng/mL in inflammatory states) or transferrin saturation (TSAT) < 20%. In adult men and postmenopausal women, IDA is GI tract blood loss until proven otherwise; bidirectional endoscopy (EGD and colonoscopy) is strongly recommended by AGA guidelines to rule out occult gastrointestinal malignancy (detected in 10-15%). Oral iron supplementation (oral ferrous sulfate 65 mg elemental iron on alternate days) optimizes fractional iron absorption by limiting hepcidin surges. Intravenous iron formulations (ferric carboxymaltose, ferumoxytol, iron sucrose) are indicated for oral intolerance, malabsorption (celiac, IBD, bariatric surgery), third-trimester pregnancy, or heavy ongoing bleeding.
patient_plain_language: Iron deficiency anemia occurs when your body does not have enough iron mineral to build hemoglobin, the iron-rich protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen to your muscles and brain. Without enough iron, you feel exhausted, look pale, become short of breath with stairs, and may crave chewing ice.

name: Vitamin B12 Deficiency (Pernicious / Megaloblastic Anemia)
overview: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency causes megaloblastic macrocytic anemia (MCV often > 100-110 fL) with hypersegmented neutrophils, and irreversible neuropsychiatric pathology (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord: bilateral peripheral neuropathy, loss of vibratory and position sense, spastic ataxia, and cognitive decline). Etiologies include autoimmune pernicious anemia (destruction of gastric parietal cells; anti-intrinsic factor antibodies), malabsorption (terminal ileal disease, Crohn's, bariatric resection), prolonged metformin or PPI use, and strict veganism. Serum B12 < 200 pg/mL confirms deficiency; borderline levels (200-350 pg/mL) require metabolic confirmation via elevated serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) and homocysteine (distinguishing B12 from folate deficiency, where MMA remains normal). Cochrane review shows oral high-dose cyanocobalamin (1,000-2,000 mcg daily) is as effective as intramuscular injections (1,000 mcg weekly then monthly) for hematologic recovery, though IM is preferred for severe neurologic impairment.
patient_plain_language: Vitamin B12 deficiency is a shortage of a vital nutrient needed to produce healthy red blood cells and maintain the protective coating (myelin) around your nerves. Low B12 causes anemia as well as numbness, pins-and-needles tingling in your feet, clumsiness, and memory fog.

name: Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)
overview: Primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an acquired autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia (platelet count < 100 x 10⁹/L) caused by autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction (anti-GPIIb/IIIa) and impaired megakaryocyte thrombopoiesis, in the absence of other cytopenias or underlying disorders. Presentation ranges from asymptomatic bruising/petechiae to mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia) and catastrophic intracranial hemorrhage (1-2%). First-line therapy for platelets < 20-30 x 10⁹/L or active bleeding consists of oral corticosteroids: high-dose dexamethasone (40 mg daily for 4 days; achieves faster initial responses and higher sustained remission rates than prednisone) or prednisone (1 mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks tapered). IVIG (1 g/kg single dose) rapidly raises platelets within 24-48 hours during emergency bleeding. Second-line therapies for persistent/chronic ITP include Thrombopoietin Receptor Agonists (TPO-RAs: romiplostim, eltrombopag, avatrombopag; sustained response >70-80%), rituximab, or laparoscopic splenectomy.
patient_plain_language: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is a condition where your immune system mistakenly creates antibodies that tag your blood-clotting cells (platelets) for removal in your spleen. With fewer platelets in your blood, you bruise very easily, develop tiny red pinpoint rash dots (petechiae), and bleed longer from small cuts.

name: Multiple Myeloma
overview: Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma cell malignancy characterized by bone marrow plasmacytosis (≥10%) and the presence of CRAB criteria (Hypercalcemia > 11 mg/dL, Renal insufficiency [creatinine > 2 mg/dL or CrCl < 40], Anemia [Hb < 10 g/dL], Bone lytic lesions) or myeloma-defining biomarkers (SLiM: ≥60% clonal marrow plasma cells, serum involved/uninvolved free light chain ratio ≥ 100, >1 focal MRI bone lesion). Workup requires serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (SPEP/UPEP/IFE), serum free light chains (sFLC), and whole-body low-dose CT or PET-CT. Triplet and quadruplet induction regimens incorporating the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab, proteasome inhibitor bortezomib, immunomodulatory drug lenalidomide, and dexamethasone (Dara-VRd or Dara-Rd) produce deep responses and unprecedented progression-free survival (MAIA and GRIFFIN trials). Autologous stem cell transplant (ASCT) remains standard for eligible patients, followed by lenalidomide maintenance.
patient_plain_language: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of the plasma cells, which are the white blood cells that make antibodies. When abnormal plasma cells multiply uncontrollably inside your bone marrow, they crowd out healthy blood cells, dissolve weak holes in bones, and produce abnormal proteins that can damage your kidneys.

name: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)
overview: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is the most prevalent adult leukemia in Western countries, defined by persistent clonal B-cell lymphocytosis in peripheral blood (≥ 5 x 10⁹/L) co-expressing CD5, CD19, CD20 (dim), and CD23 on flow cytometry. Staged via Rai (0 to IV) or Binet (A to C) systems. Asymptomatic early-stage disease (Rai 0, Binet A) managed with active surveillance ('watch and wait'), as randomized trials showed early chemotherapy does not improve overall survival. Treatment indications (iwCLL criteria): constitutional 'B' symptoms, progressive bone marrow failure, massive splenomegaly, or lymphocyte doubling time < 6 months. Targeted front-line oral therapies targeting Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK inhibitors: acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib) or BCL-2 (venetoclax combined with anti-CD20 antibody obinutuzumab) have completely displaced traditional chemoimmunotherapy (FCR), achieving superior progression-free survival even in high-risk TP53-mutated or del(17p) disease.
patient_plain_language: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a slow-growing cancer of the blood and bone marrow involving white blood cells called B-lymphocytes. In its early stages, it often causes no symptoms and is found on routine blood tests; many people live normal active lives for years under careful monitoring without ever needing chemotherapy.

name: Polycythemia Vera (PV)
overview: Polycythemia vera is a Philadelphia-chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by autonomous erythrocytosis, driving hyperviscosity and major thrombotic complications (arterial and venous, including Budd-Chiari and portal vein thrombosis). >98% of patients harbor the activating JAK2 V617F or exon 12 driver mutation. Diagnostic criteria require: elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit (>16.5 g/dL / 49% in men; >16.0 g/dL / 48% in women), hypercellular bone marrow with trilineage panmyelosis, JAK2 mutation, and subnormal serum erythropoietin (EPO). Landmark CYTO-PV trial proved that strict hematocrit maintenance < 45% reduced cardiovascular death and major thrombosis fourfold compared to a 45-50% target (HR 3.91, 95% CI 1.45-10.53, p=0.007). All patients receive low-dose aspirin (81-100 mg daily; ECLAP trial). High-risk patients (age ≥60 or prior thrombosis) require cytoreductive therapy (hydroxyurea or ropeginterferon alfa-2b; ruxolitinib in refractory cases). Aquagenic pruritus (itching triggered by warm showers) is a hallmark symptom.
patient_plain_language: Polycythemia vera is a rare chronic bone marrow condition where a gene mutation instructs your marrow factories to produce far too many red blood cells. The extra cells make your blood unusually thick and sluggish, like motor oil in winter, increasing the danger of blood clots.

name: Rosacea
overview: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory centrofacial dermatosis characterized by neurovascular dysregulation and innate immune hyperreactivity (cathelicidin LL-37 processing by kallikrein 5, Demodex folliculorum mite hypersensitivity). Phenotypes include: Erythematotelangiectatic (persistent centrofacial erythema, flushing, telangiectasias), Papulopustular (dome-shaped red papules and pustules without comedones, distinguishing it from acne vulgaris), Phymatous (sebaceous hyperplasia, rhinophyma), and Ocular rosacea (blepharitis, conjunctivitis, burning/grittiness; present in >50%). First-line topical therapies for papulopustular rosacea: ivermectin 1% cream (superior to metronidazole; anti-parasitic against Demodex and anti-inflammatory), azelaic acid 15% gel, or metronidazole 0.75-1%. Subantimicrobial-dose oral doxycycline (40 mg modified-release daily; anti-inflammatory without antibacterial resistance) is indicated for moderate-to-severe disease. Persistent facial erythema responds to topical alpha-agonists (brimonidine 0.33%, oxymetazoline 1%) or vascular pulsed-dye laser (PDL).
patient_plain_language: Rosacea is a chronic skin condition causing persistent facial redness, flushing, and small acne-like bumps across your nose, cheeks, and forehead. Unlike teenage acne, there are no blackheads, and flare-ups are often triggered by sun, heat, spicy foods, or hot coffee.

name: Alopecia Areata
overview: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition caused by collapse of immune privilege in anagen hair follicles, mediated by CD8+ NKG2D+ T-cell infiltration and IFN-gamma/IL-15 signaling. Classic presentation is sudden onset of well-circumscribed, smooth, circular patches of non-scarring hair loss on the scalp or beard, showing pathognomonic exclamation-mark hairs and yellow/black dots on dermoscopy (trichoscopy). May progress to alopecia totalis (entire scalp) or alopecia universalis (complete body hair loss). Severity of Alopecia Tool (SALT) scores extent of hair loss. For limited patchy disease (SALT < 20-30%), first-line therapy is intralesional corticosteroid injections (triamcinolone acetonide 2.5-5 mg/mL into the dermis every 4-6 weeks) or potent topical corticosteroids. Landmark BRAVE-AA1 and BRAVE-AA2 phase 3 trials established oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors (baricitinib 2-4 mg daily; ritlecitinib 50 mg daily) as breakthrough FDA-approved therapies for severe disease (SALT score ≥ 50), producing significant scalp hair regrowth (SALT score ≤ 20 achieved in ~35-40% of patients vs 3-5% placebo at 36 weeks).
patient_plain_language: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition where your body's immune cells mistakenly attack the roots of your hair follicles, causing them to suddenly drop into a resting phase. This results in smooth, round, coin-shaped bald spots on your scalp or beard without any skin scarring.

name: Hidradenitis Suppurativa
overview: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic, painful, inflammatory follicular occlusion disorder predominantly affecting apocrine gland-bearing intertriginous skin (axillae, inguinal, perineal, inframammary regions). Manifests as recurrent painful inflammatory nodules, sterile abscesses, discharging epithelialized sinus tracts (tunnels), and dense bridged scarring. Staged using Hurley classification: Stage I (isolated nodules/abscesses, no sinus tracts), Stage II (recurrent abscesses with sinus tracts and scarring, separated), Stage III (diffuse coalescent tracts and interconnected abscesses across an entire anatomic area). Medical therapy: Topical clindamycin 1% for mild Hurley I; oral combination antibiotics (clindamycin 300 mg BID + rifampin 300 mg BID for 10-12 weeks) for Hurley II flares. Pivotal Phase 3 trials demonstrated that biological therapy targeting TNF (adalimumab 40 mg weekly, PIONEER trials) or IL-17A (secukinumab 300 mg every 2-4 weeks, SUNSHINE/SUNRISE trials) significantly achieves HiSCR (Hidradenitis Suppurativa Clinical Response: ≥50% reduction in inflammatory nodules without abscess increase). Deroofing or wide surgical excision is required for established chronic epithelialized tunnels.
patient_plain_language: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a painful, chronic inflammatory skin condition where clogged hair follicles in sensitive sweat-prone areas—like your armpits, groin, and under breasts—turn into deep, tender boils that can rupture, drain, and form under-the-skin tunnels.

name: Vitiligo
overview: Vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune depigmenting disorder characterized by progressive destruction of epidermal melanocytes, mediated by autoreactive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells driven by IFN-gamma and JAK1/JAK2 signaling. Clinically presents as well-demarcated, amelanotic milky-white macules and patches without epidermal atrophy or scale, exhibiting bright blue-white fluorescence under Wood's lamp. Segmental (unilateral, dermatomal) vs Non-segmental (bilateral, symmetric; ~90% of cases). Koebner phenomenon (depigmentation at sites of cutaneous friction/trauma) indicates active disease. The landmark TRuE-V1 and TRuE-V2 randomized phase 3 trials established the topical JAK inhibitor ruxolitinib 1.5% cream (applied twice daily) as the first FDA-approved disease-directed therapy for non-segmental vitiligo in patients ≥ 12 years, achieving ≥75% improvement in Facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index (F-VASI75) in ~30% of patients at 24 weeks and ~50% at 52 weeks. Narrowband ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) phototherapy (2-3 times/week) synergizes with medical therapy to stimulate melanocyte stem cell migration from hair follicles.
patient_plain_language: Vitiligo is an autoimmune condition where your body's immune defense system attacks its own pigment-producing cells (melanocytes) in your skin. This causes smooth, chalk-white patches to appear on your hands, face, or body where pigment has been lost.

research_papers.key_findings: Vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune depigmenting disorder characterized by progressive destruction of epidermal melanocytes, mediated by autoreactive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells driven by IFN-gamma and JAK1/JAK2 signaling. name: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
overview: Obsessive-compulsive disorder is characterized by recurrent, persistent, intrusive, and distressing thoughts, urges, or images (obsessions) and/or repetitive physical behaviors or mental acts (compulsions) that the individual feels driven to perform to reduce anxiety, consuming > 1 hour/day or causing clinically significant distress. Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) circuit hyperactivity underlies pathophysiology. First-line evidence-based psychotherapeutic treatment is specialized Cognitive Behavioral Therapy incorporating Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP; effect size g=1.39). First-line pharmacotherapy mandates high-dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs: fluoxetine 60-80 mg, sertraline 200 mg, escitalopram 20-40 mg, or fluvoxamine 200-300 mg daily), requiring higher doses and longer trial durations (10-12 weeks at maximum tolerated dose) than required for major depressive disorder. Clomipramine (tricyclic with potent serotonin reuptake inhibition) is second-line; augmentation with atypical antipsychotics (aripiprazole 5-10 mg, risperidone 1-2 mg) improves refractory cases.
patient_plain_language: OCD is a mental health condition where your brain gets stuck on distressing, intrusive thoughts, doubts, or fears (obsessions). To quiet the intense anxiety, you feel an overwhelming urge to perform repetitive routines, checks, or mental rituals (compulsions), which only temporarily relieves the anxiety before the cycle repeats.

name: Panic Disorder
overview: Panic disorder is characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks—abrupt surges of intense fear or intense discomfort reaching a peak within minutes, accompanied by ≥ 4 somatic and cognitive symptoms (palpitations, sweating, trembling, dyspnea, choking sensation, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat sensations, paresthesias, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control, fear of dying)—followed by ≥ 1 month of persistent concern about additional attacks or maladaptive behavioral changes (avoidance). First-line treatment consists of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT with interoceptive exposure to panic-related sensations) or SSRIs/SNRIs (sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, venlafaxine). SSRIs should be initiated at half standard starting doses (e.g., sertraline 25 mg) because panic disorder patients exhibit heightened sensitivity to initial jitteriness/anxiety. Benzodiazepines provide rapid acute relief but carry risks of physical dependence, tolerance, cognitive blunting, and increased relapse rates upon discontinuation, and are not recommended for long-term maintenance.
patient_plain_language: Panic disorder is a condition where your body's 'fight-or-flight' alarm system misfires without any real danger, flooding your system with adrenaline. Within minutes, your heart pounds, your chest tightens, and you feel dizzy and terrified that you are having a heart attack or losing your mind.

name: Social Anxiety Disorder (Social Phobia)
overview: Social anxiety disorder is characterized by marked, persistent fear or anxiety about one or more social situations in which the individual is exposed to possible scrutiny by others (social interactions, being observed eating/drinking, performing in front of others), fearing negative evaluation, embarrassment, or humiliation. The largest comprehensive network meta-analysis (Lancet Psychiatry, 101 trials, 13,164 participants) demonstrated that individual Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT based on the Clark and Wells or Heimberg models with video feedback and behavioral experiments) has the largest effect size and longest-lasting benefits. First-line pharmacotherapy for generalized social anxiety disorder is SSRIs (sertraline 50-200 mg, paroxetine 20-50 mg, escitalopram 10-20 mg) or SNRIs (venlafaxine XR 75-225 mg). For discrete performance-only social anxiety (e.g., public speaking, musical performances), as-needed non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol 10-40 mg orally taken 30-60 minutes before the event) effectively suppress peripheral autonomic somatic symptoms (tremors, tachycardia, voice shaking) without cognitive sedation.
patient_plain_language: Social anxiety disorder is far more intense than ordinary shyness. It is an intense, paralyzing fear of being watched, judged, scrutinized, or embarrassed in social or performance situations, causing sweating, trembling, blushing, and leading people to avoid conversations, meetings, or public speaking.

name: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD)
overview: Diagnostic criteria (DSM-5) require ≥ 2 of 11 criteria over a 12-month period, categorized into mild (2-3), moderate (4-5), and severe (≥6 criteria: tolerance, withdrawal, craving, inability to cut down, spending excess time obtaining/using, neglecting social/occupational roles). Acute alcohol withdrawal is managed with protocolized symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (CIWA-Ar protocol). First-line FDA-approved pharmacotherapies for maintaining abstinence and reducing heavy drinking days: Oral naltrexone (50 mg daily) or once-monthly extended-release injectable naltrexone (Vivitrol 380 mg IM; opioid receptor antagonist reducing the dopamine-mediated reinforcing reward of alcohol; Cochrane review confirms 28% reduction in heavy drinking days; contraindicated in patients taking opioid analgesics or in acute hepatitis/liver failure); and Acamprosate (666 mg TID; modulates NMDA glutamate neurotransmission, ideal for maintaining abstinence in patients with liver disease; cleared renally, contraindicated if CrCl < 30 mL/min). Disulfiram is second-line. Combining pharmacotherapy with evidence-based psychosocial interventions (Motivational Interviewing, CBT, Twelve-Step Facilitation) optimizes recovery outcomes.
patient_plain_language: Alcohol use disorder is a chronic medical brain disease where changes in brain chemistry make it extremely difficult to control or stop drinking alcohol despite harm to your health, relationships, or career. It is a treatable condition, and modern medications can significantly reduce cravings.

name: Uterine Leiomyomas (Fibroids)
overview: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign monoclonal smooth muscle neoplasms of the myometrium, occurring in up to 70-80% of women by age 50. Symptoms depend on anatomical location (FIGO classification: submucosal [Types 0-2], intramural [Types 3-5], subserosal [Types 6-7]). Submucosal and intramural fibroids distorting the uterine cavity cause heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB / menorrhagia) leading to iron deficiency anemia; large fibroids cause pelvic pressure, urinary frequency, and hydronephrosis. Transvaginal ultrasonography is first-line imaging; saline-infusion sonohysterography (SIS) or pelvic MRI defines submucosal mapping. Medical therapy for HMB: Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD (52 mg LNG-IUD; reduces menstrual blood loss by >80%), tranexamic acid (1,300 mg TID during heavy flow), or oral GnRH antagonists combined with add-back hormone therapy (elagolix or relugolix combination therapy; FDA-approved, suppresses HMB while preventing bone loss). Uterine artery embolization (UAE), hysteroscopic/laparoscopic myomectomy, or radiofrequency ablation provide fertility-preserving or uterine-preserving procedural options; hysterectomy is definitive.
patient_plain_language: Uterine fibroids are non-cancerous muscular growths that develop in the wall of your uterus. While many cause zero symptoms, depending on their size and location they can cause very heavy or prolonged periods, pelvic pressure, bloating, and fatigue from low iron.

name: Postpartum Depression (PPD)
overview: Postpartum depression affects ~10-15% of women following childbirth, defined as a major depressive episode occurring during pregnancy or within the first 12 months postpartum (distinguished from transient 'postpartum blues' which peak at 3-5 days and resolve by 10-14 days without functional impairment). Presentation features persistent sadness, profound emotional detachment or anhedonia toward the newborn, excessive guilt, sleep disturbance unrelated to infant wakings, severe anxiety, and obsessive fears of infant harm. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is the validated screening standard (score ≥ 10-12 indicates positive screen). Mild-to-moderate PPD responds well to evidence-based psychotherapy (Interpersonal Psychotherapy [IPT] or CBT). Moderate-to-severe PPD warrants pharmacotherapy: SSRIs (sertraline is preferred during breastfeeding due to minimal infant breastmilk excretion and low relative infant dose <0.5%). The breakthrough GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator zuranolone (50 mg orally once nightly with fatty food for 14 days; SKYLARK phase 3 trial) demonstrated rapid, statistically significant reduction in HAM-D depression scores by day 3 with sustained remission at day 45.
patient_plain_language: Postpartum depression is a medical complication of childbirth caused by massive hormonal drops and chemical shifts in the brain. It is not a sign of personal weakness or being a 'bad mother'. It causes deep sadness, feeling disconnected from your baby, and overwhelming anxiety that can be effectively treated.

name: Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis)
overview: Croup is an acute viral infection of the upper airway primarily caused by human parainfluenza virus type 1 (70-80%), peaking in infants and toddlers aged 6 months to 3 years during autumn/early winter. Inflammatory subglottic edema leads to the hallmark clinical triad: barking cough (resembling a seal or dog), inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness, characteristically worsening at night. Severity is stratified via the Westley Croup Score (evaluating stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and level of consciousness). Cochrane meta-analyses definitively prove that a single dose of oral dexamethasone (0.15-0.6 mg/kg, max 16 mg) significantly reduces hospital admissions (RR 0.52), shortens length of emergency department stay, reduces return visits, and decreases the need for nebulized epinephrine across all severity grades (mild, moderate, and severe). For moderate-to-severe croup with resting stridor and retractions, nebulized racemic epinephrine (0.5 mL of 2.25% solution) or L-epinephrine provides rapid subglottic vasoconstriction and symptom relief within 10-30 minutes, requiring a 2-4 hour observation window to monitor for post-epinephrine rebound stridor.
patient_plain_language: Croup is a common childhood viral infection that causes swelling in the voice box and windpipe just below the vocal cords. The narrowed airway produces a very distinctive deep, barking cough that sounds like a barking seal, along with a high-pitched squeaking noise when breathing in (stridor).

name: Pediatric Bronchiolitis (RSV)
overview: Bronchiolitis is the leading cause of hospitalization in infants < 12 months, predominantly caused by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV, 70-80%). Viral necrosis of bronchiolar epithelium, mucus plugging, and submucosal edema produce air trapping, tachypnea, expiratory wheezing, diffuse crackles, and increased work of breathing (nasal flaring, subcostal retractions). AAP evidence-based guidelines emphasize supportive care as the foundation of management: nasal suctioning (saline drops and bulb suction) and maintenance of adequate hydration (oral feeds or IV/nasogastric fluids if tachypneic with respiratory rate > 60-70 breaths/min risking aspiration). The AAP guideline explicitly recommends AGAINST the routine use of bronchodilators (albuterol), systemic corticosteroids, or chest physiotherapy, as randomized trials demonstrate they do not alter disease progression, reduce hospitalizations, or shorten stay. Supplemental oxygen is indicated only if pulse oximetry persistently falls below 90%. High-risk infants benefit from immunoprophylaxis with the long-acting monoclonal antibody nirsevimab (Beyfortus; single IM injection providing >75-80% protection against RSV lower respiratory infection; MELODY trial; NEJM 2022).
patient_plain_language: Bronchiolitis is a common winter viral infection (most often caused by RSV) that clogs the tiniest breathing branches (bronchioles) in an infant's lungs with mucus. Babies start with common cold symptoms before developing fast breathing, wheezing, and a chest that sucks in when inhaling.

name: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
overview: BPPV is the most common cause of peripheral vertigo, caused by otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) dislodged from the utricular macula migrating into a semicircular canal (canalithiasis; posterior canal involved in 85-95%). Pathognomonic presentation is brief (<1 minute), intense episodes of rotational spinning vertigo provoked by head position changes relative to gravity (rolling over in bed, looking up at a high shelf, bending forward). Gold standard diagnosis is the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, which elicits torsional, upbeating nystagmus with a 2-5 second latency and duration < 60 seconds that fatigues upon repeated testing. First-line definitive therapy is the canalith repositioning procedure (Epley maneuver; Cochrane systematic review proves >80-90% resolution of vertigo and negative Dix-Hallpike after 1-2 treatments vs 30% control, NNT=1.5). Vestibular suppressant medications (meclizine, benzodiazepines) are explicitly NOT recommended for routine treatment because they impair central compensation, cause cognitive blunting, and do not resolve otoconia displacement.
patient_plain_language: BPPV is a common inner-ear balance disorder where tiny calcium 'ear stones' come loose from their normal spot and float into the semicircular balance canals. When you tilt your head or roll over in bed, the loose crystals slosh the ear fluid, tricking your brain into feeling like the room is violently spinning.

name: Diabetic Retinopathy
overview: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults, caused by chronic microvascular damage from hyperglycemia leading to retinal capillary basement membrane thickening, pericyte loss, microaneurysms, retinal hemorrhages, and vascular leakage. Classified into Non-Proliferative (NPDR: mild, moderate, severe based on 4-2-1 rule: retinal hemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 quadrants, IRMA in 1 quadrant) and Proliferative (PDR: pathological neovascularization of the disc [NVD] or retina [NVE] driven by VEGF ischemia, risking vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment). Diabetic macular edema (DME: fluid accumulation in the fovea) can occur at any stage. Foundational systemic control (UKPDS and DCCT trials) reduces retinopathy progression: HbA1c < 7.0%, blood pressure < 130/80 mmHg, and lipid management. First-line therapy for center-involved DME with visual impairment is intravitreal anti-VEGF injections (aflibercept, ranibizumab, or faricimab; Protocol T trial showed aflibercept achieved superior visual gains in eyes with initial visual acuity 20/50 or worse). Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) laser or anti-VEGF therapy stabilizes high-risk PDR.
patient_plain_language: Diabetic retinopathy is damage to the delicate blood vessels in the light-sensing retina at the back of your eye caused by high blood sugar. In its early stages, weak spots leak fluid into the center of vision; in later stages, abnormal fragile blood vessels sprout that can bleed into the eye, causing dark floaters or vision loss.

name: Mitral Valve Regurgitation
overview: In the landmark COAPT trial (n=614 heart failure patients with secondary mitral regurgitation), transcatheter mitral-valve repair (MitraClip) plus guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) significantly reduced annual hospitalization for heart failure compared with GDMT alone (35.8% vs 67.9% per patient-year; HR 0.53; 95% CI 0.40-0.70; p<0.001) and all-cause 24-month mortality (29.1% vs 46.1%; HR 0.62; 95% CI 0.46-0.82; p<0.001). Number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent 1 death was 5.9.
patient_plain_language: The mitral valve is like a one-way swinging door that lets blood flow forward from your heart's upper chamber to the lower pump. In mitral regurgitation, the door does not seal completely tightly, allowing blood to leak backwards into your lungs with every heartbeat.

name: Infective Endocarditis
overview: The landmark POET trial (n=400 randomized patients with left-sided endocarditis stabilized on initial IV therapy) proved that transitioning to step-down oral antibiotics was non-inferior to continued intravenous antibiotic therapy for the composite primary outcome of all-cause mortality, unplanned cardiac surgery, embolic events, or relapsed bacteremia (9.0% oral vs 12.1% IV; difference -3.1 percentage points; 95% CI -8.8 to 2.5; p=0.40). Modified Duke Criteria remain the gold standard for clinical diagnosis (sensitivity >80%).
patient_plain_language: Infective endocarditis is a serious infection of the smooth inner lining and valves of your heart. Bacteria or microbes enter your bloodstream (often from the gums, skin, or medical lines) and settle on heart valves, creating clumps of bacteria that damage the heart flaps.

name: Acute Pericarditis
overview: In the landmark multicenter double-blind ICAP trial (n=240 patients with first-episode acute pericarditis), adding weight-adjusted colchicine (0.5 mg once or twice daily for 3 months) to standard anti-inflammatory therapy significantly reduced the rate of recurrent pericarditis at 18 months from 37.5% in the placebo group to 16.7% in the colchicine group (relative risk reduction 56%; absolute risk reduction 20.8 percentage points; NNT = 5; p<0.001). Colchicine also reduced symptom persistence at 72 hours (19.2% vs 40.0%; p=0.001).
patient_plain_language: Pericarditis is an inflammation of the pericardium, the protective fluid-filled double-layered sac that surrounds and cushions your heart. When inflamed, the two layers rub against each other like sandpaper, causing sharp chest pain that feels worse when breathing deeply or lying flat, but eases when leaning forward.

name: Cardiac Tamponade
overview: Cardiac tamponade is a life-threatening hemodynamic emergency where pericardial fluid accumulation under high pressure impairs diastolic filling. Beck's triad (hypotension, jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds) has high specificity (>90%) but low sensitivity (<30%). The single most sensitive clinical sign is pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg inspiratory drop in systolic blood pressure, sensitivity 98%). Echocardiographic hallmark is right ventricular early diastolic collapse (specificity 95%) and right atrial late diastolic collapse. Immediate pericardiocentesis resolves hemodynamics in >98% of cases.
patient_plain_language: Cardiac tamponade is a medical emergency where fluid rapidly builds up inside the sac wrapped around your heart. The fluid squeezes your heart like a tight vise grip, preventing the heart chambers from opening wide enough to fill with blood. This causes blood pressure to plunge dangerously low.

name: Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)
overview: In the multicenter VANISH trial (n=259 patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy and recurrent VT despite baseline antiarrhythmic therapy), catheter ablation significantly reduced the primary composite outcome of death, VT storm (>=3 episodes in 24 hours), or appropriate ICD shocks compared with escalated antiarrhythmic drug therapy (59.1% vs 68.5%; HR 0.72; 95% CI 0.53-0.98; p=0.04). Catheter ablation reduced VT storm by 42% (HR 0.58; p=0.04) and ICD shocks by 35% without excess procedural mortality.
patient_plain_language: Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a dangerously fast heartbeat that starts in the bottom pumping chambers (ventricles) of the heart. The ventricles fire off rapid electrical pulses (over 100-200 beats a minute), beating so fast that they quiver and do not have time to fill with blood before squeezing, causing blood pressure to drop rapidly.

name: Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT)
overview: The multicenter REVERT trial (n=428 emergency department patients with acute SVT) proved that a modified Valsalva maneuver (40 mmHg forced strain for 15 seconds in semi-recumbent position followed immediately by supine repositioning with 45-degree passive leg raise for 15 seconds) achieved cardioversion to normal sinus rhythm in 43% of patients compared with only 17% with standard Valsalva (odds ratio 3.7; 95% CI 2.3-5.8; p<0.0001; NNT = 3.8). This simple maneuver halved the need for intravenous adenosine (50% vs 69%). Definitive catheter radiofrequency ablation achieves >95% long-term cure.
patient_plain_language: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is a condition where an extra electrical short-circuit in the top chambers of your heart suddenly causes your pulse to race like a runaway freight train (often 150 to 220 beats per minute) out of nowhere. It starts and stops abruptly like flipping an electrical light switch.

name: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm
overview: The comprehensive 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline establishes strict diameter thresholds for elective surgical intervention in thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA). For ascending aortic aneurysms in low-surgical-risk centers of excellence, elective repair is recommended at >=5.0 cm (Class 2a) or >=5.5 cm in standard centers (Class 1). In patients with genetic aortopathies (Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz, bicuspid aortic valve), the threshold drops to 4.5-5.0 cm, or an aortic cross-sectional area to height ratio >10 cm2/m. Strict blood pressure control with beta-blockers and ARBs reduces rate of aortic expansion by >30%.
patient_plain_language: A thoracic aortic aneurysm is a bulge or ballooning in the aorta, the large main highway artery carrying oxygen-rich blood directly out of your heart through your chest. When the artery wall weakens, high blood pressure causes it to stretch outward like an over-inflated tire.

name: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)
overview: The landmark UK EVAR-1 trial (n=1252 patients with AAA >=5.5 cm followed for 15 years) demonstrated that endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) produced a 73% reduction in 30-day operative mortality compared with open surgical repair (1.8% vs 4.3%; p=0.02). Beyond 8 years, aneurysm-related mortality became similar, but EVAR required higher rates of reintervention for endoleaks (HR 2.42; p<0.0001). USPSTF recommends 1-time screening ultrasound in all men aged 65-75 who have ever smoked (Grade B; reduces rupture mortality by 50%).
patient_plain_language: An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a balloon-like swelling in the lower part of the aorta, the main blood vessel running through your belly to supply your legs. Most people have no symptoms until the aneurysm becomes very large. Smoking and high blood pressure are the leading causes of the blood vessel wall thinning out.

name: Raynaud's Phenomenon
overview: In a comprehensive Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 randomized controlled trials (n=296 participants), oral dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (predominantly nifedipine) significantly reduced the frequency of vasospastic attacks by 33% compared with placebo (mean difference -2.8 attacks per week; 95% CI -3.9 to -1.7; p<0.0001). Attack severity was also significantly reduced by 33%. In severe secondary Raynaud's resistant to CCBs, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) reduce attack frequency by a further 45% and accelerate digital ulcer healing.
patient_plain_language: Raynaud's phenomenon is an over-reactive response in the small blood vessels of your fingers and toes when exposed to cold or emotional stress. The tiny arteries suddenly spasm and shut down tightly, turning your fingers white, then blue as oxygen runs low, and finally bright red, throbbing, and tingling as blood rushes back in.

name: Buerger's Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans)
overview: Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) is a non-atherosclerotic segmental inflammatory vaso-occlusive vasculopathy affecting small and medium-sized arteries and veins of the extremities, almost exclusively in young tobacco smokers (<45 years). Complete and permanent cessation of all tobacco and nicotine products is the single proven intervention that halts disease progression and prevents limb loss. Continued smoking leads to amputation in 43% of patients at 10 years, compared to <5% in those who achieve complete smoking cessation (p<0.001). IV iloprost significantly improves ulcer healing and relieves ischemic rest pain (85% vs 17% placebo; p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: Buerger's disease is an inflammatory disease that causes swelling, inflammation, and tiny blood clots in the blood vessels of your hands and feet. This blocks blood flow to your fingers and toes, causing pain, coldness, and sores that can lead to tissue death (gangrene). It is directly linked to tobacco use—stopping smoking completely is the only way to save your fingers and toes.

name: Cor Pulmonale
overview: Cor pulmonale represents right ventricular (RV) hypertrophy, dilation, and systolic dysfunction resulting directly from severe pulmonary hypertension secondary to intrinsic lung disease (COPD, IPF, OSA). Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) in patients with chronic resting hypoxemia (PaO2 <=55 mmHg or SaO2 <=88%) significantly reduces pulmonary vascular resistance, prevents RV deterioration, and improves 5-year survival by 48% (NOTT and MRC trials). Judicious loop diuretic titration relieves RV volume overload without causing pre-renal azotemia.
patient_plain_language: Cor pulmonale is heart enlargement and weakness on the right side of your heart caused by chronic lung disease. When damaged lungs cannot absorb enough oxygen, the lung blood vessels clamp down tight. This forces the right side of your heart to work overtime against high resistance, causing it to stretch and weaken.

name: Spontaneous Pneumothorax
overview: In the open-label noninferiority PSP trial (n=316 patients aged 14-50 with a first large primary spontaneous pneumothorax [>=32% on chest radiograph]), conservative observation alone (analgesia and serial clinical review without interventional drainage) was noninferior to routine interventional chest drain insertion with respect to radiographic lung re-expansion at 8 weeks (94.4% conservative vs 98.5% interventional; difference -4.1 percentage points; 95% CI -8.6 to 0.5; p=0.02 for noninferiority). patient_plain_language: A spontaneous pneumothorax is a collapsed lung that occurs suddenly without any injury. name: Pleural Effusion (Exudative vs Transudative)
overview: Diagnostic thoracentesis evaluated using Light's Criteria has 98% sensitivity for distinguishing exudative from transudative pleural effusions. An effusion is exudative if any of the following 3 criteria are met: pleural fluid protein to serum protein ratio >0.5; pleural fluid LDH to serum LDH ratio >0.6; or pleural fluid LDH > two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Transudative effusions are driven by systemic hydrostatic/oncotic imbalances (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrosis) and resolve with medical diuresis. Parapneumonic effusions with pH <7.20, glucose <40 mg/dL, or positive Gram stain mandate prompt chest tube drainage.
patient_plain_language: A pleural effusion is an abnormal buildup of extra fluid in the space between your lung and the chest wall (the pleural space). As fluid collects, it pushes against your lung, squishing it down like a sponge submerged under water. This makes it hard to take a full deep breath and causes a dry cough.

name: Silicosis (Occupational Pneumoconiosis)
overview: Silicosis is an irreversible fibrotic occupational lung disease caused by the inhalation of respirable crystalline silica (quartz) particles (<5 microns). Silica particles ingested by alveolar macrophages trigger persistent activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, releasing interleukin-1-beta and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta), producing classical fibrotic silicotic nodules in upper lung zones. Patients with silicosis have a 30-fold increased risk of developing active tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis) and a 2.5-fold increased risk of lung cancer (IARC Group 1 human carcinogen). Primary prevention through engineering controls (wet-cutting, HEPA ventilation, N95/P100 respirators) is the only definitive intervention.
patient_plain_language: Silicosis is a chronic, permanent lung condition caused by breathing in tiny, invisible specks of mineral dust called crystalline silica, common in construction, stone masonry, quartz countertop cutting, sandblasting, and mining. Over time, the razor-sharp dust particles scar the lung tissue, making it stiff like leather and causing chronic shortness of breath.

High-resolution CT (HRCT) hallmarks include bilateral calcified pleural plaques (parietal pleura along diaphragm and lateral chest wall) and subpleural bibasilar reticular opacities with honeycombing. Smoking combined with asbestos exposure exhibits a supra-multiplicative synergistic effect, increasing bronchogenic lung carcinoma risk by 50- to 60-fold compared to unexposed non-smokers. Annual low-dose CT (LDCT) lung cancer screening reduces lung cancer mortality by 20% in this high-risk population.
patient_plain_language: Asbestosis is long-term scarring and inflammation of the lungs caused by breathing in asbestos fibers, a heat-resistant mineral widely used in old insulation, pipefitting, shipbuilding, and construction. The microscopic fibers lodge deep inside the air sacs, causing stiff scar tissue and chalky calcium patches (pleural plaques) along the lung lining.

name: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
overview: The 2020 international guideline categorizes Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis (HP) into non-fibrotic and fibrotic phenotypes. HP is an immune-mediated interstitial disease triggered by inhaled environmental antigens (avian proteins in bird fanciers, thermophilic actinomycetes in farmer's lung, mold in water-damaged buildings). High-resolution chest CT shows ground-glass opacities, centrilobular nodules, and the pathognomonic 'three-density sign' (headcheese sign: mosaic attenuation of ground glass, normal lung, and air trapping). Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) demonstrates marked lymphocytosis (>30-40% lymphocytes). Complete antigen remediation/avoidance is the cornerstone of therapy; non-fibrotic HP resolves in >80% with antigen removal alone.
patient_plain_language: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an allergic reaction deep inside the air sacs of your lungs triggered by breathing in microscopic organic dust or mold over long periods. Common culprits include feather bedding, pet birds (parakeets, pigeons), hot tubs, or damp moldy basements. The immune system treats the particles as invaders, causing widespread inflammation.

name: Pulmonary & Systemic Sarcoidosis
overview: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder characterized by noncaseating epithelioid granulomas, primarily affecting the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes (>90% of cases). Diagnostic hallmarks include bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) on chest radiography, elevated serum ACE levels (60% sensitivity), and negative microbiological stains/cultures to exclude tuberculosis and histoplasmosis. Scadding radiographic stages I through IV correlate with spontaneous remission rates (Stage I: 60-80% spontaneous remission vs Stage IV: <15%). Baseline screening must include 12-lead ECG (cardiac sarcoidosis screen), ophthalmologic slit-lamp exam (uveitis in 25-50%), and serum/urinary calcium (hypercalcemia due to 1-alpha-hydroxylase production in granulomas).
patient_plain_language: Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory disease where your immune system clusters together into tiny microscopic clumps called granulomas. While these granulomas can appear anywhere, they most commonly form in your lungs and chest lymph nodes. In many people, the clumps clear up on their own, but in others, they can cause coughing, chest ache, skin rashes, and joint stiffness.

name: Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP)
overview: Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP, formerly BOOP) is a distinct clinicopathologic entity characterized by intra-alveolar buds of granulation tissue (Masson bodies) extending into alveolar ducts. Unlike idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), COP is predominantly an inflammatory and reversible condition rather than a permanent fibrotic disease. Classic HRCT findings show bilateral patchy peripheral subpleural and peribronchovascular ground-glass consolidation, often with the pathognomonic 'reverse halo sign' (atoll sign: central ground glass surrounded by a crescentic or complete ring of consolidation, specificity >90%). First-line systemic corticosteroid therapy produces dramatic clinical and radiographic clearance in >80% of patients within 48 to 72 hours, though relapse occurs in 30-50% during steroid tapering.
patient_plain_language: Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP) is a non-infectious inflammatory lung condition where plugs of healing scar-like tissue and white blood cells form inside your lung's tiny air sacs. It often mimics pneumonia with dry cough, fever, and shortness of breath, but standard antibiotics fail to cure it because it is not caused by bacteria. Fortunately, it responds rapidly to steroid medications.

name: Pulmonary Arteriovenous Malformation (PAVM)
overview: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs) are abnormal direct low-resistance vascular conduits between pulmonary arteries and pulmonary veins that bypass the capillary bed, creating a right-to-left shunt. Over 80-90% of cases occur in the setting of Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT / Osler-Weber-Rendu disease). Because the normal pulmonary capillary filtration barrier is absent, paradoxical embolization occurs, leading to cryptogenic ischemic stroke (in 10-20%) and cerebral brain abscesses (in 5-10%). Transcatheter coil or microvascular plug embolization of all feeding arteries >=2-3 mm is the gold-standard therapy, reducing ischemic stroke and brain abscess incidence by >90% while improving arterial oxygenation.
patient_plain_language: A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (PAVM) is an abnormal direct tangle between a blood vessel carrying blood into your lungs and one carrying it away, bypassing the lung's normal microscopic filtering net (capillaries). Because this natural filter is skipped, tiny blood clots or bacteria can slip straight through to your brain, causing strokes or brain infections. Treating it involves plugging the abnormal connection with tiny coils.

name: Barrett's Esophagus
overview: In the landmark multicenter sham-controlled AIM Dysplasia trial (n=127 patients with dysplastic Barrett's esophagus), radiofrequency ablation (RFA) resulted in complete eradication of low-grade dysplasia in 90.5% of patients (vs 22.7% sham; p<0.001) and complete eradication of high-grade dysplasia in 81.0% (vs 19.0% sham; p<0.001) at 12 months. RFA was associated with less disease progression (3.6% vs 16.3%; p=0.03) and fewer esophageal adenocarcinomas (1.2% vs 9.3%; p=0.045). Continuous high-dose proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy reduces risk of progression to neoplastic dysplasia by 71% (OR 0.29; 95% CI 0.12-0.79).
patient_plain_language: Barrett's esophagus is a condition where chronic acid reflux from the stomach damages the lower lining of your food pipe (esophagus). Over years of acid exposure, the normal pale pink esophageal lining changes into a salmon-pink tissue that resembles the lining of your intestines. It requires regular camera checks (endoscopies) because of a small risk of developing cancer.

name: Achalasia
overview: In the landmark multicenter randomized noninferiority trial (n=221 patients with treatment-naive achalasia followed for 2 years), peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) was noninferior to laparoscopic Heller myotomy (LHM) plus Dor fundoplication with respect to clinical treatment success (Eckardt score <=3: 83.0% POEM vs 81.7% LHM; difference 1.4 percentage points; 95% CI -8.7 to 11.4; p=0.007 for noninferiority). Reflux esophagitis was more common after POEM at 2 years (44% vs 29%; p=0.03). High-resolution esophageal manometry (HRM) using the Chicago Classification (Type I, II, III) is the diagnostic gold standard; Type II achieves the highest treatment response (>90%).
patient_plain_language: Achalasia is a rare swallowing disorder where the nerves in your food pipe (esophagus) become damaged and stop working. The food pipe loses its normal muscular squeezing waves, and the muscular valve at the bottom entrance to the stomach (lower esophageal sphincter) fails to relax and open. Food and liquids get stuck in your chest and back up into your throat.

name: Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE)
overview: In the landmark 3-part multicenter Phase 3 trial (n=321 patients aged >=12 with active EoE despite high-dose PPI therapy), subcutaneous dupilumab (300 mg weekly) achieved histologic remission (<=6 eosinophils per high-power field [HPF]) in 60% of patients compared to only 5% with placebo in Part A (p<0.001) and 59% vs 6% in Part B (p<0.001). Dupilumab significantly improved dysphagia symptom scores (-21.9 vs -9.6 points; p<0.001) and increased esophageal distensibility while reducing endoscopic visual scores (trachealization rings, furrows, exudates, and strictures). Swallowed topical fluticasone or budesonide suspension achieves histologic remission in 65-75% of patients.
patient_plain_language: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is an allergic inflammatory condition of your food pipe (esophagus). Certain foods you eat trigger specialized allergy white blood cells called eosinophils to gather in the lining of your esophagus. This causes the lining to swell, develop stiff circular rings, and narrow down, making dense foods like chicken, steak, or bread catch and feel stuck in your chest.

name: Gastroparesis (Diabetic & Idiopathic)
overview: The ACG Gastroparesis Guidelines establish standardized 4-hour solid-phase gastric emptying scintigraphy (GES) with a low-fat egg meal as the diagnostic standard. Gastric retention >10% at 4 hours (or >60% at 2 hours) confirms delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction. In diabetic gastroparesis, optimizing glycemic control (targeting HbA1c <7.0%) is critical, as acute hyperglycemia (>200 mg/dL) directly inhibits antral contractions. Metoclopramide remains the only FDA-approved oral prokinetic medication, but therapy must be limited to <12 weeks due to risk of tardive dyskinesia.
patient_plain_language: Gastroparesis is a condition where the muscles in your stomach work too slowly or stop squeezing altogether, delaying the normal movement of food down into your intestines. Even when there is no physical blockage, food sits in your stomach for hours, leading to premature fullness after just a few bites, nausea, bloating, and vomiting.

name: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (Gastrinoma)
overview: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES) is caused by a neuroendocrine gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma), located predominantly within the 'gastrinoma triangle' (duodenum and pancreas). Approximately 25-30% of cases occur as part of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1). Hypergastrinemia causes marked hyperchlorhydria, resulting in severe refractory peptic ulcerations, gastroesophageal reflux, and secretory diarrhea (inactivation of pancreatic lipase by low pH). Diagnosis is established by fasting serum gastrin >1,000 pg/mL (in the presence of gastric pH <2) or a positive secretin stimulation test (rise in serum gastrin >120 pg/mL). High-dose PPI therapy eliminates acid hypersecretion and peptic complications in >98% of patients.
patient_plain_language: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a rare digestive disorder where tiny tumors called gastrinomas form in your pancreas or the first part of your small intestine. These tumors release large surges of a hormone called gastrin. The gastrin stimulates your stomach to produce massive amounts of burning acid, causing severe recurrent ulcers and chronic watery diarrhea.

name: Microscopic Colitis (Collagenous & Lymphocytic)
overview: In a Cochrane systematic review of 11 randomized controlled trials (n=556 patients with collagenous or lymphocytic colitis), oral budesonide (9 mg daily for 6-8 weeks) was highly effective for induction of clinical remission compared with placebo (73% vs 22%; relative risk 3.01; 95% CI 2.18-4.14; p<0.00001; NNT = 2). Budesonide also provided significant histologic remission (RR 2.76; p<0.0001) and substantial quality of life improvements. Low-dose budesonide (3-6 mg daily) maintained clinical remission in 75% at 6 months (vs 25% placebo; p<0.0001). Diagnosis requires routine mucosal biopsies of normal-appearing colon (showing subepithelial collagen band >10 microns in collagenous colitis, or >20 intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 enterocytes in lymphocytic colitis).
patient_plain_language: Microscopic colitis is an inflammatory bowel disorder that causes frequent, watery, non-bloody diarrhea, especially in older adults. When a doctor looks inside your colon with a camera, the colon lining looks completely normal and healthy to the naked eye. However, when small pinch biopsies are examined under a microscope, inflammation or an abnormal band of scar protein (collagen) is revealed.

name: Short Bowel Syndrome (Intestinal Failure)
overview: In the landmark double-blind Phase 3 STEPS trial (n=86 short bowel syndrome patients dependent on parenteral nutrition/IV support), subcutaneous teduglutide (a GLP-2 analogue, 0.05 mg/kg/day for 24 weeks) significantly reduced weekly parenteral nutrition volume requirements by >=20% in 63% of patients (vs 30% placebo; p=0.002). The absolute reduction in weekly parenteral volume was 4.4 L in teduglutide vs 2.3 L in placebo (p<0.001), with 54% of treated patients able to eliminate >=1 day of parenteral support per week. Teduglutide enhances intestinal mucosal hyperplasia, expands crypt depth and villus height, and boosts intestinal fluid and nutrient absorption.
patient_plain_language: Short bowel syndrome occurs when you are missing a large portion of your small intestine (usually after surgeries for bowel clots, Crohn's disease, or injury). Because the intestine is much shorter than normal, your body cannot absorb enough fluids, calories, vitamins, and minerals from eating, resulting in severe diarrhea, dehydration, and the need for liquid nutrition through an intravenous vein drip.

name: Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO)
overview: The landmark double-blind Phase 3 TARGET 1 and TARGET 2 trials (n=1260 patients with IBS-D/SIBO) demonstrated that a 14-day course of oral rifaximin (550 mg three times daily) significantly improved global IBS/SIBO symptoms (40.7% vs 31.7% placebo; p<0.001) and relieved bloating (40.2% vs 30.3%; p<0.001) for up to 10 weeks post-treatment. Retreatment with rifaximin upon symptom recurrence maintains efficacy without generating antimicrobial resistance (TARGET 3). Standardized glucose or lactulose breath testing showing an early rise in hydrogen >=20 ppm within 90 minutes (or methane >=10 ppm, diagnostic of Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth [IMO]) confirms the diagnosis.
patient_plain_language: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) occurs when bacteria that normally live harmlessly in your large colon back up and multiply inside your small intestine. When you eat foods containing sugars and carbohydrates, these out-of-place bacteria rapidly ferment the food, producing massive clouds of hydrogen or methane gas that cause painful bloating, gas, abdominal cramping, and chronic diarrhea.

name: Autoimmune Hepatitis
overview: Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH) is characterized by hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG >1.1x ULN), circulating autoantibodies (ANA and SMA in Type 1; anti-LKM1 or anti-LC1 in Type 2), and interface hepatitis on liver biopsy. The Revised Original Score (>15 definite) and Simplified Diagnostic Criteria (>7 definite) achieve >95% diagnostic sensitivity and specificity. Combined induction therapy with prednisone (30-60 mg/day tapered) plus azathioprine (1-2 mg/kg/day) or budesonide (9 mg/day) produces complete biochemical remission (normalization of transaminases and IgG) in >85% of patients while minimizing corticosteroid adverse events. 10-year survival exceeds 90% with sustained biochemical remission.
patient_plain_language: Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic disease where your body's immune defense system mistakenly identifies your own liver cells as foreign invaders and attacks them. This causes continuous inflammation, swelling, and scarring of the liver. Without medication to quiet down the overactive immune system, it can eventually lead to permanent liver cirrhosis.

name: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)
overview: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC, formerly cirrhosis) is an autoimmune destruction of intrahepatic interlobular bile ducts, characterized by antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA titer >=1:40, specificity >98%) and elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP). First-line therapy with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA 13-15 mg/kg/day) normalizes survival when biochemical response is achieved (Paris II or Toronto criteria: ALP <1.67x ULN and normal bilirubin). In the landmark Phase 3 POISE trial (n=217 patients with inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA), adding obeticholic acid (5-10 mg daily) achieved the composite biochemical endpoint in 46-47% vs 10% placebo (p<0.001) with marked reductions in ALP, bilirubin, and liver fibrosis markers.
patient_plain_language: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is an autoimmune condition where your immune system slowly attacks and destroys the microscopic bile ducts inside your liver. These ducts are tiny drainage tubes that carry bile (digestive fluid) out of the liver. When the tubes are damaged, toxic bile backs up inside the liver, causing liver scarring, deep fatigue, and severe skin itching.

name: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)
overview: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) is a progressive fibro-obliterative disease of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD, present in 70-80% of patients, predominantly ulcerative colitis). Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice, showing characteristic multifocal strictures and segmental dilatations ('beading' pattern) without diagnostic autoantibodies. Patients face a 400-fold increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma (lifetime risk 10-20%) and a marked risk of colorectal carcinoma (4-fold higher than IBD alone). Surveillance with annual MRCP + CA 19-9 and annual colonoscopy with random biopsies is mandatory.
patient_plain_language: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is an inflammatory disease that causes scarring and narrowing in the medium and large bile ducts both inside and outside your liver. The bile tubes become stiff, blocked, and beaded like a string of knotted ropes. Because bile cannot drain into the intestines, it backs up, causing liver damage. It is closely linked to ulcerative colitis.

name: Wilson's Disease (Hepatolenticular Degeneration)
overview: Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and defective ceruloplasmin incorporation. Toxic copper accumulates sequentially in the liver, brain (basal ganglia/lenticular nuclei), cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings present in >95% of neurologic cases), and kidneys. Diagnostic hallmarks include decreased serum ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL), elevated 24-hour urinary copper excretion (>40-100 mcg/24h), and hepatic parenchymal copper concentration >250 mcg/g dry weight on liver biopsy. Leipzig diagnostic score >=4 establishes definitive diagnosis. Chelation therapy with penicillamine or trientine halts disease progression and reverses hepatic/neurologic deficits in >80%.
patient_plain_language: Wilson's disease is an inherited genetic condition where your body cannot get rid of excess copper from the foods you eat. Instead of releasing extra copper into your digestive bile, the copper builds up in your liver and then spills over into your brain and eyes. This can cause liver damage, tremors, difficulty speaking, mood changes, and a distinctive golden-brown ring around the iris of your eye (Kayser-Fleischer ring).

name: Hereditary Hemochromatosis
overview: Hereditary hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive iron overload disorder caused primarily by homozygous C282Y mutations (or C282Y/H63D compound heterozygosity) in the HFE gene on chromosome 6, resulting in deficiency of the iron-regulatory peptide hepcidin. Unchecked ferroportin activity causes progressive intestinal iron hyperabsorption (2-4 mg/day vs 1 mg normal). Progressive iron deposition in hepatocytes, pancreatic islets, myocardium, pituitary, and synovium causes the classic 'bronze diabetes' tetrad (cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, hyperpigmentation, and arthropathy). Diagnostic screening begins with fasting transferrin saturation (>45% in women, >50% in men) and serum ferritin (>200 ng/mL in women, >300 ng/mL in men), followed by HFE genetic testing. Therapeutic phlebotomy initiated prior to cirrhosis development restores normal life expectancy.
patient_plain_language: Hereditary hemochromatosis is a genetic 'iron overload' disorder where your digestive system absorbs far more iron from your food than your body can ever use. Because your body has no natural way to get rid of extra iron, the iron builds up over decades in your liver, heart, pancreas, and joints. The standard treatment is simple and life-saving: regularly donating a pint of blood (therapeutic phlebotomy) to pull the excess iron out.

name: Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS-AKI)
overview: Hepatorenal syndrome acute kidney injury (HRS-AKI) is a severe form of functional renal failure occurring in advanced cirrhosis with ascites, driven by extreme splanchnic arterial vasodilation that triggers reflex renal vasoconstriction. In the landmark multicenter double-blind Phase 3 CONFIRM trial (n=300 patients with HRS-AKI), terlipressin plus IV albumin was significantly superior to placebo plus albumin in achieving verified HRS reversal (sustained serum creatinine <=1.5 mg/dL without renal replacement therapy for at least 10 days: 32% vs 17%; p=0.006). Terlipressin also improved renal function before liver transplantation (34% vs 17%; p=0.002). Definitive curative therapy remains orthotopic liver transplantation.
patient_plain_language: Hepatorenal syndrome is a severe medical emergency where the kidneys suddenly stop functioning properly because of advanced liver disease (cirrhosis). The damaged liver causes large blood vessels in your abdomen to widen excessively, stealing blood away from your kidneys. The kidneys react by clamping down their own blood vessels, shutting down urine production.

name: Hepatic Encephalopathy
overview: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a spectrum of neuropsychiatric abnormalities in patients with liver dysfunction and portosystemic shunting, driven by hyperammonemia crossing the blood-brain barrier and causing astrocyte swelling. In the landmark multicenter double-blind Phase 3 trial (n=299 patients in remission from recurrent HE), combination therapy with rifaximin (550 mg BID) plus lactulose significantly reduced the risk of an acute HE breakthrough episode by 58% compared with placebo over 6 months (22.1% vs 45.9%; hazard ratio 0.42; 95% CI 0.28-0.64; p<0.001; NNT = 4). Rifaximin also reduced HE-related hospitalizations by 50% (HR 0.50; p=0.01). First-line lactulose titration targeting 2-3 soft bowel movements daily remains the cornerstone.
patient_plain_language: Hepatic encephalopathy is a decline in brain function that happens when your liver is too damaged to filter out normal toxins from your blood. Toxic substances, especially ammonia produced by gut bacteria when digesting protein, build up in your bloodstream and travel to your brain. This causes forgetfulness, day-night sleep reversal, sluggish thinking, flapping hand tremors (asterixis), and confusion.
