name: Chronic Pancreatitis
overview: Chronic pancreatitis is an irreversible fibro-inflammatory syndrome resulting in progressive destruction of pancreatic exocrine parenchyma and islet architecture. Alcohol consumption and tobacco smoking act synergistically as the leading etiologic drivers (TIGAR-O classification). Cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI/MRCP, or endoscopic ultrasound [EUS]) establishes the diagnosis via classic structural hallmarks: parenchymal calcifications, ductal dilatations with strictures (chain of lakes appearance), and intraductal calculi. Smoking cessation reduces the rate of disease progression and reduces the 12-fold elevated risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Antioxidant supplementation and high-dose pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) relieve pain and malabsorption.
patient_plain_language: Chronic pancreatitis is long-term, permanent inflammation and scarring of your pancreas, the organ tucked behind your stomach that makes digestive juices and insulin. Over time, the constant inflammation destroys healthy pancreas tissue and causes chalky stones to form inside the pancreatic ducts. This leads to persistent upper belly pain, malabsorption, and weight loss.

name: Pancreatic Exocrine Insufficiency (PEI)
overview: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI) results when functional pancreatic enzyme secretion drops below 10% of physiological capacity, leading to severe fat and protein maldigestion. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 randomized controlled trials (n=518 patients), enteric-coated pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) significantly increased the coefficient of fat absorption (CFA) by 13.9 percentage points compared with placebo (mean CFA 83.7% vs 69.8%; 95% CI 9.9-17.9; p<0.00001). PERT also improved coefficient of nitrogen absorption, relieved steatorrhea, and produced substantial weight gain. Fecal elastase-1 (FE-1) <200 mcg/g stool (severe if <100 mcg/g) is the non-invasive diagnostic standard (sensitivity 95% in moderate-to-severe PEI).
patient_plain_language: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI) means your pancreas does not produce enough digestive enzymes to break down the food you eat. Because dietary fats cannot be digested and absorbed, they pass straight through your bowels. This leads to large, greasy, pale, foul-smelling stools that float in the toilet bowl (steatorrhea), along with stomach rumbles, weight loss, and vitamin deficiencies.

name: Cushing's Syndrome & Disease
overview: Cushing's syndrome results from prolonged, inappropriate tissue exposure to excess glucocorticoids, most commonly iatrogenic, or endogenous (Cushing's disease due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma in 70-80% of endogenous cases). Diagnostic confirmation requires at least two concordant first-line tests: 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC >3x ULN), late-night salivary cortisol (>2 elevated measurements, sensitivity/specificity >95%), or 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (serum cortisol post-dex >1.8 mcg/dL / >50 nmol/L). Plasma ACTH differentiates ACTH-dependent (>20 pg/mL) from ACTH-independent (<5 pg/mL, adrenal source) disease. First-line therapy for Cushing's disease is transsphenoidal pituitary adenomectomy (initial cure rate 70-85%).
patient_plain_language: Cushing's syndrome is a hormone disorder caused by having too much cortisol (the body's primary stress hormone) in your bloodstream for long periods. Cortisol is essential for life, but excessive amounts cause a rounded 'moon face', fat buildup on the back of the neck ('buffalo hump'), wide purple stretch marks across the belly, fragile skin that bruises easily, muscle weakness, and high blood pressure.

name: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's Disease)
overview: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's disease) is the destruction or dysfunction of the entire adrenal cortex, leading to combined deficiency of glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone). Autoimmune adrenalitis (marked by 21-hydroxylase antibodies) accounts for >80-90% of cases in developed nations. Diagnostic gold standard is the high-dose synthetic ACTH (Cosyntropin 250 mcg) stimulation test; a peak serum cortisol <18 mcg/dL (<500 nmol/L) at 30 or 60 minutes establishes adrenal insufficiency, with plasma ACTH markedly elevated (>2x ULN). Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and generalized cutaneous hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, vermilion border, buccal mucosa) are pathognomonic hallmarks.
patient_plain_language: Addison's disease is an autoimmune condition where your adrenal glands (tiny hormone factories sitting on top of your kidneys) become damaged and stop producing vital hormones called cortisol and aldosterone. Cortisol helps you handle stress and keep blood pressure steady, while aldosterone balances salt and water. Without these hormones, you develop deep fatigue, weight loss, salt cravings, low blood pressure, and a darkened skin tan.

name: Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome)
overview: Primary Aldosteronism (PA) is the most common cause of secondary hypertension, accounting for 5-10% of all hypertensive patients and >20% of resistant hypertension. Autonomous aldosterone secretion by an adrenal adenoma (Conn's syndrome, 35%) or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (60%) suppresses renin, causing sodium retention, potassium wasting, and target-organ damage disproportionate to blood pressure elevation (4-fold higher stroke, 6-fold higher myocardial infarction, and 12-fold higher atrial fibrillation risk). Initial screening requires the plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR >20-30 with plasma aldosterone >10-15 ng/dL). Confirmatory testing (oral sodium loading or saline infusion test) followed by adrenal venous sampling (AVS) accurately distinguishes unilateral from bilateral disease with >95% accuracy.
patient_plain_language: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) is a hormonal cause of severe high blood pressure. Your adrenal glands produce far too much of a hormone called aldosterone. Aldosterone tells your kidneys to hold onto excessive amounts of salt and water while dumping potassium into your urine. This drives blood pressure high and makes it resistant to standard blood pressure medications.

name: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
overview: In the landmark double-blind Phase 3 MCI-186 trial (n=137 patients with early definite or probable ALS), intravenous edaravone (a free-radical scavenger, 60 mg daily in 28-day cycles) significantly slowed functional motor decline over 24 weeks compared with placebo, as measured by the Revised ALS Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R mean difference 2.49 points; 95% CI 0.99-3.98; p=0.0013). Riluzole (50 mg BID) prolongs median survival or time to tracheostomy by 2-3 months (hazard ratio 0.65; p=0.002). Multidisciplinary specialized ALS clinic care and early non-invasive ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) when upright FVC <50% or sniff nasal pressure <40 cm H2O prolongs quality survival by >12 months.
patient_plain_language: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, often called Lou Gehrig's disease) is a progressive nervous system disease that affects motor nerve cells in your brain and spinal cord. These motor nerves control all your voluntary muscles. As the nerves gradually degenerate, the muscles they signal become weak, twitch (fasciculations), and shrink, making it difficult to walk, talk, swallow, and breathe.

name: Huntington's Disease
overview: Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat (>36 repeats; fully penetrant at >=40 repeats) in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, resulting in toxic huntingtin protein aggregation and profound striatal (caudate and putamen) GABAergic medium spiny neuron loss. The clinical triad comprises motor chorea, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbances. In the multicenter double-blind Phase 3 First-HD trial (n=90 patients), deuterated tetrabenazine (deutetrabenazine, a vesicular monoamine transporter 2 [VMAT2] inhibitor) significantly improved the Total Maximal Chorea score from baseline to week 12 compared with placebo (mean difference -2.5 units; 95% CI -3.7 to -1.3; p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: Huntington's disease is a genetic brain disorder caused by an inherited error in a single gene. Over time, it damages nerve cells in the central movement-control centers of your brain. It causes involuntary dancing or jerking movements (chorea), changes in personality, irritability, and gradual memory and reasoning challenges. Each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the gene.

name: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH)
overview: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) is a reversible cause of dementia characterized by the classic clinical triad of gait disturbance ('magnetic' gait: slow, wide-based, shuffling, glued to the floor), cognitive decline (subcortical psychomotor slowing), and urinary incontinence ('wet, wacky, and wobbly'). MRI demonstrates ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal atrophy (Evans index >0.30) with tight high-convexity sulci and enlarged Sylvian fissures (Disproportionately Enlarged Subarachnoid-space Hydrocephalus [DESH]). Diagnostic CSF tap test (removal of 30-50 mL CSF via lumbar puncture) producing an objective >=20% improvement in 10-meter timed walking speed has >90% positive predictive value for surgical shunt success. Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting with a programmable valve achieves long-term clinical gait improvement in >80% of patients.
patient_plain_language: Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is a condition where normal fluid (cerebrospinal fluid) builds up inside the open fluid chambers (ventricles) of your brain. As the fluid chambers swell, they stretch the brain tissue that controls your walking, memory, and bladder control. The classic signs are a shuffling 'magnetic' walk (feet feeling glued to the floor), mild forgetfulness, and urgent bladder leaks. It is one of the few forms of dementia that can be reversed with a small drainage tube (shunt).

name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)
overview: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated post-infectious polyradiculoneuropathy (most commonly following Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV, or Zika virus infection) characterized by molecular mimicry attacking peripheral nerve myelin (AIDP) or axolemma (AMAN/AMSAN). Clinical hallmark is acute, rapidly progressive, symmetric ascending flaccid paralysis with areflexia. Lumbar puncture demonstrates classic 'albuminocytological dissociation' (elevated CSF protein >0.45 g/L with normal white blood cell count <10 cells/mcL). In a Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials (n=585 patients), intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days) was equally effective as plasma exchange (PE 200-250 mL/kg over 5 sessions) in accelerating motor recovery and reducing mechanical ventilation (RR 1.05; 95% CI 0.73-1.53), with fewer adverse events. Corticosteroids alone are ineffective and harmful.
patient_plain_language: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is a rare neurological disorder where your body's immune system, usually triggered by a recent stomach bug or respiratory virus, gets confused and mistakenly attacks the protective coating of your peripheral nerves. It causes tingling and numbness that starts in your toes and feet and rapidly spreads upward into your legs, arms, and chest, causing temporary weakness or paralysis.

name: Myasthenia Gravis
overview: Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission caused predominantly by pathogenic autoantibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (AChR-Ab, present in 85%), muscle-specific kinase (MuSK-Ab, 5-8%), or LRP4. Hallmark is fatigable muscle weakness that worsens with repetitive activity and improves with rest. In the landmark international randomized trial of thymectomy (MGTX, n=126 patients with non-thymomatous generalized AChR-positive MG aged 18-65), extended transsternal thymectomy combined with prednisone significantly improved the Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis (QMG) score over 3 years (mean score 6.15 vs 8.99; p<0.001) and lowered average daily prednisone dose (44 mg vs 60 mg; p<0.001) compared with prednisone alone. In refractory generalized MG, complement C5 inhibition (eculizumab) or neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) blockers (efgartigimod) produce rapid, robust clinical improvements.
patient_plain_language: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder where your immune system mistakenly blocks or destroys the receptors on your muscles that receive signals from your nerves. Without these communication receptors, your muscles get tired and weak very quickly when used. The most common signs are a droopy eyelid (ptosis), double vision, difficulty chewing solid food, slurred speech, and muscle fatigue that improves after a short nap.

name: Trigeminal Neuralgia
overview: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN, tic douloureux) is characterized by paroxysmal, brief (lasting fractions of a second to 2 minutes), severe, unilateral, electric shock-like, shooting facial pains strictly distributed along one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve (most commonly V2 maxillary and V3 mandibular). Pain is triggered by innocuous light cutaneous touch (brushing teeth, light breeze, chewing, talking). Classic TN is driven by neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root entry zone by an aberrant arterial loop (most commonly the superior cerebellar artery [SCA]), identifiable on 3D high-resolution T2/constructive interference MRI (3D-CISS/FIESTA). First-line pharmacological therapy with sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine 200-1200 mg/day or oxcarbazepine 600-1800 mg/day) achieves initial pain control in >80% of patients. Microvascular decompression (MVD, Janetta procedure) achieves long-term pain freedom without sensory loss in >70-80% at 5 years.
patient_plain_language: Trigeminal neuralgia is an intense facial nerve pain condition often described as one of the most painful conditions known. A pulsating blood vessel presses against the trigeminal nerve, the main sensation cable connecting your face to your brain. This wears away the nerve's protective insulation, so even the lightest brush—like a gentle gust of wind, chewing food, or brushing your teeth—triggers blinding, lightning-bolt pain across your cheek, jaw, or mouth.

name: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri)
overview: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH, formerly pseudotumor cerebri) is characterized by elevated intracranial pressure (>250 mm H2O in adults) without hydrocephalus, mass lesion, or abnormal CSF composition, predominantly affecting young obese females of childbearing age. Modified Dandy criteria require papilledema, normal neurological exam (except 6th cranial nerve abducens palsy), and MRI showing neuroimaging signs of raised ICP (empty sella turcica, flattening of posterior sclerae, distension of perioptic subarachnoid space, and bilateral transverse venous sinus stenosis). In the landmark multicenter double-blind IIHTT trial (n=165 patients with mild visual field loss), high-dose acetazolamide (titrated up to 4 g daily) plus a low-sodium weight-reduction diet produced significantly greater improvement in visual field perimetric mean deviation (MD: +1.43 dB; p=0.04) and papilledema grade (mean reduction -0.70 Frisén units; p<0.001) compared with diet alone. Weight reduction of 10-15% cures IIH in >70%.
patient_plain_language: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) is a condition where high pressure builds up inside your skull, acting just like a brain tumor even though no actual tumor exists. The fluid that cushions your brain (cerebrospinal fluid) cannot drain away quickly enough, putting high pressure on your optic nerves (the cables connecting your eyes to your brain). This causes daily throbbing headaches, whooshing sounds in your ears (pulsatile tinnitus), and brief blackouts in your vision when bending over.

name: Cluster Headache
overview: Cluster headache is the most severe primary headache disorder, classified as a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia (TAC) characterized by strictly unilateral, excruciating, piercing/boring orbital or supraorbital pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes, accompanied by prominent ipsilateral cranial autonomic features (conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, forehead sweating, and partial Horner's syndrome [ptosis and miosis]). In the landmark double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial (n=109 patients with 150 attacks treated), high-flow 100% normobaric oxygen (12 L/min via non-rebreather face mask for 15 minutes) rendered 78% of patients pain-free at 15 minutes compared with only 20% on medical air placebo (p<0.001; NNT = 1.7). Subcutaneous sumatriptan (6 mg) provides rapid abortion in >75% within 15 minutes. First-line preventative therapy is high-dose verapamil (240-960 mg/day).

name: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
overview: A Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) is a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, without acute infarction on diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI). TIA carries an immediate 10-15% risk of disabling ischemic stroke within 90 days, with half occurring within the first 48 hours. In the landmark POINT (n=4881) and CHANCE (n=5170) trials in high-risk TIA (ABCD2 score >=4) or minor stroke, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT: Aspirin 81 mg + Clopidogrel 300-600 mg load then 75 mg daily) initiated within 12-24 hours and continued for exactly 21 days significantly reduced subsequent major ischemic stroke by 25-32% compared with aspirin monotherapy (HR 0.68-0.75; p<0.001) without a significant excess in major hemorrhage when capped at 21 days.
patient_plain_language: A transient ischemic attack (TIA), often called a 'warning stroke' or 'mini-stroke', occurs when blood flow to part of your brain is briefly blocked by a small traveling blood clot. The symptoms—such as a droopy face, weak arm, or slurred speech—may disappear completely after a few minutes, but a TIA is an emergency warning that a major, permanent stroke could strike within the next 48 hours.

name: Vascular Dementia
overview: Vascular Cognitive Impairment and Dementia (VCID) is the second most common form of dementia, encompassing multi-infarct dementia, strategic single-infarct dementia, and subcortical ischemic vascular dementia (Binswanger's disease driven by arteriolosclerosis). Brain MRI is the diagnostic modality of choice, revealing extensive confluent periventricular white matter hyperintensities (Fazekas Grade 3), multiple lacunar infarcts, and microbleeds on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI). Unlike the insidious memory-predominant course of Alzheimer's, vascular dementia classically presents with stepwise cognitive decline, prominent dysexecutive syndrome (impaired planning, sequencing, processing speed), and early psychomotor and gait slowing. Aggressive vascular risk reduction (BP <130/80 mmHg with ACEi/ARBs, statins, and antiplatelet therapy) halts further microvascular accumulation.
patient_plain_language: Vascular dementia is memory and thinking loss caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, often following multiple silent 'mini-strokes' or long-term narrowing of tiny blood vessels in the brain. Unlike other dementias that primarily start with memory loss, vascular dementia often starts with slowed thinking, difficulty planning and organizing daily tasks, and a hesitant, unsteady walking gait.

name: Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB)
overview: Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB) is pathologically characterized by widespread neuronal alpha-synuclein inclusions (Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites) throughout the neocortex, paralimbic, and brainstem structures. Core clinical features require: (1) fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness; (2) recurrent, complex, well-formed visual hallucinations (present in >80%); (3) REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD: dream enactment, kicking/punching during sleep, preceding dementia by years); and (4) one or more spontaneous cardinal features of parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor). Indicative biomarkers include reduced dopamine transporter (DaT) uptake in basal ganglia on DaTscan SPECT (sensitivity 78%, specificity 90%) and preserved temporal lobe structures on MRI. Patients exhibit severe neuroleptic sensitivity (up to 50% suffer acute severe parkinsonism, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, or death when exposed to typical antipsychotics).
patient_plain_language: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is a progressive brain condition caused by abnormal microscopic protein deposits called Lewy bodies forming inside your brain cells. It causes memory and thinking problems that fluctuate dramatically from hour to hour, realistic visual hallucinations (often seeing people or animals that are not there), physically acting out dreams while asleep (kicking or shouting), and Parkinson's-like stiffness and shuffling.

name: Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD)
overview: Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD / Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration [FTLD]) is the most common cause of early-onset dementia in patients <65 years, pathologically driven by tau inclusions (Pick bodies), TDP-43, or FUS aggregates. The behavioral variant (bvFTD) is diagnosed via the international FTDC criteria requiring at least 3 of 6 core features: (1) early behavioral disinhibition (socially inappropriate actions, loss of manners); (2) early apathy or inertia; (3) early loss of empathy or sympathy; (4) early perseverative, stereotyped, or compulsive behavior; (5) hyperorality and dietary changes (gluttony, sweet cravings); and (6) executive cognitive deficits with relative sparing of episodic memory and visuospatial function. Structural MRI shows asymmetric knife-blade atrophy of frontal and anterior temporal lobes. Genetic mutations (C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion, GRN, MAPT) account for 30-40% of familial cases.
patient_plain_language: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a group of brain disorders caused by nerve cell damage and shrinking in the front and side regions of your brain (the frontal and temporal lobes). Because these areas govern your personality, behavior, judgment, empathy, and language, FTD typically starts with major personality shifts—such as socially inappropriate comments, loss of sympathy for family, obsessive rituals, or a craving for sweets—often while memory remains intact.

name: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
overview: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by intrusive, distressing, ego-dystonic thoughts, urges, or images (obsessions) that trigger repetitive mental or physical behaviors (compulsions) performed to neutralize anxiety, consuming >1 hour daily. In a comprehensive network meta-analysis of 54 randomized trials (n=6652 patients), Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) behavioral therapy combined with high-dose Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) was significantly superior to either intervention alone for reduction in Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) scores (standardized mean difference -1.18; 95% CI -1.45 to -0.91; p<0.0001). SSRI doses required for OCD are typically substantially higher than for major depression (e.g. Fluoxetine up to 80 mg/day, Sertraline up to 200 mg/day) and require 8-12 weeks to assess clinical response.
patient_plain_language: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a mental health condition driven by a cycle of obsessions and compulsions. Obsessions are unwanted, intrusive, frightening thoughts or doubts (like fears of germs, harm, or symmetry) that get stuck on repeat in your mind, triggering intense anxiety. Compulsions are repetitive mental acts or physical behaviors (like washing hands, checking door locks, or tapping) you feel driven to perform to relieve the anxiety.

name: Panic Disorder & Agoraphobia
overview: Panic disorder is characterized by recurrent unexpected panic attacks (abrupt surges of intense fear or intense discomfort reaching a peak within minutes, with at least 4 of 13 autonomic symptoms: palpitations, sweating, trembling, dyspnea, choking sensation, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat, paresthesias, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control, and fear of dying) followed by at least 1 month of persistent worry about further attacks or maladaptive avoidance behavior (agoraphobia). In a network meta-analysis of 87 randomized controlled trials (n=12,823 patients), Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT with interoceptive exposure) combined with an SSRI/SNRI achieved superior remission of panic attacks and reduction in agoraphobic avoidance compared with either treatment alone (odds ratio 2.45; 95% CI 1.72-3.48; p<0.0001). Long-term benzodiazepine monotherapy is discouraged due to tolerance and rebound panic.
patient_plain_language: Panic disorder is an anxiety condition where you experience sudden, terrifying surges of overwhelming fear and physical sensations called panic attacks. Out of nowhere, your heart pounds rapidly, your chest tightens, you gasp for breath, and you feel like you are having a heart attack, fainting, or dying. Because these attacks strike without warning, many people develop agoraphobia—avoiding crowded places, stores, or driving out of fear of having another attack.

name: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD)
overview: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is characterized by a pervasive pattern of emotional dysregulation, instability of interpersonal relationships, unstable self-image, marked impulsivity (spending, sex, substance abuse), recurrent suicidal behavior, gestures, or self-harm (NSSI), and chronic feelings of emptiness. In a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of 33 randomized controlled trials (n=2256 patients), specialized psychotherapies—most notably Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT, standardized mean difference -0.34; p=0.005) and Mentalization-Based Therapy (MBT)—significantly reduced self-harm, suicidal gestures, emergency department visits, and BPD core symptom severity compared with treatment as usual. Pharmacotherapy has no primary disease-modifying FDA approval; low-dose second-generation antipsychotics or mood stabilizers offer modest adjunctive control for severe affective lability.
patient_plain_language: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a mental health condition characterized by intense emotional sensitivity and difficulty regulating emotions. Sufferers experience emotions like emotional third-degree burns—feeling emotional pain far more intensely and for longer than others. This leads to dramatic mood shifts, intense fears of abandonment, rocky relationships, impulsive actions, and self-harm when distress becomes overwhelming.

name: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
overview: Meniere's disease is an inner ear disorder pathologically characterized by endolymphatic hydrops (fluid distension of the endolymphatic system in the cochlea and vestibular labyrinth). The definitive diagnostic criteria established by AAO-HNS and the Bárány Society require: (1) two or more spontaneous episodes of rotational vertigo lasting between 20 minutes and 12 hours; (2) audiometrically documented low-to-medium frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the affected ear on at least one occasion before, during, or after an episode; and (3) fluctuating aural fullness or tinnitus in the affected ear. First-line conservative management with dietary sodium restriction (<1,500-2,000 mg/day) and oral diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide/triamterene) or betahistine reduces vertigo attack frequency in >70-80% of patients. Intratympanic dexamethasone or gentamicin is effective in refractory cases.
patient_plain_language: Meniere's disease is an inner ear disorder caused by excess fluid pressure building up inside the hearing and balance chambers of your inner ear. This fluid buildup triggers sudden attacks of violent room-spinning dizziness (vertigo) that last for hours, accompanied by nausea, a roaring sound in your ear (tinnitus), a clogged feeling of pressure in the ear, and temporary loss of low-pitched hearing.

name: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL)
overview: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL) is an otologic emergency defined as a rapid sensorineural hearing loss of >=30 decibels (dB) across at least 3 contiguous audiometric frequencies occurring within a 72-hour window. Approximately 90% of cases are idiopathic, with vascular ischemia, viral labyrinthitis, or cochlear autoimmune reactions implicated. Immediate initiation of high-dose systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, maximum 60 mg daily for 7-14 days followed by a taper) or intratympanic corticosteroid injections (dexamethasone 10-24 mg/mL or methylprednisolone) within the first 14 days achieves meaningful hearing recovery in 65-80% of patients. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) within 1 month of onset provides significant additional hearing gain (odds ratio 1.43). Gadolinium-enhanced brain MRI of the internal auditory canal (IAC) is mandatory to rule out vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma, found in 3-5%).
patient_plain_language: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (often called sudden deafness) is an ear emergency where you suddenly wake up with one ear completely blocked or hearing muffled, or notice the hearing vanish over a few hours. Many people mistakenly think their ear is just plugged with earwax or water, but it is actually damage to the nerve hair cells in your inner ear. Beginning steroid treatment within the first few days gives you the highest chance of getting your hearing back permanently.

name: Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION)
overview: Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION) is infarction of the optic nerve head supplied by the short posterior ciliary arteries, presenting as sudden, painless, unilateral vision loss accompanied by optic disc edema. It is critically bifurcated into: (1) Arteritic AION (A-AION, accounting for 10-15%), an ophthalmic emergency caused by Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) in patients >=50 years, marked by high ESR (>50-100 mm/h) and elevated CRP; and (2) Non-Arteritic AION (NA-AION, 85-90%), driven by nocturnal arterial hypotension and microvascular hypoperfusion in structurally crowded optic discs ('disc-at-risk': small or absent optic cup). Visual field testing classically reveals an inferior altitudinal visual field defect. In A-AION, emergent high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days) is mandatory to prevent fellow eye blindness (which occurs in up to 50% within days if untreated).
patient_plain_language: Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION) is often described as a 'stroke of the optic nerve'. The small blood vessels carrying oxygen to the optic nerve (the main visual cable transmitting images from your eye to your brain) suddenly become blocked. This causes sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye, typically leaving the lower or upper half of your vision completely dark.

name: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)
overview: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) is an acute ischemic stroke of the eye, characterized by sudden, painless, profound monocular vision loss (visual acuity counting fingers or worse in >90%). Fundoscopy reveals a pale, edematous retina with the classic 'cherry-red spot' at the fovea (where the thin foveal retina allows the underlying red choroid to shine through). The AHA scientific statement emphasizes that CRAO must be triaged as an acute ischemic stroke code; the retina suffers irreversible ischemic infarction within 240 minutes (4 hours) of complete occlusion. Over 70% of CRAO patients have concurrent high-grade ipsilateral carotid artery stenosis or cardioembolic sources. Emergency intravenous thrombolysis (IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg) within 4.5 hours of symptom onset produces visual recovery in 37% vs 17% conventional conservative therapy (p=0.002).
patient_plain_language: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is an eye stroke. Just like an ischemic stroke in the brain, a small traveling blood clot gets stuck in the main artery supplying blood and oxygen to your retina (the visual film lining the back of your eye). This causes sudden, painless blindness in one eye, like a dark window shade pulling shut. It is a critical medical emergency requiring immediate emergency room stroke evaluation.

name: Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment
overview: Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RRD) is an ophthalmic surgical emergency occurring when a full-thickness retinal tear or break (rhegma), most commonly triggered by posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) or lattice degeneration in myopic eyes, allows liquefied vitreous fluid to dissect into the subretinal space, separating the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Cardinal premonitory symptoms include sudden photopsia (flashes of light), sudden shower of black floaters, and a progressive dark peripheral curtain/shadow advancing toward the central vision. In the primary repair of uncomplicated RRD, surgical reattachment via pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) or scleral buckle achieves primary anatomic reattachment in >85-90% of cases and final attachment in >95%. Preserving visual acuity depends critically on whether the macula is still attached ('macula-on' status).
patient_plain_language: A retinal detachment occurs when the thin, light-sensitive tissue at the back of your eye (the retina) peels away from its normal position and blood supply, like wallpaper peeling off a damp wall. It often begins with sudden bursts of flashing lights and a shower of dark floating specks, followed by a dark shadow or curtain spreading across your field of vision. Prompt surgical repair is needed to prevent permanent blindness.

name: IgA Nephropathy (Berger's Disease)
overview: In the landmark multicenter Phase 3 TESTING trial (n=503 patients with IgA nephropathy, proteinuria >=1 g/day, and eGFR 20-120 mL/min/1.73m2 despite optimized renin-angiotensin system blockade), reduced-dose oral methylprednisolone (0.4 mg/kg/day with Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis) significantly reduced the primary composite renal outcome (40% eGFR decline, end-stage kidney disease [ESKD], or renal death) by 47% compared with placebo over 4.2 years (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.39-0.72; p<0.001). Targeted-release budesonide (Nefecon, NefIgArd trial) and dual endothelin/angiotensin receptor antagonists (sparsentan, PROTECT trial) achieve robust proteinuria reduction (>40%) and preserve eGFR.
patient_plain_language: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) is an autoimmune kidney disease where an abnormal form of an antibody called Immunoglobulin A (IgA)—which normally protects you from throat and lung infections—clumps together and gets trapped in the microscopic filters of your kidneys (glomeruli). This causes inflammation, microscopic bleeding into the urine (often turning urine pink or tea-colored during a cold), and slow kidney scarring.

name: Membranous Nephropathy
overview: Primary Membranous Nephropathy (pMN) is an autoimmune podocytopathy and the leading cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults, driven in 70-80% by circulating autoantibodies against the M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R1-Ab) or thrombospondin type-1 domain-containing 7A (anti-THSD7A-Ab). In the landmark randomized MENTOR trial (n=130 patients with proteinuria >=5 g/day despite 3 months of RAS blockade), intravenous rituximab (1,000 mg on days 1 and 15, repeated at 6 months if proteinuria declined by >25%) was noninferior to cyclosporine at 12 months and vastly superior at 24 months in maintaining complete or partial clinical remission (60% rituximab vs 20% cyclosporine; p<0.001). Relapse rates were dramatically lower with rituximab (5% vs 46%). Monitoring anti-PLA2R antibody titers predicts clinical proteinuria remission by 3-6 months.
patient_plain_language: Membranous nephropathy is an autoimmune kidney disease where your body produces antibodies (most commonly anti-PLA2R antibodies) that attack the outside surface of your kidney's filtering units. The filters become thickened and leaky, allowing large amounts of protein (albumin) to spill out into your urine. Losing this protein causes fluid to pool in your body, producing heavy swelling (edema) in your legs, ankles, and face.

name: Minimal Change Disease
overview: Minimal Change Disease (MCD) is the predominant cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (70-90%) and accounts for 10-15% of adult nephrotic syndrome. It is characterized clinically by abrupt-onset massive selective proteinuria (predominantly albuminuria), profound hypoalbuminemia (<2.5 g/dL), severe generalized anasarca, and hypercholesterolemia, with normal blood pressure and preserved eGFR. Light microscopy reveals normal-appearing glomeruli, immunofluorescence is negative for immune complexes, and electron microscopy demonstrates pathognomonic diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes. Oral corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, max 80 mg daily) achieve complete remission in >90% of children (within 4 weeks) and 75-80% of adults (within 12-16 weeks), though 50-70% experience steroid-dependent or frequent relapses requiring calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/cyclosporine) or rituximab.
patient_plain_language: Minimal change disease is a kidney condition that causes your kidneys to suddenly leak massive amounts of protein into your urine. When viewed under an ordinary optical microscope, the kidney filters look almost completely normal (minimal change). However, under a powerful electron microscope, the tiny interlocking foot-like cells (podocytes) that act as the kidney's strainer are swollen and flattened out. Fortunately, it usually responds very quickly to steroid medication.

name: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
overview: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a clinicopathologic pattern of podocyte injury characterized by sclerosis in portions (segmental) of some (focal) glomeruli, categorized by the Columbia classification into collapsing, tip, cellular, perihilar, and not-otherwise-specified (NOS) variants. In the multicenter randomized double-blind Phase 2/3 DUET trial (n=109 patients with biopsy-proven primary FSGS), the first-in-class dual endothelin type A and angiotensin II receptor antagonist sparsentan produced a significantly greater reduction in proteinuria at 8 weeks compared with active irbesartan control (-45% vs -19%; p=0.006), with 28% achieving complete or partial remission (vs 9% irbesartan; p=0.02). Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine/tacrolimus) achieve remission in 50-60% of steroid-resistant primary FSGS. Secondary/adaptive FSGS (driven by hyperfiltration from obesity, reduced nephron mass, or reflux) is non-immunologic and managed with maximal hemodynamic RAS/SGLT2 inhibition.
patient_plain_language: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a kidney disease that causes scarring in the microscopic filters of your kidneys. 'Focal' means only some of the filters are damaged, and 'segmental' means only a section of each filter is scarred. Because the filters are scarred and torn, protein leaks out into your urine, causing heavy swelling in your legs and belly, high cholesterol, and gradual decline in kidney function.

name: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)
overview: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) is the most common monogenic kidney disorder, caused by mutations in PKD1 (chromosome 16, 78% of cases, more severe with median ESKD age 58) or PKD2 (chromosome 4, 15%, median ESKD age 79), leading to progressive cystogenesis that destroys renal parenchyma. In the landmark Phase 3 TEMPO 3:4 trial (n=1445 patients with total kidney volume [TKV] >=750 mL and CrCl >=60 mL/min), tolvaptan (a selective vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist, titrated to 45/15 to 90/30 mg daily) significantly slowed the annual rate of TKV growth over 3 years (2.8% per year vs 5.5% with placebo; p<0.001) and significantly reduced annual eGFR decline (-2.72 vs -3.70 mL/min/1.73m2; p<0.001). The REPRISE trial confirmed preserved eGFR benefit in later-stage disease (eGFR 25-65 mL/min/1.73m2). Baseline Mayo Classification (Classes 1A-1E based on height-adjusted TKV) reliably predicts rapid disease progression.
patient_plain_language: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is an inherited genetic condition that causes hundreds of fluid-filled cysts to grow and enlarge inside your kidneys over time. As the cysts multiply and expand, the kidneys can grow to the size of footballs, crowding out healthy kidney tissue and causing high blood pressure, flank pain, kidney stones, and gradual kidney failure. Each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the gene.

name: Lupus Nephritis
overview: Lupus nephritis (LN) is a major organ-threatening manifestation of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), occurring in up to 50% of patients and classified by ISN/RPS into Classes I through VI (Class III focal and Class IV diffuse proliferative carrying the highest risk of progression to end-stage renal disease). In the landmark Phase 3 BLISS-LN trial (n=448 patients with active Class III, IV, or V LN receiving standard therapy with mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide), adding intravenous belimumab (a BLyS/BAFF inhibitor, 10 mg/kg) significantly increased Primary Efficacy Renal Response at 2 years compared with standard therapy alone (43% vs 32%; odds ratio 1.6; 95% CI 1.0-2.3; p=0.03) and halved the risk of a renal-related event or death (hazard ratio 0.51; p=0.001). The Phase 3 AURORA trial demonstrated that adding voclosporin (a novel calcineurin inhibitor) to mycophenolate doubled the complete renal response rate at 1 year (41% vs 23%; p<0.0001).
patient_plain_language: Lupus nephritis is kidney inflammation caused by systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), an autoimmune disease. In lupus, your immune system generates autoantibodies that mistakenly attack your own organs. When these antibody complexes lodge inside your kidney's filters, they cause swelling, inflammation, protein leakage, and high blood pressure. Left untreated, it can permanently scar the kidneys.

name: ANCA-Associated Vasculitis (Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis)
overview: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener's) and Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA) are necrotizing small-vessel vasculitides associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (PR3-ANCA / c-ANCA in 85% of GPA; MPO-ANCA / p-ANCA in 70% of MPA). In the landmark Phase 3 ADVOCATE trial (n=330 patients with active ANCA vasculitis), the oral complement C5a receptor antagonist avacopan (30 mg BID) was noninferior to prednisone at week 26 and significantly superior to standard tapering prednisone in achieving sustained disease remission at 52 weeks (Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score [BVAS] of 0 without relapse: 65.7% vs 54.9%; difference 12.5 percentage points; 95% CI 2.6-22.3; p=0.007 for superiority). Avacopan also significantly improved eGFR (+7.3 vs +4.1 mL/min/1.73m2; p=0.029) and eliminated glucocorticoid-related toxicity. In the RAVE trial, Rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 doses) was proven noninferior to cyclophosphamide for induction and superior in relapsing disease (67% vs 42%; p=0.01).
patient_plain_language: ANCA-associated vasculitis (such as Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis) is an autoimmune disorder where your immune system produces abnormal autoantibodies called ANCA that cause severe swelling and inflammation in your small blood vessels. The inflammation attacks blood vessels in your nose, sinuses, lungs, and kidneys. Symptoms often start like a severe sinus infection with bloody crusting, coughing up blood, and rapid kidney inflammation.

name: Ankylosing Spondylitis (Axial Spondyloarthritis)
overview: Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS / radiographic axial spondyloarthritis) is a chronic inflammatory arthritis predominantly affecting the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints, strongly associated with HLA-B27 (>85-90%). Inflammatory back pain criteria (Calin/ASAS criteria: onset <45 years, insidious onset, improvement with exercise, no improvement with rest, pain at night) distinguish it from mechanical back pain. Pelvic radiography demonstrating bilateral Grade >=2 or unilateral Grade >=3 sacroiliitis (modified New York criteria) or active sacroiliac bone marrow edema on STIR MRI confirms the diagnosis. In the landmark Phase 3 MEASURE 1 and 2 trials (n=590 patients), secukinumab (an anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody, 150 mg subcutaneous) significantly improved ASAS20 response rates at week 16 compared with placebo (61% vs 28%; p<0.001) and sustained clinical remission and spinal mobility out to 5 years. First-line therapy with continuous NSAIDs reduces radiographic spinal syndesmophyte progression.
patient_plain_language: Ankylosing spondylitis is an inflammatory arthritis that primarily attacks the joints of your spine and pelvis (sacroiliac joints). Unlike ordinary mechanical back pain that gets worse with exercise, ankylosing spondylitis causes deep lower back stiffness that feels worst when resting in bed and dramatically improves after you get up and move around. Over years, the chronic inflammation can cause the spinal vertebrae to fuse together into a stiff 'bamboo spine'.

name: Psoriatic Arthritis
overview: Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) is a multifaceted inflammatory musculoskeletal disease occurring in up to 30% of patients with plaque psoriasis, involving six clinical domains: peripheral arthritis (often asymmetric, involving distal interphalangeal [DIP] joints), axial disease, enthesitis (inflammation at tendon insertion sites, e.g. Achilles tendonitis), dactylitis ('sausage digits'), skin psoriasis, and nail dystrophy (nail pitting and onycholysis in >80%). Classification Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis (CASPAR score >=3) provides 91% sensitivity and 99% specificity. In the landmark Phase 3 DISCOVER-2 trial (n=739 biologic-naive patients with active PsA), the IL-23 p19-subunit inhibitor guselkumab (100 mg SC every 4 or 8 weeks) significantly improved ACR20 response rates at week 24 compared with placebo (64% vs 33%; p<0.0001) with marked complete clearance of skin psoriasis (PASI 90 in 70%), resolution of dactylitis/enthesitis, and significant inhibition of radiographic joint destruction.
patient_plain_language: Psoriatic arthritis is an autoimmune condition that causes joint pain, swelling, and stiffness in people who have the skin condition psoriasis. It causes painful inflammation in your finger and toe joints, swollen 'sausage-like' fingers and toes (dactylitis), tender heels where the Achilles tendon attaches, and pitted, crumbly fingernails. Early treatment prevents permanent joint damage.

name: Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma)
overview: Systemic Sclerosis (SSc / Scleroderma) is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by microvascular obliteration, immune activation, and widespread progressive tissue fibrosis of the skin and internal organs. Subdivided into Limited Cutaneous SSc (lcSSc: CREST syndrome; anti-centromere antibodies [ACA] in 60-80%; high risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension) and Diffuse Cutaneous SSc (dcSSc: skin thickening proximal to elbows/knees; anti-Scl-70/topoisomerase I or anti-RNA polymerase III; high risk of interstitial lung disease and scleroderma renal crisis). In the landmark Phase 3 SENSCIS trial (n=576 patients with SSc-ILD), the intracellular tyrosine kinase inhibitor nintedanib (150 mg BID) significantly reduced the annual rate of decline in Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) by 44% compared with placebo (-52.4 mL/year vs -93.3 mL/year; difference 41.0 mL/year; 95% CI 2.9-79.0; p=0.04). In early progressive dcSSc, tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) preserves lung function.
patient_plain_language: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is an autoimmune disorder that causes your body to produce far too much collagen, a tough scar-like protein. Extra collagen builds up in your skin, blood vessels, and internal organs. It causes the skin on your fingers, hands, and face to become tight, hard, and shiny, makes fingers turn white in the cold (Raynaud's), causes chronic acid reflux, and can cause stiff scarring in your lungs.

name: Sjögren's Syndrome
overview: Primary Sjögren's Syndrome is a systemic autoimmune exocrinopathy characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of salivary and lacrimal glands, resulting in classic sicca syndrome (xerophthalmia [dry eyes] and xerostomia [dry mouth]). Diagnostic classification requires a weighted score >=4 based on: positive anti-SSA/Ro antibodies (weight 3); labial salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with focus score >=1 focus per 4 mm2 (weight 3); ocular staining score >=5 or van Bijsterveld score >=4 (weight 1); Schirmer's test <=5 mm in 5 minutes (weight 1); and unstimulated whole saliva flow rate <=0.1 mL/min (weight 1). Patients face a 15- to 20-fold increased lifetime risk of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (predominantly MALT lymphoma in parotid glands), heralded by persistent parotid swelling, purpura, monoclonal gammopathy, and low complement C4.
patient_plain_language: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune disease where your body's immune system attacks its own moisture-producing glands, primarily the tear glands in your eyes and the saliva glands in your mouth. This leads to chronic, severe dry eyes (feeling like grit or sand is trapped under your eyelids), dry mouth (difficulty swallowing dry crackers or speaking without sipping water), rampant tooth decay, and joint stiffness.

name: Dermatomyositis & Polymyositis
overview: Dermatomyositis (DM) and Polymyositis (PM) are idiopathic inflammatory myopathies characterized by symmetric, progressive, proximal muscle weakness (neck flexors, deltoids, hip flexors) and elevated skeletal muscle enzymes (creatine kinase [CK] typically 10-50x ULN, aldolase, LDH). Dermatomyositis features pathognomonic cutaneous signs: heliotrope rash (violaceous erythema with periorbital edema), Gottron's papules (violaceous scaly papules over MCP and PIP joints), and shawl/V-sign rashes. In the landmark international Phase 3 ProDERM trial (n=95 patients with active dermatomyositis), high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 2.0 g/kg every 4 weeks for 16 weeks) achieved a Total Improvement Score (TIS) >=20 in 78.7% of patients compared with 43.8% on placebo (difference 34.9 percentage points; 95% CI 16.7-52.8; p=0.001) with marked recovery in muscle strength (MMT-8) and skin disease (CDASI). Extensive age-appropriate cancer screening (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, mammography, colonoscopy) is mandatory, as DM carries a 5- to 6-fold increased risk of paraneoplastic malignancy (particularly with anti-TIF1-gamma or anti-NXP2 autoantibodies).
patient_plain_language: Dermatomyositis is a rare inflammatory disease marked by muscle weakness and distinctive skin rashes. Your immune system attacks blood vessels and muscle fibers, causing weakness in the muscles closest to the center of your body—making it hard to lift your arms to wash your hair, climb stairs, or stand up from a deep chair. In dermatomyositis, it also causes a reddish-purple rash around the eyelids (heliotrope rash) and purple bumps across the knuckles (Gottron's papules).

name: Behçet's Disease
overview: Behçet's disease is a variable-vessel systemic vasculitis characterized by recurrent, painful aphthous oral ulcers (present in >98%), recurrent genital ulcers, cutaneous lesions (erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis), and sight-threatening posterior uveitis / retinal vasculitis. International Criteria for Behçet's Disease (ICBD score >=4) provides 94% sensitivity and 96% specificity; strong genetic association with HLA-B*51. Pathergy testing (sterile pustule developing 24-48h after skin needle prick) is highly specific. In the multicenter double-blind Phase 3 RELIEF trial (n=207 patients with active oral ulcers), the oral phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor apremilast (30 mg BID) significantly reduced the daily area under the curve for number of oral ulcers over 12 weeks compared with placebo (129.5 vs 222.1; p<0.001) and cleared oral ulcers in 52.9% vs 22.3% (p<0.001) with marked pain relief. In sight-threatening uveitis, TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab/adalimumab) achieve remission in >85%.
patient_plain_language: Behçet's disease is a rare autoimmune disorder that causes inflammation in blood vessels throughout your body. The most common hallmark is having recurrent, painful canker sores in your mouth that look like normal ulcers but occur frequently and take longer to heal. It also causes painful ulcers in the genital area, acne-like skin bumps, swollen joints, and inflammation inside the eye that can threaten vision if not treated promptly.

name: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN)
overview: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN) is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized and small muscular arteries, classically sparing the venous system, pulmonary arteries, and glomeruli (not ANCA-associated). A significant subset is secondary to chronic Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Pathology shows transmural fibrinoid necrosis and segmental aneurysmal dilatations with thrombosis. Catheter-directed visceral angiography or CT angiography characteristically demonstrates multiple microaneurysms and arterial occlusions ('string-of-beads' appearance) in mesenteric, renal, and hepatic vasculatures. Clinical hallmarks include mononeuritis multiplex (asymmetric foot/wrist drop in >60%), livedo reticularis, testicular pain, and renovascular hypertension. Prognosis is stratified using the Five-Factor Score (FFS: proteinuria >1g/day, renal insufficiency, cardiomyopathy, severe GI involvement, CNS involvement). Remission is achieved in >80% with combined high-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide.
patient_plain_language: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a serious autoimmune condition where your immune system attacks and inflames medium-sized blood vessels in your body, particularly in your nerves, kidneys, skin, and bowels. As the inflamed artery walls weaken, tiny balloon-like pouches (aneurysms) form along the blood vessels like beads on a string, cutting off blood flow. Common signs include severe nerve pain and sudden weakness (like being unable to lift your foot, called foot drop), deep muscle aches, and purplish lace-like skin discoloration.

name: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (IgA Vasculitis)
overview: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP, now classified as IgA Vasculitis [IgAV]) is the most common systemic vasculitis of childhood (over 90% of cases in children <10 years), characterized by immune complex deposition of galactose-deficient IgA1 in small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles). The validated EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria mandate palpable purpura (non-thrombocytopenic petechiae and raised purpura distributed predominantly on dependent lower extremities and buttocks) plus at least one of four features: (1) acute diffuse colicky abdominal pain; (2) any biopsy showing predominant IgA deposition; (3) acute arthritis or arthralgia; and (4) renal involvement (hematuria >5 RBCs/HPF, red blood cell casts, or proteinuria >0.3 g/24h). The disease is self-limiting in >85% of cases within 4 to 8 weeks. Long-term morbidity is entirely determined by the severity of nephritis (HSP nephritis), which develops in 30-50% and requires longitudinal urinalysis surveillance.
patient_plain_language: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is an illness that causes tiny blood vessels in the skin, joints, intestines, and kidneys to become swollen and leaky. It often strikes children and young adults a couple of weeks after a simple cold or respiratory virus. The classic sign is a raised, bumpy, reddish-purple spotted rash (palpable purpura) on the legs and buttocks, accompanied by aching knees and ankles and crampy belly pain.

name: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (Hypermobile & Vascular)
overview: Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes (EDS) are a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of hereditary connective tissue disorders characterized by joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, and generalized tissue fragility. Hypermobile EDS (hEDS) is the most prevalent, diagnosed clinically using the 2017 International Consortium criteria (Beighton generalized hypermobility score >=5 in adults, soft/velvety hyperextensible skin, piezogenic papules, recurrent joint subluxations, and chronic musculoskeletal pain). Vascular EDS (vEDS) is the severe life-threatening subtype caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the COL3A1 gene (type III procollagen), characterized by translucent thin skin, easy bruising, and spontaneous arterial dissections/ruptures (aorta, iliac, mesenteric, carotid) or hollow organ perforation (colon, gravid uterus). In the landmark randomized BBEST trial in vEDS (n=53), the cardioselective beta-blocker with beta-2 agonist properties celiprolol (up to 400 mg daily) significantly reduced the composite endpoint of arterial rupture, dissection, or death by 64% over 5 years (hazard ratio 0.36; 95% CI 0.15-0.88; p=0.018).
patient_plain_language: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) is a group of inherited genetic conditions that affect collagen, the fibrous 'glue' that gives strength and support to your joints, skin, ligaments, and blood vessels. In hypermobile EDS, joints are extremely loose and flexible ('double-jointed'), easily popping out of place, accompanied by chronic pain and velvety skin. In the rare vascular type, blood vessel walls are fragile, requiring careful blood pressure control to protect internal arteries.

name: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
overview: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS, formerly Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy [CRPS Type 1] and Causalgia [CRPS Type 2 with defined major nerve lesion]) is a debilitating chronic neuropathic pain condition, typically developing after a limb trauma, fracture, or surgery, characterized by continuing pain disproportionate in time or degree to the inciting event. The validated IASP Budapest Clinical Diagnostic Criteria (sensitivity 99%, specificity 68%) require continuing disproportionate pain plus at least 1 symptom in 3 of 4 categories and at least 1 sign in 2 of 4 categories: (1) Sensory: hyperalgesia or allodynia; (2) Vasomotor: temperature asymmetry (>1°C) or skin color changes; (3) Sudomotor/Edema: edema or sweating changes; (4) Motor/Trophic: decreased range of motion, motor weakness, tremor, or dystonia, and abnormal hair, nail, or skin trophic changes. Early functional physical therapy combined with graded motor imagery (GMI) and mirror therapy reduces pain scores significantly.
patient_plain_language: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is a severe, chronic nerve pain condition that usually develops in an arm or leg after an injury, sprain, fracture, or surgery. The pain is far more intense, burning, and longer-lasting than the original injury. The affected limb becomes hypersensitive to touch (even a light bedsheet brushing against the skin feels agonizing), swells, changes color (turning red, purple, or mottled), and feels hot or ice-cold compared to the other limb.

research_papers.key_findings: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS, formerly Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy [CRPS Type 1] and Causalgia [CRPS Type 2 with defined major nerve lesion]) is a debilitating chronic neuropathic pain condition, typically developing after a limb trauma, fracture, or surgery, characterized by continuing pain disproportionate in time or degree to the inciting event. name: Cervical Radiculopathy (Cervical Spondylosis)
overview: Cervical radiculopathy is neurological dysfunction caused by mechanical compression or inflammatory irritation of a cervical spinal nerve root, most commonly resulting from cervical disk herniation (20-25%) or degenerative foraminal stenosis from uncovertebral/facet spondylosis (70-75%), predominantly involving C6 (biceps reflex, thumb sensation, wrist extension) and C7 (triceps reflex, middle finger sensation, elbow extension). Clinical provocative testing (Spurling's neck compression test [specificity 93%], shoulder abduction relief test [Bakody sign, specificity 90%], and upper limb tension test of Elvey [sensitivity 97%]) has high diagnostic accuracy. In high-quality randomized trials, conservative multimodal therapy (cervical mechanical traction, physical therapy, short-course NSAIDs/oral steroids) resolves radicular symptoms in 75-90% of patients without surgery over 2 to 3 months. Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) achieves rapid, reliable pain relief in refractory cases.
patient_plain_language: Cervical radiculopathy, commonly called a 'pinched nerve in the neck', occurs when a nerve root leaving your spinal cord in your neck is squeezed or irritated by a bulging spinal disc or arthritic bone spur. This pinched nerve sends sharp, electric, shooting pain, numbness, and tingling travelling down your neck and shoulder, through your arm, and into your fingers.

name: Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder)
overview: Adhesive Capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is a progressive fibro-inflammatory contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule, characterized by capsular thickening, volume reduction, and obliteration of the axillary recess, strongly associated with diabetes mellitus (prevalence up to 20%), thyroid disorders, and prolonged immobilization. It progresses classically through 3 distinct phases: (1) Freezing phase (2-9 months, severe pain worse at night); (2) Frozen phase (4-12 months, profound restriction of both active AND passive glenohumeral motion in a capsular pattern [external rotation > abduction > internal rotation]); and (3) Thawing phase (5-24 months, gradual restoration of motion). Cochrane systematic reviews confirm that ultrasound-guided intra-articular corticosteroid injection (triamcinolone 40 mg) combined with gentle home stretching provides superior early pain relief and functional motion recovery compared with physical therapy alone (standardized mean difference -0.73; p<0.001). Image-guided capsular distension (hydrodilatation) provides rapid capsular mechanical stretching.
patient_plain_language: Adhesive capsulitis, commonly known as 'frozen shoulder', is a condition where the strong connective tissue capsule surrounding your shoulder joint becomes thick, tight, and severely inflamed. The capsule shrinks and loses its normal lubricating fluid, making the shoulder joint physically 'freeze' in place. It becomes agonizingly painful to reach overhead, fasten a seatbelt, or put your arm through a jacket sleeve, and the arm cannot be moved even when someone else gently tries to lift it for you.

name: Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome (Trochanteric Bursitis)
overview: Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome (GTPS, formerly trochanteric bursitis) is an umbrella term encompassing gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy, partial or full-thickness tears, and trochanteric bursal inflammation, predominantly affecting women aged >50. Diagnostic hallmark is point tenderness elicited directly over the greater trochanter of the femur, exacerbated by lying on the affected side, prolonged standing, single-leg stance for 30 seconds (reproduction of pain, sensitivity 100%), and resisted hip abduction in 90 degrees flexion. In the landmark randomized clinical trial (n=204 patients), load management education plus targeted isometric/eccentric gluteal strengthening exercises achieved superior global recovery at 1 year compared with corticosteroid injection (78% vs 58%; difference 20 percentage points; 95% CI 7-34; p=0.003) and had a vastly lower recurrence rate. Radial extracorporeal shockwave therapy (rESWT) provides significant clinical improvement in recalcitrant tendinopathy.
patient_plain_language: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (often called trochanteric bursitis) is a condition that causes sharp or aching pain on the outside of your hip and upper thigh. While previously thought to just be an inflamed fluid sac (bursa), it is most often caused by wear-and-tear or micro-tears in the strong gluteal hip tendons that anchor your buttock muscles to the hip bone. The pain is triggered by lying on that side in bed, climbing stairs, or walking long distances.

name: Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)
overview: Primary Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an acquired autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100,000/mcL) resulting from antibody-mediated platelet destruction and impaired megakaryocyte thrombopoiesis. In the landmark multicenter double-blind Phase 3 RAISE trial (n=197 patients with chronic refractory ITP), the oral thrombopoietin receptor agonist (TPO-RA) eltrombopag (50-75 mg daily) maintained target platelet counts between 50,000 and 400,000/mcL in 79% of patients vs 28% placebo (odds ratio 8.2; 95% CI 3.6-18.7; p<0.0001). Eltrombopag reduced clinically significant bleeding by 76% (HR 0.24; p=0.0002) and allowed 59% of patients to discontinue or reduce concomitant steroids. ASH guidelines recommend first-line corticosteroids (dexamethasone 40 mg daily for 4 days or prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) or IVIG for platelet counts <20,000-30,000/mcL with bleeding.
patient_plain_language: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune blood condition where your immune system mistakenly destroys your body's platelets (tiny cell fragments that stick together to form blood clots and stop bleeding). Because your platelet count drops far below normal, you bruise easily, develop clusters of tiny red or purple pinpoint spots under your skin (petechiae), and experience frequent nosebleeds or heavy gums.

In the landmark multicenter double-blind Phase 3 RAISE trial (n=197 patients with chronic refractory ITP), the oral thrombopoietin receptor agonist (TPO-RA) eltrombopag (50-75 mg daily) maintained target platelet counts between 50,000 and 400,000/mcL in 79% of patients vs 28% placebo (odds ratio 8.2; 95% CI 3.6-18.7; p<0.0001). Eltrombopag reduced clinically significant bleeding by 76% (HR 0.24; p=0.0002) and allowed 59% of patients to discontinue or reduce concomitant steroids. ASH guidelines recommend first-line corticosteroids (dexamethasone 40 mg daily for 4 days or prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) or IVIG for platelet counts <20,000-30,000/mcL with bleeding.

name: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)
overview: Immune Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (iTTP) is a life-threatening hematologic emergency characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA with abundant schistocytes on blood smear) and severe consumptive thrombocytopenia, driven by acquired autoantibodies neutralizing the von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease ADAMTS13 (activity <10%). Ultra-large vWF multimers spontaneously bind platelets, producing widespread microvascular thrombi that cause organ ischemia (brain, heart, kidneys). In the landmark Phase 3 HERCULES trial (n=145 patients), the anti-vWF nanobody caplacizumab (10 mg daily) added to plasma exchange (PEX) and immunosuppression significantly accelerated time to platelet count normalization (rate ratio 1.55; p=0.01) and reduced the composite endpoint of TTP-related death, recurrence, or major thromboembolic event by 74% (12.7% vs 49.3%; p<0.001) while eliminating refractory disease (0% vs 4.2%). Mortality without immediate PEX exceeds 90%, dropping to <10-15% with modern triple therapy (PEX + caplacizumab + rituximab/corticosteroids).
patient_plain_language: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a critical, life-threatening blood emergency where your immune system knocks out an enzyme called ADAMTS13. Without this molecular scissor to trim down long sticky protein ropes in your blood, tiny blood clots form in small vessels all throughout your body. These clots block blood flow to your brain and kidneys while chewing up and destroying red blood cells (hemolytic anemia) and using up all your platelets.

name: Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS)
overview: Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS) is a genetic, life-threatening thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) driven by uncontrolled chronic dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway (mutations in CFH, CFI, MCP/CD46, C3, or CFB, or autoantibodies against complement factor H). Unchecked activation of the terminal complement cascade leads to continuous endothelial cell damage, platelet consumption, and microvascular thrombosis, with profound predilection for the renal microvasculature. In prospective multicenter Phase 2/3 trials (n=67 patients), the humanized monoclonal anti-C5 antibody eculizumab produced a rapid, sustained hematologic normalization (platelets and LDH normal in 88%) and achieved a dramatic, durable improvement in renal function (eGFR increased by >=15 mL/min in 80%; 80% of dialysis-dependent patients discontinued dialysis permanently). Long-acting C5 inhibition (ravulizumab every 8 weeks) achieves equivalent complement suppression with reduced infusion frequency.
patient_plain_language: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) is a rare, severe blood and kidney disorder caused by a genetic malfunction in your immune system's 'complement' defense system. The complement system is like a chemical alarm system that attacks bacteria. In aHUS, the off-switch is broken, so the system stays stuck in the 'attack' mode, destroying healthy blood cells and creating tiny blood clots that rapidly shut down your kidneys.

name: Polycythemia Vera
overview: Polycythemia Vera (PV) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm driven in >95-98% by a gain-of-function somatic mutation in JAK2 (V617F in exon 14, or exon 12 mutations), resulting in autonomous trilineage bone marrow proliferation, marked erythrocytosis, and hyperviscosity. The WHO diagnostic criteria require: elevated hemoglobin (>16.5 g/dL in men, >16.0 g/dL in women) or hematocrit (>49% in men, >48% in women); hypercellular bone marrow with trilineage hyperplasia (panmyelosis); and presence of JAK2 mutation. In the landmark multicenter randomized Phase 3 CYTO-PV trial (n=365 patients), maintaining a strict hematocrit target <45% via therapeutic phlebotomy and cytoreduction significantly reduced the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death or major thrombosis by 73% compared with a hematocrit target of 45-50% (hazard ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.11-0.66; p=0.007). In hydroxyurea-resistant patients, the JAK1/2 inhibitor ruxolitinib achieved hematocrit control without phlebotomy in 60% vs 20% control (RESPONSE trial, p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: Polycythemia vera is a rare, slow-growing blood cancer where your bone marrow produces far too many red blood cells. The extra red blood cells thicken your blood like sludge, slowing down circulation and making it much more likely for dangerous blood clots to form in your brain, heart, or legs. Classic symptoms include a reddish or purplish face, burning pain in hands and feet, and intense, stinging skin itching immediately after a warm bath or shower (aquagenic pruritus).

name: Essential Thrombocythemia (ET)
overview: Essential Thrombocythemia (ET) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by sustained megakaryocytic proliferation, thrombocytosis (platelets >=450,000/mcL), and an elevated risk of arterial/venous thrombosis and hemorrhagic complications (due to acquired von Willebrand syndrome at platelet counts >1,000,000/mcL). Mutational driver landscape comprises JAK2 V617F (55-60%), calreticulin (CALR exon 9 indels, 25-30%, associated with lower thrombosis risk and higher platelet counts), and MPL W515 (3-5%). In the landmark multicenter randomized PT1 trial (n=809 high-risk ET patients), hydroxyurea plus low-dose aspirin was significantly superior to anagrelide plus aspirin in preventing arterial thrombosis (odds ratio 0.43; p=0.004), major hemorrhage (OR 0.39; p=0.003), and myelofibrotic transformation (OR 0.36; p=0.01), establishing hydroxyurea as the first-line cytoreductive standard.
patient_plain_language: Essential thrombocythemia (ET) is a rare blood disorder where your bone marrow produces too many platelets. Platelets are the cell fragments responsible for forming blood clots. Having too many platelets can cause them to clump together and block blood vessels, causing blood clots in your brain, heart, or legs. Paradoxically, if platelet counts climb extremely high (over one million), they can consume clotting proteins and cause unusual bleeding.

name: Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS)
overview: Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS) are a heterogeneous group of clonal hematopoietic stem cell neoplasms characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis, peripheral blood cytopenias (refractory anemia in >85%), prominent morphological dysplasia in bone marrow lineages, and a propensity for transformation into acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Prognosis is established via the Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R) based on marrow blast percentage, cytogenetics, and cytopenia depth. In the landmark open-label Phase 3 COMMANDS trial (n=356 patients with transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS), the erythroid maturation agent luspatercept (1.0-1.75 mg/kg subcutaneous every 3 weeks) was significantly superior to epoetin alfa in achieving red blood cell transfusion independence for >=12 weeks with concurrent hemoglobin increase >=1.5 g/dL (58.5% vs 31.2%; p<0.0001). In higher-risk MDS (IPSS-R >3.5), the hypomethylating agent azacitidine (75 mg/m2/day for 7 days every 28 days) prolongs median overall survival compared with conventional care (24.5 vs 15.0 months; hazard ratio 0.58; p=0.0001; AZA-001).
patient_plain_language: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of bone marrow disorders sometimes described as 'bone marrow failure'. Your bone marrow produces defective, immature blood cells that die prematurely inside the marrow instead of maturing into healthy red cells, white cells, and platelets. This causes chronic severe fatigue from anemia, frequent infections due to low white blood cells, and easy bruising. Some forms can progress into acute leukemia.

name: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)
overview: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) and Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL) are mature B-cell clonal lymphoproliferative neoplasms characterized by absolute monoclonal B-lymphocytosis (>=5,000/mcL for >=3 months) co-expressing CD5, CD19, CD20 (dim), and CD23, with surface immunoglobulin light chain restriction. High-risk genomic markers include TP53 deletion (del[17p]) or mutation, and unmutated IGHV status. In the landmark Phase 3 ELEVATE-TN trial (n=535 treatment-naive CLL patients), continuous monotherapy with the second-generation selective Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor acalabrutinib (100 mg BID) significantly prolonged progression-free survival (PFS) compared with chemoimmunotherapy (24-month PFS 87% vs 47%; hazard ratio 0.20; 95% CI 0.13-0.30; p<0.0001). Fixed-duration targeted therapy with venetoclax (a BCL-2 inhibitor) plus obinutuzumab for 12 months (CLL14 trial) achieves high rates of undetectable minimal residual disease (uMRD <10^-4 in 76%) and durable 5-year progression-free survival without continuous therapy.
patient_plain_language: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a slow-growing cancer of the white blood cells (lymphocytes). The bone marrow produces abnormal, long-lived B-cells that do not fight infections properly and slowly crowd out normal blood cells. Many people with CLL have zero symptoms for years and do not need immediate treatment—a standard, safe medical approach called 'active surveillance' or watchful waiting.

name: Multiple Myeloma
overview: Multiple Myeloma is a clonal plasma cell malignancy characterized by the neoplastic proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow (>10% clonal marrow plasma cells or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) producing a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein). End-organ damage is defined by the CRAB criteria: Hypercalcemia (serum calcium >11 mg/dL), Renal insufficiency (serum Cr >2 mg/dL or eGFR <40 mL/min), Anemia (hemoglobin <10 g/dL), and Bone lesions (one or more osteolytic lesions on whole-body low-dose CT or PET/CT); or biomarker criteria (SLiM: >=60% clonal bone marrow plasma cells, involved-to-uninvolved serum free light chain [sFLC] ratio >=100, or >1 focal lesion on MRI). In the landmark Phase 3 MAIA trial (n=737 transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma patients), adding the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab to lenalidomide and dexamethasone (D-Rd) reduced the risk of disease progression or death by 44% (hazard ratio 0.56; 95% CI 0.43-0.73; p<0.001) with 5-year progression-free survival of 52.5% vs 28.7%. In transplant-eligible patients, quadruplet induction (D-RVd) followed by autologous stem cell transplantation achieves deep minimal residual disease negativity.
patient_plain_language: Multiple myeloma is a type of blood cancer that develops in plasma cells, a type of white blood cell in your bone marrow that normally makes antibodies to fight infections. In myeloma, abnormal plasma cells multiply uncontrollably and produce large amounts of a faulty antibody protein (M-protein). The myeloma cells weaken and eat away at your bones (causing bone pain and fractures), cause high calcium levels, damage your kidneys, and cause severe anemia.

name: Hodgkin Lymphoma
overview: Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma (cHL) is a B-cell-derived lymphoid malignancy characterized by binucleated or multinucleated giant Reed-Sternberg cells (CD30+, CD15+, CD20-) set within a rich inflammatory background, with a bimodal age distribution (peak in young adults aged 15-35 and >55). In the landmark multicenter randomized Phase 3 ECHELON-1 trial (n=1334 patients with stage III or IV cHL), replacing bleomycin with the antibody-drug conjugate brentuximab vedotin (A+AVD: brentuximab vedotin, doxorubicin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) significantly improved 5-year overall survival compared with standard ABVD (94.9% vs 88.9%; hazard ratio for death 0.59; 95% CI 0.40-0.88; p=0.009), while completely eliminating bleomycin-induced pulmonary toxicity. Interim PET/CT scan (Deauville 5-point score) after 2 cycles allows risk-adapted response-guided therapy.
patient_plain_language: Hodgkin lymphoma is a cancer of the lymphatic system, which is part of your body's germ-fighting immune network. Cancerous white blood cells called Reed-Sternberg cells multiply in your lymph nodes. It typically presents as a painless, firm, rubbery lump or swelling in your neck, armpit, or collarbone, accompanied by drenching night sweats, unexplained fevers, and rapid weight loss (known as 'B symptoms'). Hodgkin lymphoma is one of the most curable cancers known, with cure rates over 90%.
