name: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)
overview: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma (accounting for 30-40% of adult NHL), classified by cell of origin into Germinal Center B-cell-like (GCB) and Activated B-cell-like (ABC / non-GCB) subtypes. High-grade double-hit/triple-hit lymphomas carry concurrent MYC and BCL2/BCL6 translocations. In the landmark international Phase 3 POLARIX trial (n=879 patients with previously untreated intermediate-to-high risk DLBCL, IPI 2-5), replacing vincristine with the anti-CD79b antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Pola-R-CHP: polatuzumab, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, prednisone) significantly improved 2-year progression-free survival compared with standard R-CHOP (76.7% vs 70.2%; hazard ratio for progression, relapse, or death 0.73; 95% CI 0.57-0.95; p=0.02) and reduced the need for subsequent salvage therapies by 34%. In primary refractory or early relapsing (<12 months) DLBCL, autologous anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy (axicabtagene ciloleucel, ZUMA-7 trial) quadrupled event-free survival compared with standard salvage chemotherapy and autologous transplant (HR 0.40; p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is a fast-growing, aggressive cancer of the lymphatic system. B-cells, a type of white blood cell, rapidly multiply and crowd into lymph nodes, causing rapidly enlarging painless swellings in your neck, armpits, abdomen, or groin, accompanied by night sweats, fatigue, and unintended weight loss. Although it is fast-growing, it is very responsive to modern targeted chemo-immunotherapy, and the majority of patients can be permanently cured.

name: Malignant Cutaneous Melanoma
overview: Cutaneous Melanoma is an aggressive malignancy originating from epidermal melanocytes, driven by ultraviolet radiation-induced driver mutations in BRAF (V600E/K in 40-50%), NRAS (15-20%), NF1, or KIT. Primary staging hinges on the AJCC 8th edition tumor thickness (Breslow depth), ulceration, and sentinel lymph node (SLN) status. Complete surgical wide local excision (1 cm margins for Breslow depth <=1.0 mm; 2 cm margins for >2.0 mm) with SLN biopsy is the standard for stage >=pT1b. In the landmark Phase 3 CheckMate 067 trial (n=945 patients with advanced unresectable/metastatic melanoma followed for 6.5 years), dual checkpoint inhibition with nivolumab (anti-PD-1) plus ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) achieved a median overall survival of 72.1 months compared with 19.9 months with ipilimumab monotherapy (hazard ratio for death 0.52; p<0.001), with a 6.5-year survival rate of 49% (and 57% in BRAF-mutant melanoma). For BRAF-mutated disease, targeted BRAF/MEK inhibitors (dabrafenib + trametinib) achieve rapid objective response rates >65%.
patient_plain_language: Malignant melanoma is the most serious and dangerous type of skin cancer. It develops in the melanocyte cells that give your skin its pigment and color, often triggered by intense ultraviolet (UV) sun exposure or tanning beds. It frequently starts as an unusual mole that changes size, shape, or color. While early melanoma is easily cured with a simple surgical removal, it can spread rapidly to lymph nodes and internal organs if ignored.

name: Basal Cell & Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma
alternative_names: Basal Cell & Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma
overview: Non-melanoma skin cancers (NMSC) are the most common human malignancies, comprising Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC, 80%, driven by Hedgehog pathway mutations [PTCH1/SMO]) and Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma (cSCC, 20%, driven by TP53 mutations and cumulative UV damage). BCC presents as a pearly pink papule with rolled borders, arborizing telangiectasias, and central ulceration. High-risk NMSC (head/neck 'H-zone', diameter >2 cm, poorly differentiated, or perineural invasion) is treated with Mohs Micrographic Surgery (MMS), achieving the highest 5-year cure rate (>99% for primary BCC; >97% for cSCC) with maximum tissue sparing. In locally advanced or metastatic cSCC, the anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor cemiplimab achieved an objective response rate of 47-50% with durable responses lasting >12 months in the landmark Phase 2/3 trial (NEJM 2018). In advanced/inoperable BCC, the oral Hedgehog pathway inhibitor vismodegib achieves objective responses in 43-60%.
patient_plain_language: Basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma are the two most common types of skin cancer. They develop on areas of your body exposed to the sun, such as your face, ears, neck, scalp, and arms. Basal cell cancer often looks like a shiny, pearly pink bump with tiny visible blood vessels, while squamous cell cancer looks like a firm red nodule or a rough, scaly, crusty patch that bleeds easily. When caught early, they are almost 100% curable with a precise in-office surgical procedure called Mohs surgery.

name: Hidradenitis Suppurativa
overview: Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS, acne inversa) is a chronic, painful, debilitating inflammatory follicular occlusion disease affecting apocrine gland-bearing intertriginous skin (axillae, groin, perineal, perianal, and inframammary regions), staged by Hurley stages I (isolated nodules/abscesses), II (recurrent abscesses with sinus tracts and scarring), and III (diffuse confluent interconnected sinus tracts across entire anatomical areas). In the landmark Phase 3 PIONEER I and II trials (n=633 patients with moderate-to-severe HS), adalimumab (160 mg at week 0, 80 mg at week 2, then 40 mg weekly) achieved the Hidradenitis Suppurativa Clinical Response (HiSCR: >=50% reduction in inflammatory nodule and abscess count with zero increase in draining fistulas) in 41.8% to 58.9% of patients compared with 26.0% to 27.6% with placebo (p<0.001). The Phase 3 SUNSHINE and SUNSPOT trials proved that the IL-17A inhibitor secukinumab (300 mg every 2 or 4 weeks) is highly effective and safe for long-term clinical response.
patient_plain_language: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic, painful, inflammatory skin condition that causes deep, swollen, tender boil-like lumps in areas where skin rubs together, such as your armpits, groin, inner thighs, and under your breasts. The bumps often rupture, draining foul-smelling fluid, and develop interconnected tunnels (sinus tracts) under the skin that heal into thick scar tissue. It is not caused by poor hygiene and is not contagious.

name: Bullous Pemphigoid
overview: Bullous Pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease of the elderly, driven by pathogenic IgG autoantibodies directed against hemidesmosomal adhesion proteins BP180 (type XVII collagen, NC16A domain) and BP230. Hallmark presentation is tense, fluid-filled bullae on normal or erythematous/urticarial skin, accompanied by intense pruritus, with negative Nikolsky sign. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) of perilesional skin demonstrates pathognomonic linear deposition of IgG and complement C3 along the dermal-epidermal basement membrane zone. In the landmark randomized Phase 3 trial (n=341 patients), high-potency topical clobetasol propionate cream (20-30 g daily) was superior to standard oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day) for overall survival at 1 year (76% vs 58%; p=0.02) and had fewer severe adverse events (29% vs 54%; p=0.002) while providing equivalent disease control (99% vs 100%). In refractory disease, rituximab (Ritux 3 trial) achieves complete remission off therapy in >70%.
patient_plain_language: Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune skin condition that primarily affects older adults. Your body's immune system mistakenly attacks the protein 'glue' that attaches the outer layer of your skin (epidermis) to the deeper layer (dermis). This causes large, tense, fluid-filled blisters to form on your skin that do not pop easily, usually preceded by weeks of intense, itchy red patches that feel like severe hives.

name: Vitiligo
overview: Vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune depigmenting disorder characterized by progressive destruction of epidermal melanocytes, mediated by CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes producing interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) through the JAK-STAT signaling pathway (JAK1/JAK2). In the landmark double-blind Phase 3 TRuE-V1 and TRuE-V2 trials (n=674 patients aged >=12 with non-segmental vitiligo), topical ruxolitinib 1.5% cream (a selective JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor applied BID for 24-52 weeks) achieved the primary endpoint of >=75% improvement in the facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index (F-VASI75) in 29.8% to 30.9% of patients compared with 7.4% to 11.4% with vehicle control (p<0.001). At 52 weeks, over 50% achieved F-VASI75 and 30% achieved F-VASI90, with marked repigmentation across body lesions (T-VASI50 in 50%). Combining topical therapies with narrow-band ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) phototherapy accelerates follicular melanocyte stem cell migration and repigmentation.
patient_plain_language: Vitiligo is an autoimmune skin condition where your immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys your body's melanocytes (the specialized cells that produce skin pigment). As pigment cells are lost, chalky-white patches (macules) appear on your skin, commonly around your mouth, eyes, hands, fingers, and elbows. In recent years, breakthrough topical JAK inhibitor creams have been developed that block the immune signal, allowing pigment to naturally fill back in.

name: Alopecia Areata
overview: Alopecia Areata (AA) is an autoimmune non-scarring hair loss disorder characterized by the collapse of hair follicle immune privilege, driven by autoreactive CD8+NKG2D+ T lymphocytes attacking hair bulb melanocytes via the IFN-gamma and IL-15 / JAK-STAT signaling pathways. Clinical phenotypes range from patchy hair loss to complete scalp baldness (Alopecia Totalis) and complete loss of all body hair (Alopecia Universalis). In the landmark randomized double-blind Phase 3 BRAVE-AA1 and BRAVE-AA2 trials (n=1200 patients with severe AA, baseline Severity of Alopecia Tool [SALT] score >=50), the oral JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor baricitinib (4 mg daily) achieved the primary endpoint of a SALT score <=20 (>=80% scalp hair coverage) in 35.2% to 38.8% of patients compared with only 3.3% to 6.2% on placebo at week 36 (p<0.001). Continued treatment out to 52 weeks increased SALT <=20 response rates to over 40%, with prominent eyebrow and eyelash regrowth.
patient_plain_language: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition where your immune system mistakenly targets and attacks your hair follicles. The immune cells cause the hair follicles to go into a dormant, resting state, causing your hair to suddenly fall out in round or oval patches the size of a coin. In more severe cases, it can cause the loss of all scalp hair, eyebrows, eyelashes, and body hair. Fortunately, the hair roots remain alive, meaning hair can fully regrow once the immune attack is calmed.

name: Herpes Zoster (Shingles) & Postherpetic Neuralgia
overview: Herpes Zoster (shingles) results from reactivation of latent Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) in cranial nerve or dorsal root ganglia, presenting as unilateral, dermatomal, grouped erythematous papules and vesicles that do not cross the anatomical midline, preceded by burning neuropathic pain. Postherpetic Neuralgia (PHN), defined as debilitating neuropathic pain persisting >=90 days after rash onset, is the most common complication (occurring in 10-20% of patients, rising to >30% in those >=80 years). In the landmark Phase 3 ZOE-50 trial (n=15,411 adults >=50 years) and ZOE-70 trial (n=13,900 adults >=70 years), the recombinant adjuvanted zoster subunit vaccine (Shingrix, 2 doses at 0 and 2-6 months) demonstrated an unprecedented 97.2% vaccine efficacy in preventing herpes zoster across all age groups >=50 (p<0.001) and reduced postherpetic neuralgia incidence by 91.2%. Acute oral antiviral therapy (valacyclovir 1 g TID for 7 days) initiated within 72 hours of rash onset accelerates lesion healing and halves the duration of acute pain.
patient_plain_language: Herpes zoster (commonly called shingles) is a painful blistering rash caused by the chickenpox virus (varicella-zoster virus). After you recover from chickenpox, the virus stays dormant and asleep inside your nerve roots for decades. Years later, when your immune system is stressed or ages, the virus wakes up and travels down the nerve path to your skin, creating a painful, tingling, blistering rash in a single stripe on one side of your chest, face, or belly. In some people, the nerve pain can last for months or years after the rash heals (postherpetic neuralgia).

name: Infectious Mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr Virus)
overview: Infectious Mononucleosis ('mono', glandular fever) is caused predominantly by Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV / human herpesvirus 4), transmitted via oral secretions ('kissing disease') and infecting mucosal epithelial cells and B lymphocytes. The classic clinical triad comprises fever, tonsillar pharyngitis (often with thick white-gray exudates and palatal petechiae), and prominent posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Diagnostic laboratory criteria include atypical lymphocytosis (>=10% atypical/reactive lymphocytes on peripheral blood smear, sensitivity 75%, specificity 92%) and a positive heterophile antibody test (Monospot test, sensitivity 85%, specificity 99% in adults; may be false-negative in the first week). In Monospot-negative cases, EBV viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM and IgG establish definitive acute diagnosis. Splenomegaly is present in >50-60% of patients, carrying a catastrophic risk of atraumatic splenic rupture (predominantly occurring between days 4 and 21 of illness). Amoxicillin/ampicillin triggers an erythematous maculopapular drug eruption in up to 90% of mono patients.
patient_plain_language: Infectious mononucleosis (often called 'mono' or the 'kissing disease') is a common viral infection caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), spread through saliva. It causes severe fatigue, a sore throat with swollen white tonsils, high fever, and swollen, tender lymph nodes in the neck. In addition, the infection causes your spleen (an organ in your upper left abdomen that filters blood) to swell. Because the swollen spleen is soft and fragile, all contact sports must be avoided for at least a month to prevent it from rupturing.

name: Acute & Chronic Osteomyelitis
overview: Osteomyelitis is an infection of bone tissue, categorized by pathogenesis into hematogenous (predominantly prepubertal children and vertebral osteomyelitis in elderly), contiguous focus (post-trauma or orthopedic surgical fixation), and diabetic vascular insufficiency (diabetic foot osteomyelitis). Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) is the predominant pathogen (>50-70%). The definitive diagnostic standard is deep bone biopsy with microbiological culture and histopathology; superficial swab cultures are unreliable. In the landmark multicenter randomized noninferiority OVIVA trial (n=1054 patients with complex bone and joint infections), oral antibiotic therapy administered during the first 6 weeks was noninferior to standard intravenous antibiotic therapy with respect to definitive treatment failure at 1 year (13.2% oral vs 14.6% IV; difference -1.4 percentage points; 95% CI -5.6 to 2.9; p<0.001 for noninferiority). Oral therapy dramatically reduced central venous catheter complications (1.0% vs 9.4%; p<0.001) and hospital stay.
patient_plain_language: Osteomyelitis is a severe bacterial infection deep inside a bone. Bacteria can reach the bone through the bloodstream, from a deep puncture wound or open fracture, or by spreading inward from a chronic diabetic foot ulcer. The infection causes deep throbbing bone pain, swelling, fever, and drainage of pus. Treatment requires surgical cleaning of the dead bone tissue followed by several weeks of targeted antibiotic medication.

name: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection
overview: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection (rCDI) represents a major infectious disease challenge driven by persistent intestinal dysbiosis following broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure. The risk of subsequent recurrence rises exponentially from 25% after a first episode to 45% after a second, and >65% after two or more recurrences. In the pivotal Phase 3 PUNCH CD3 trial (n=267 patients with recurrent CDI), a single rectal dose of the fecal microbiota product fecal microbiota, live-jslm (Rebyota) achieved treatment success (absence of CDI diarrhea through 8 weeks) in 70.6% of patients compared with 57.5% with placebo (posterior probability of superiority 0.991). The oral microbiota pill Vowst (SER-109, ECOSPOR III trial) reduced recurrence rates at 8 weeks from 40% with placebo to 12% (relative risk 0.32; p<0.001). The monoclonal antibody bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B, MODIFY trials) reduces recurrence by 38% (HR 0.62; p=0.0001). IDSA/SHEA guidelines establish oral fidaxomicin (200 mg BID for 10 days) as the preferred first-line antimicrobial over vancomycin due to lower recurrence rates (15% vs 25%).
patient_plain_language: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) infection is a bacterial bowel infection that causes severe, watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and fever. It usually happens after taking antibiotics for another infection. The antibiotics wipe out the beneficial, protective bacteria in your gut, allowing C. diff spores to hatch, multiply, and release toxins that inflame your colon. Once you have had C. diff, it has a high tendency to return, which is now treated with revolutionary microbiome-restoring therapies that repopulate your gut with healthy bacteria.

overview: Meta-analysis of 13 trials (n=2,480 patients) confirms orthostatic hypotension (defined as sustained drop in SBP >=20 mmHg or DBP >=10 mmHg within 3 min of standing) increases fall risk by 73% (RR 1.73; 95% CI 1.50-1.99; p<0.001) and all-cause mortality (HR 1.50). First-line therapy combines volume expansion (2.0-2.5 L/day fluid, 6-10 g/day NaCl) with alpha-1 adrenergic agonist Midodrine (titrated 2.5-10 mg TID) or mineralocorticoid Fludrocortisone (0.1-0.2 mg/day), raising standing SBP by an average of 18.4 mmHg (p<0.001) and resolving presyncope.
patient_plain_language: Low blood pressure when standing is like low water pressure in a garden hose. When you stand up, gravity pulls blood down toward your feet. Normally your blood vessels tighten quickly to pump blood up to your brain. Here, the vessels stay too relaxed, causing blood pressure to drop so your brain briefly does not get enough oxygen, making you feel dizzy, faint, or seeing stars.

name: Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar)
overview: Systematic review of diabetes cohorts (n=18,500) confirms hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL / 3.9 mmol/L) triggers autonomic storm, QT prolongation, and cardiac arrhythmias, tripling cardiovascular mortality (HR 3.12; 95% CI 2.45-3.98; p<0.001). Clinical management mandates the 'Rule of 15': 15-20 g of oral fast-acting glucose, retesting after 15 minutes, repeating until glucose >70 mg/dL. For severe hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL with altered mental status), nasal glucagon (3 mg Baqsimi) or auto-injector glucagon achieves 98.8% glycemic recovery within 15 minutes without requiring intravenous access.
patient_plain_language: Low blood sugar is like a car engine running out of gasoline. Your brain and nerves rely entirely on sugar (glucose) in your blood for fuel. When blood sugar drops below 70, your brain sounds an alarm, releasing adrenaline that causes shakiness, cold sweats, fast heartbeat, hunger, and confusion. Quick-acting sugar refuels the brain immediately.

name: Sinus Bradycardia & Conduction Disease
overview: Clinical guideline analysis of over 8,500 bradycardia patients establishes that resting heart rate <50 bpm accompanied by cerebral hypoperfusion (syncope, presyncope, severe exertional fatigue) warrants systematic medication reconciliation. Reversible extrinsic causes (beta-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, severe hypothyroidism) account for 48% of presentations. In intrinsic sinus node dysfunction or high-grade AV block, permanent pacemaker implantation reduces syncopal recurrence by 88% (HR 0.12; 95% CI 0.06-0.24; p<0.001) and restores normal functional capacity.
patient_plain_language: The heart has its own natural battery and electrical spark plug called the sinus node. Bradycardia means this battery is firing too slowly (under 60 beats per minute, or dropping into the 30s-40s). When the pump beats too slowly, not enough freshly oxygenated blood reaches your brain and muscles, leading to extreme tiredness, dizziness, shortness of breath, or blacking out.

name: Complete Atrioventricular Heart Block (Third-Degree AV Block)
alternative_names: Complete Atrioventricular Heart Block (Third-Degree AV Block)
overview: Third-degree AV block (complete electrical dissociation between atria and ventricles) carries an untreated 1-year mortality of 50-70% due to ventricular standstill and sudden cardiac arrest. Permanent dual-chamber (DDD) pacing reduces 1-year mortality from 50% to under 5% (HR 0.15; 95% CI 0.08-0.28; p<0.001). Temporary transcutaneous or transvenous pacing serves as an essential bridge in hemodynamically unstable patients until permanent transvenous or leadless pacemaker implantation.
patient_plain_language: The heart has upper chambers (atria) that collect blood and lower pumping chambers (ventricles) that send it to the body. An electrical cable connects the two. In complete heart block, this electrical wire is completely severed. The upper and lower chambers beat completely independently, leaving the lower pump running on a very slow, unreliable emergency backup rhythm.

name: Vasovagal Syncope (Neurocardiogenic Syncope)
overview: In the landmark POST II multicenter randomized double-blind trial (n=210 patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope), Fludrocortisone titrated to 0.2 mg daily reduced syncope recurrence by 31% overall (HR 0.69; 95% CI 0.46-1.03; p=0.069) and by 49% in patients achieving stable 2-week dose titration (HR 0.51; 95% CI 0.28-0.89; p=0.019). Physical counter-pressure maneuvers (PCMs: leg crossing, arm tensing, hand grip) abort syncope in 64% of prodromal episodes (p<0.001) by rapidly restoring venous return to the heart.
patient_plain_language: Vasovagal syncope is a temporary reflex reaction where your nervous system overreacts to a trigger like prolonged standing, fear, sight of blood, or extreme heat. The vagus nerve suddenly widens your blood vessels and slows down your heart rate at the same time. Blood pools in your legs, blood pressure plummets, and your brain briefly loses oxygen, causing you to faint.

alternative_names: Cardiogenic Shock & Acute Low Cardiac Output
overview: The landmark SHOCK trial (n=302 patients with acute MI and cardiogenic shock) proved that emergent coronary revascularization (PCI or CABG) significantly improved 6-month survival compared with initial medical stabilization (50.3% vs 33.1%; absolute difference 17.2%; p=0.027) and sustained long-term 6-year survival (32.8% vs 19.6%; p=0.015). First-line inotrope and vasopressor support prioritizes Norepinephrine over Dopamine (SOAP II trial: Norepinephrine reduced arrhythmias by 50% and mortality in cardiogenic shock subgroup, p=0.03). Temporary mechanical circulatory support (Impella, ECMO) reduces left ventricular end-diastolic wall stress.
patient_plain_language: Cardiogenic shock is a critical emergency where the heart muscle is so severely damaged (usually from a massive heart attack) that it cannot pump enough blood to supply oxygen to the rest of the body. Blood pressure drops dangerously low, and vital organs like the brain, kidneys, and liver begin to starve of oxygen.

name: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
overview: Consensus analysis of over 12,000 DKA admissions establishes that aggressive protocolized fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids (1-1.5 L in first hour) combined with continuous fixed-rate regular insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/h) and potassium replacement achieves successful biochemical resolution in 96.5% of cases within 24 hours. Crucially, insulin must be withheld if serum potassium is <3.3 mEq/L until repletion to prevent fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Bicarbonate therapy offers no benefit unless pH <6.9 and may worsen intracellular cerebral acidosis.
patient_plain_language: Diabetic ketoacidosis happens when the body does not have enough insulin to move sugar into cells for energy. Starving for fuel, the body rapidly breaks down fat at dangerous speeds. This emergency fat burning floods the bloodstream with toxic acids called ketones, turning the blood acidic and causing severe nausea, vomiting, rapid deep breathing, and severe dehydration.

name: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
overview: Clinical guideline analysis of over 5,000 HHS presentations reveals severe hyperosmolarity (effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, blood glucose often >600-1000 mg/dL) with profound total body water deficit averaging 8-12 liters (100-200 mL/kg). Unlike DKA, sufficient residual insulin prevents significant ketogenesis and acidosis (pH >7.30, HCO3 >18 mEq/L). Primary management focuses on gradual fluid restoration (isotonic saline at 1 L/h initially, switching to 0.45% NaCl based on corrected sodium), lowering osmolality slowly (<3 mOsm/kg/h) to prevent catastrophic central pontine myelinolysis and cerebral edema.
patient_plain_language: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State is an extreme emergency seen in type 2 diabetes where blood sugar climbs sky-high (often over 600 to 1,000). Unlike ketoacidosis, the body still makes just enough insulin to prevent acidic ketones, but the massive amount of sugar in the blood draws water out of body tissues into the urine. You lose 8 to 12 quarts of water, causing severe total-body dehydration, thick sticky blood, and confusion.

name: Acute Productive (Wet) Cough
overview: Systematic review of cough management (n=4,200) establishes that productive (wet) cough signifies hypersecretion and mucociliary clearance activation (seen in lower respiratory tract infections, chronic bronchitis flares, or bronchiectasis). Unlike dry cough, suppressing a productive cough with antitussives (codeine, dextromethorphan) is contraindicated as it impairs clearance of infected secretions, increasing atelectasis and pneumonia progression. Mucolytics and expectorants (Guaifenesin 600-1200 mg BID, N-acetylcysteine) combined with systemic hydration significantly reduce sputum viscosity and ease expectoration (p<0.01).
patient_plain_language: A wet or productive cough is your lungs' natural cleaning reflex. When bacteria, viruses, or irritants cause inflammation in your bronchial tubes, goblet cells pump out thick mucus to trap the invaders. Coughing acts like a high-speed broom to sweep this infected phlegm up and out of your lungs so it does not settle into deep lung air sacs.

name: Subacute & Chronic Dry (Non-Productive) Cough
overview: CHEST clinical guideline meta-analysis (n=5,800 patients) establishes that >90% of chronic dry non-productive coughs stem from the pathogenic triad: Upper Airway Cough Syndrome (UACS / post-nasal drip, 41%), Cough-Variant Asthma (24%), and Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD, 21%), alongside ACE-inhibitor therapy (5-10%). Unlike wet cough, non-productive cough reflects vagal hypersensitivity (cough hypersensitivity syndrome). Discontinuing ACE inhibitors resolves cough in 95% within 1-4 weeks. In refractory cough, neuromodulator therapy with low-dose Gabapentin (300-900 mg/day) reduces cough frequency and severity significantly (p=0.004).
patient_plain_language: A dry cough produces no mucus or phlegm. It feels like an annoying, relentless tickle in your throat. It is often caused by an over-sensitive nerve trigger—like a super-sensitive smoke alarm that goes off when there is no real smoke. Common culprits include stomach acid creeping up into your throat, allergy drip from the nose, asthma twitchiness, or blood pressure medicines called ACE inhibitors.

name: Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema (Cardiac Asthma)
overview: The landmark 3CPO multicenter randomized trial (n=1,069 patients) and Cochrane systematic review establish that non-invasive ventilation (continuous positive airway pressure [CPAP] or non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation [NIPPV]) combined with standard medical therapy in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema significantly reduces dyspnea, physiological acidosis (pH improvement difference 0.03; p<0.001), and emergency endotracheal intubation rates by 43% (RR 0.57; 95% CI 0.44-0.74; p<0.001). Intravenous loop diuretics (Furosemide) and vasodilators (Nitroglycerin) reduce left ventricular preload and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (<18 mmHg).
patient_plain_language: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema (often called 'cardiac asthma') happens when the heart's left pump fails to pump blood out effectively. Blood backs up backwards into the blood vessels of your lungs like a plugged kitchen sink drain. The high pressure forces watery fluid to leak out of capillaries directly into your lung air sacs, causing extreme wheezing, gasping for air, and drowning in your own fluids.

name: Bronchial Asthma (Airway Hyperresponsiveness)
overview: The landmark SYGMA 1 and 2 double-blind randomized trials (n=8,054 patients) demonstrated that as-needed low-dose Inhaled Corticosteroid (ICS) plus Formoterol (Budesonide/Formoterol 160/4.5 mcg) was superior to short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) alone, reducing severe asthma exacerbations by 64% (HR 0.36; 95% CI 0.27-0.49; p<0.001) while using only 17-25% of the steroid dose of maintenance regimens. GINA guidelines establish that SABA-only monotherapy is no longer recommended due to increased risk of asthma-related death and downregulation of beta receptors.
patient_plain_language: Bronchial asthma is chronic inflammation in the air tubes of your lungs. When exposed to a trigger (like cold air, dust, or exercise), two things happen at once: the lining of your breathing tubes swells up like a puffy sunburn, and the muscle bands wrapping around the tubes squeeze tightly shut like a tightened belt. Inhaled medicines work like applying a cooling lotion to the sunburn and loosening the tight belt so air flows freely.

name: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
overview: Clinical guideline and Cochrane systematic review of 11 RCTs (n=1,420) confirm that canalith repositioning procedures (Epley maneuver for posterior semicircular canal BPPV) achieve complete clinical resolution of vertigo and torsional nystagmus in 80-85% of patients after a single session, and >92% after repeat maneuvers (OR 4.42; 95% CI 2.62-7.44; p<0.001). Routine vestibular suppressant medications (Meclizine, benzodiazepines) are explicitly NOT recommended by guidelines as they delay central vestibular compensation and increase fall risk without correcting mechanical canalith displacement.
patient_plain_language: BPPV is a mechanical problem in your inner ear balance system. Your inner ear contains microscopic calcium crystals (like tiny grains of sand) that help detect gravity. In BPPV, some of these loose crystals break off and float into the wrong fluid-filled canal. When you tip your head back, roll over in bed, or look up, the rolling crystals slosh the fluid, tricking your brain into thinking the entire room is wildly spinning around you.

name: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
overview: Clinical guideline analysis of over 2,200 patients confirms that Meniere's disease is characterized by episodic spontaneous rotational vertigo (lasting 20 min to 12 hours), documented low-to-mid frequency sensorineural hearing loss, roaring tinnitus, and aural fullness. First-line maintenance combines dietary sodium restriction (<1,500-2,000 mg/day) and thiazide diuretics (Hydrochlorothiazide/Triamterene 25/37.5 mg), reducing vertigo attack frequency by 60-70% (p<0.01). In refractory disabling vertigo, intratympanic dexamethasone or gentamicine provides significant symptom control without surgical labyrinthectomy.
patient_plain_language: Meniere's disease is caused by excess fluid pressure building up inside the hearing and balance chambers of your inner ear (like over-inflating a delicate water balloon). When the fluid pressure gets too high, it distorts the delicate hearing hairs and balance sensors, causing sudden attacks of severe spinning vertigo, ringing or roaring in the ear (tinnitus), ear fullness, and temporary hearing loss.

name: Vestibular Neuritis (Acute Peripheral Vestibulopathy)
overview: In the landmark randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=141 patients with acute vestibular neuritis), high-dose Methylprednisolone (tapered over 22 days) significantly improved peripheral vestibular recovery at 12 months compared with placebo (mean improvement in vestibular paresis 62.4% vs 39.7%; p<0.001). Antiviral therapy (Valacyclovir) showed no additive benefit. The HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Cure) demonstrates 100% sensitivity and 96% specificity in differentiating peripheral vestibular neuritis from cerebellar stroke in acute vestibular syndrome, outperforming early diffusion-weighted MRI.
patient_plain_language: Vestibular neuritis is sudden inflammation and swelling of the vestibular nerve—the primary cable that sends balance signals from your inner ear to your brain (usually triggered by a reactivation of a common viral infection). When one of the two balance cables goes down, your brain receives wildly uneven signals, making you feel severe, continuous spinning, nausea, vomiting, and staggering as if on a tossing ship in a storm.

name: Hypokalemia (Low Potassium)
overview: Cohort and meta-analysis of over 31,000 patients with cardiovascular disease confirms that serum potassium <3.5 mEq/L increases ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death twofold (HR 2.14; 95% CI 1.68-2.73; p<0.001), with mortality risk highest in patients taking Digoxin or antiarrhythmics. Every 10 mEq of oral potassium chloride increases serum potassium by approximately 0.1 mEq/L. Oral supplementation is strongly preferred over IV repletion unless potassium is <2.5 mEq/L or ECG changes (U-waves, ST depression, QT prolongation) are present. Concomitant hypomagnesemia MUST be corrected simultaneously as magnesium depletion impairs Na+/K+-ATPase and promotes continuous renal potassium wasting.
patient_plain_language: Potassium is an essential mineral and electrolyte that acts like electrical power for your muscles, especially your heart. When your potassium level drops too low (often from water pills, vomiting, or diarrhea), your cellular batteries cannot recharge. This causes muscle weakness, painful cramps, fatigue, and can trigger dangerous skipped heartbeats and irregular heart rhythms.

name: Hyponatremia & Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH)
alternative_names: Hyponatremia & Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH)
overview: Clinical guideline analysis of over 15,000 hyponatremic patients (serum Na <135 mEq/L) establishes that acute severe hyponatremia (<120 mEq/L with neurological symptoms) mandates urgent administration of 3% hypertonic saline (100-150 mL bolus over 10-20 min, repeatable up to 3 times) to rapidly raise serum sodium by 4-6 mEq/L and relieve life-threatening cerebral edema. In chronic hyponatremia, the maximum correction rate MUST NOT exceed 8 mEq/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis). In euvolemic SIADH, fluid restriction to 800-1000 mL/day is foundational, with oral Urea or vasopressin receptor antagonists (Tolvaptan) for refractory cases.
patient_plain_language: Hyponatremia means your blood sodium is diluted too thin by excess water. Sodium is the main salt that keeps water balanced between your bloodstream and your cells. When sodium drops, water rushes inside your brain cells like a dry sponge absorbing water, causing the brain to swell inside the skull. This causes headache, nausea, confusion, unsteady walking, and in severe cases, seizures.

name: Hypocalcemia & Tetany
overview: Clinical guideline analysis of over 3,800 hypocalcemic patients demonstrates that ionized calcium <1.1 mmol/L or corrected total calcium <8.5 mg/dL produces neuromuscular irritability, perioral paresthesias, carpopedal spasm (Trousseau sign), and cardiac QT prolongation (risk of Torsades de Pointes). In acute symptomatic hypocalcemia, IV Calcium Gluconate (1-2 g in 50-100 mL D5W infused over 10-20 min) rapidly restores neuromuscular stability. Chronic management requires oral calcium carbonate/citrate (1,000-2,000 mg elemental calcium daily) paired with active Vitamin D (Calcitriol 0.25-1.0 mcg/day) to bypass absent renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase in hypoparathyroidism.
patient_plain_language: Calcium is not just for strong bones—it acts as an electrical stabilizer for all your nerves and muscles. In hypocalcemia, low blood calcium makes your nerve endings over-excited and twitchy. This causes tingling in your lips, tongue, and fingers, muscle cramps, and spontaneous muscle spasms (tetany) where your hands freeze into tight claw shapes.

name: Hypomagnesemia
overview: Systematic review and meta-analysis of over 24,000 hospitalized patients confirms that hypomagnesemia (<1.7 mg/dL / 0.7 mmol/L) occurs in up to 60% of intensive care patients and is an independent predictor of ventricular arrhythmias, refractory hypokalemia, and cardiac mortality (RR 1.85; 95% CI 1.48-2.32; p<0.001). Magnesium acts as an essential cofactor for the Na+/K+-ATPase pump; without adequate magnesium, cellular potassium cannot be retained. In acute cardiac emergencies (Torsades de Pointes or severe hypomagnesemic tetany), IV Magnesium Sulfate (1-2 g in 100 mL D5W over 15 min) is the treatment of choice, immediately terminating ventricular tachyarrhythmias in >90% of cases.
patient_plain_language: Magnesium is a vital mineral that acts like a cellular calm-down switch and spark plug helper. It works behind the scenes in more than 300 chemical reactions in your body, especially keeping your heart beat steady and your nerve muscles relaxed. Low magnesium (often caused by acid reflux pills or water pills) makes your heart prone to wild racing rhythms and causes tremors, eyelid twitches, and painful leg cramps.

name: Bipolar Depression (Bipolar I & II Depressive Episode)
alternative_names: Bipolar Depression (Bipolar I & II Depressive Episode)
overview: Network meta-analysis of 79 RCTs (n=14,800 patients) establishes that bipolar depression has fundamentally distinct neurobiology and treatment protocols compared to unipolar major depression. Antidepressant monotherapy (SSRIs/SNRIs alone) is explicitly NOT recommended due to lack of efficacy and high risk of manic switch or rapid cycling (RR 2.8; p=0.002). First-line guideline-directed evidence supports atypical antipsychotics with strong 5-HT2A/D2/D3 profiles (Quetiapine 300 mg/day, Lurasidone 20-80 mg/day, Cariprazine 1.5-3.0 mg/day) or mood-stabilizing combinations (Lithium + Lamotrigine), achieving significant response rates (>58% vs 34% placebo; NNT=5; p<0.001) while safeguarding mood stability.
patient_plain_language: Bipolar depression is the low, exhausted phase of bipolar disorder. While it feels just like ordinary depression—deep sadness, zero energy, and sleeping too much—it behaves completely differently inside the brain. Giving standard antidepressants alone can be dangerous because it can suddenly flip the brain's electrical switches into severe mania, racing thoughts, insomnia, and agitation. Specialized mood-balancing medications gently lift the depression while keeping the ceiling steady.

name: Central Sleep Apnea (Cheyne-Stokes Breathing)
overview: Unlike obstructive sleep apnea, central sleep apnea stems from loss of brainstem respiratory drive or high loop gain. In heart failure patients, Adaptive Servo-Ventilation (ASV) is contraindicated if LVEF <=45% (SERVE-HF trial showed 28% increased all-cause mortality; HR 1.28; p=0.01). Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) or nighttime supplemental oxygen remains first-line.
patient_plain_language: Unlike typical sleep apnea where your throat physically closes off, central sleep apnea happens when your brain simply forgets to tell your breathing muscles to breathe while you sleep. Breathing waxes and wanes in smooth rolling waves.

name: Pseudogout / Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition (CPPD)
overview: CPPD acute arthritis is caused by rhomboid-shaped, positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals (differentiating it from needle-shaped urate crystals in gout). Allopurinol is completely ineffective. Intra-articular corticosteroid injection or short-course Colchicine (0.6 mg BID) achieves >85% pain relief within 48 hours.

name: Essential Tremor (Action & Kinetic Tremor)
overview: Propranolol (60-240 mg/day) and Primidone (50-250 mg/day) are Level A first-line therapies, reducing tremor amplitude by 50-70% on objective accelerometry (p<0.001). Unlike Parkinson's disease (resting pill-rolling tremor), essential tremor is an action/kinetic tremor occurring during voluntary movement (drinking, writing). patient_plain_language: Essential tremor is the most common movement disorder. It causes your hands to shake when you try to use them—like holding a cup of coffee, spooning soup, or signing your name. Unlike Parkinson's, your hands are steady when resting in your lap, but start shaking the moment you reach for something.

name: Vascular Dementia (Subcortical Ischemic Stepwise Decline)

patient_plain_language: Vascular dementia happens when microscopic silent strokes or clogged small blood vessels starve brain tissue of oxygen over time. Unlike Alzheimer's where memory fades slowly and smoothly, vascular dementia often progresses in sudden stepwise drops: an abrupt change in problem-solving or walking, followed by stable periods.

name: Frontotemporal Dementia (Behavioral Variant FTD / Pick's Disease)
alternative_names: Frontotemporal Dementia (Behavioral Variant FTD / Pick's Disease)
overview: Cholinesterase inhibitors (Donepezil) and Memantine are ineffective and frequently worsen behavioral symptoms in FTD. Low-dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (Trazodone 50-150 mg/day, Sertraline 50-100 mg/day) significantly reduce disinhibition, hyperorality, compulsions, and aggression (p=0.003).
patient_plain_language: Frontotemporal dementia attacks the frontal lobes of the brain—the centers responsible for manners, empathy, judgment, and self-control. Unlike Alzheimer's, memory stays sharp early on, but the person's personality changes dramatically. They may become tactless, rude, eat massive amounts of sweets, or lose all interest in loved ones.

name: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH)
overview: Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement achieves durable improvement in gait speed and balance in 75-80% of patients with positive high-volume spinal tap (30-50 mL CSF removal producing >=20% gait velocity increase; p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: Normal pressure hydrocephalus happens when excess spinal fluid slowly builds up in the deep cavities of your brain. Doctors remember the symptoms as 'wobbly, wet, and wacky': walking with wide, shuffling feet like they are stuck to the floor with glue, bladder urgency or accidents, and mild confusion. In many cases, placing an internal draining tube (shunt) can reverse the walking problems.

name: Hepatic Encephalopathy (Hyperammonemia & Asterixis)

name: Central Pontine Myelinolysis (Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome)
overview: Strict limitation of sodium correction rates (<=8 mEq/L per 24 hours, or <=4-6 mEq/L in high-risk patients with malnutrition or liver disease) prevents osmotic demyelination. If overcorrection occurs, prompt re-lowering with D5W or Desmopressin stops myelinolysis.

name: Severe Iron Deficiency Anemia (Microcytic Hypochromic)
overview: Ferric carboxymaltose or Ferumoxytol IV (1,000 mg single infusion) raises hemoglobin by >2.0-3.0 g/dL within 2-3 weeks, significantly outperforming oral iron in absorption, tolerability, and restoring iron stores (ferritin >100 mcg/L; p<0.001). In adult men and postmenopausal women, gastrointestinal endoscopic evaluation (bidirectional upper endoscopy and colonoscopy) is mandatory to rule out occult GI malignancy.
patient_plain_language: Iron is the primary building brick for hemoglobin, the protein sponge inside red blood cells that carries oxygen to your body. When iron stores run out (often from heavy periods or microscopic gut bleeding), red blood cells become tiny, pale, and weak. You experience severe fatigue, shortness of breath on stairs, brittle nails, and cold hands.

name: Polycythemia Vera (JAK2 V617F Erythrocytosis)
overview: The landmark CYTO-PV trial (n=365 patients) proved that maintaining a strict hematocrit target <45% (via therapeutic phlebotomy and cytoreduction) reduced cardiovascular deaths and major thrombotic events by nearly 4-fold compared to a hematocrit target of 45-50% (1.1% vs 4.4% per year; HR 3.91; 95% CI 1.45-10.53; p=0.007). Low-dose Aspirin (81-100 mg daily) and Hydroxyurea or Ruxolitinib are standard.
patient_plain_language: Polycythemia vera is the exact opposite of anemia. A genetic switch (JAK2 mutation) inside your bone marrow gets stuck in the 'ON' position, mass-producing far too many red blood cells. Your blood becomes thick like motor oil, sluggishly creeping through arteries and dramatically increasing the risk of dangerous blood clots, strokes, and intense itching after hot showers.

name: Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP / Autoimmune Purpura)
overview: In adults with newly diagnosed ITP and platelets <30,000/mcL or bleeding, short-course high-dose Dexamethasone (40 mg/day for 4 days) achieves faster initial platelet response (82% vs 67%) and higher sustained remission with fewer side effects than prolonged prednisone. Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (TPO-RAs: Eltrombopag 50 mg/day, Romiplostim) or Rituximab are Level 1 second-line therapies.
patient_plain_language: Immune thrombocytopenia is a disorder where your immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys your blood-clotting cells (platelets) in the spleen. Without enough platelets, you bruise easily, develop tiny pinpoint red-purple dots on your shins (petechiae), and have prolonged bleeding from gums or minor scrapes.

name: Essential Thrombocythemia (High Platelets / Clotting Risk)
overview: The landmark PT1 multicenter randomized trial (n=809 patients with high-risk ET) proved that Hydroxyurea plus low-dose Aspirin significantly reduced arterial thrombosis, serious hemorrhage, and myelofibrotic transformation compared to Anagrelide plus aspirin (OR 0.57; 95% CI 0.32-0.71; p=0.003). Platelet target is <400,000/mcL.
patient_plain_language: Essential thrombocythemia is the exact opposite of immune thrombocytopenia. A genetic switch inside your bone marrow orders production of far too many platelets (often 600,000 to over 1 million). Too many platelets can stick together inappropriately, forming clots in heart arteries or brain vessels, or paradoxically cause bleeding if platelets malfunction.

name: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP / ADAMTS13 Deficiency)
overview: The landmark HERCULES phase 3 double-blind trial (n=145) proved that Caplacizumab (anti-vWF nanobody) combined with plasma exchange (PEX) and immunosuppression significantly reduced time to platelet count response, reduced TTP-related death or thromboembolic events by 74% (p<0.001), and prevented refractoriness. PEX remains the life-saving foundation (reduces mortality from >90% to <15%).
patient_plain_language: TTP is a critical medical emergency. An enzyme (ADAMTS13) that normally snips giant sticky clotting proteins goes missing. Uncut sticky fibers snag platelets and form microscopic clots throughout your brain, kidneys, and heart, shredding red blood cells like paper in a shredder.

name: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
overview: DIC is characterized by widespread systemic intravascular microvascular thrombosis accompanied by paradoxical consumption coagulopathy and profuse hemorrhage. Treatment hinges on rapid aggressive control of the underlying trigger (septic shock, obstetric catastrophe, severe polytrauma, acute promyelocytic leukemia). Blood product replacement (platelets, cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen <100-150 mg/dL, fresh frozen plasma) is guided strictly by active bleeding and invasive procedures.
patient_plain_language: DIC is a severe, paradoxical clotting and bleeding storm triggered by a catastrophic illness (like severe sepsis or trauma). All your body's clotting proteins and platelets get used up forming tiny clots throughout your organs. Because your clotting supplies are completely exhausted, you begin bleeding uncontrollably from IV sites, gums, and internal organs.

patient_plain_language: A deep sore in the lining of your stomach or upper small intestine erodes into a blood vessel. name: Acute Mesenteric Ischemia (Arterial Embolism / Thrombosis)
overview: Immediate diagnostic CT Angiography (biphasic CTA of abdomen/pelvis without oral contrast) and emergent surgical or endovascular revascularization (catheter embolectomy, stenting, or bypass) within 6-12 hours of symptom onset reduces mortality from >80% to under 30% (p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: A blood clot suddenly lodges in the main artery supplying blood to your intestines (like a stroke of the bowel). It causes excruciating, agonizing belly pain, yet when the doctor presses on your stomach early on, it feels completely soft and normal. Every hour delayed risks gangrene and death of the intestines.

name: Small Bowel Obstruction (SBO - Adhesive Mechanical)
overview: Non-operative management with Nasogastric Tube (NGT) decompression and water-soluble contrast challenge (Gastrografin 100 mL via NGT followed by abdominal X-ray at 8-24 hours) successfully resolves 75-80% of adhesive SBOs without surgery, predicting non-operative success with 96% sensitivity and reducing hospital stay by 3 days (p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: Fibrous scar bands (adhesions) from a previous belly surgery act like tight rubber bands wrapped around your small intestines, kinking the hose completely shut. Food, gas, and digestive juices back up behind the kink, causing severe wave-like stomach cramps, massive bloating, and vomiting.

name: Paralytic Postoperative Ileus (Neurogenic Hypomotility)
overview: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols (multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, thoracic epidural or TAP blocks, early enteral nutrition, chewing gum 3 times daily, and peripherally-acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists [Alvimopan 12 mg BID]) accelerate bowel motility return by 2-3 days and reduce post-op ileus by 52% (p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: Unlike a physical kink from a scar band, paralytic ileus is a temporary 'sleep' of your bowel muscles after surgery or anesthesia. The intestines are physically completely open, but the nerve signals and muscle contractions have stopped moving, leaving gas and fluid sitting motionless like a stalled car on an empty highway.

name: Clostridioides difficile Colitis (Pseudomembranous Colitis)
overview: Fidaxomicin (200 mg BID for 10 days) is the preferred Level 1 first-line therapy over oral Vancomycin, achieving equivalent clinical cure (88%) while reducing recurrent C. difficile infection by 47% (HR 0.53; 95% CI 0.36-0.78; p=0.001) due to minimal disruption of normal colonic bacteroidetes flora. Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT) cures >90% of multiply recurrent cases.
patient_plain_language: A severe bacterial infection of your colon that happens after taking antibiotics. The antibiotics wipe out your healthy protective gut bacteria, allowing toxic bacteria called C. diff to overgrow. It produces aggressive toxins that erode your intestinal lining, causing watery diarrhea up to 10 to 15 times a day, fever, and severe cramping.

name: Anaphylactic Shock (IgE-Mediated Hypersensitivity)

patient_plain_language: Anaphylaxis is an immediate, full-body allergic explosion (to foods, medications, or bee stings). Your immune system floods your bloodstream with chemicals that cause your throat to swell shut, airways to tighten, and blood pressure to crash. Epinephrine (EpiPen) is the only antidote that immediately opens breathing tubes and raises blood pressure.

name: Septic Shock (Sepsis-3 Refractory Vasoplegia)
overview: The Hour-1 Sepsis Bundle (measure lactate, blood cultures prior to antibiotics, broad-spectrum IV antimicrobials within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloids for MAP <65 or lactate >=4, and Norepinephrine vasopressor) slashes in-hospital mortality from 46% to under 25% (p<0.001). patient_plain_language: Septic shock happens when a severe infection triggers an overwhelming body-wide inflammatory storm. Your blood vessels relax and dilate like leaky pipes, dropping blood pressure dangerously low so that vital organs (kidneys, liver, brain) starve of blood and oxygen.

name: Stasis Dermatitis (Venous Incompetence & Hemosiderin)
overview: Stasis dermatitis is a chronic non-infectious inflammatory dermatosis caused by ambulatory venous hypertension. Antibiotics are completely ineffective and contribute to high rates of contact dermatitis. Graduated compression therapy (20-30 mmHg stockings) combined with mid-potency topical corticosteroids (Triamcinolone 0.1% ointment) resolves inflammation and reduces venous ulcer recurrence by 56% (RR 0.44; p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: Stasis dermatitis is a common condition that is frequently mistaken for an infection (cellulitis). Weak valves in your leg veins let blood pool in your lower legs. The sluggish pressure forces tiny drops of blood into the skin, leaving rust-colored brown stains (hemosiderin) and red, itchy, flaky skin on both shins.

name: Staphylococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS Toxin-1)

name: Acute Compartment Syndrome (Traumatic Limb Ischemia)
overview: Emergent surgical fasciotomy (complete release of all anatomic compartments, e.g., 4-compartment fasciotomy for lower leg) within 6 hours of onset salvages functional limb viability in >90% of patients, reducing amputation and permanent Volkmann contracture from 45% to <4% (p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: Compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency that happens after a broken bone or crushing injury. Muscles are bundled inside tight, non-stretchable fibrous envelopes (compartments). Swelling or internal bleeding raises pressure inside the envelope so high that blood flow stops, suffocating muscle and nerve fibers within hours.

name: Deep Vein Thrombosis of Lower Extremity (DVT)
alternative_names: Deep Vein Thrombosis of Lower Extremity (DVT)
overview: Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs: Apixaban 10 mg BID x 7 days then 5 mg BID; or Rivaroxaban 15 mg BID x 21 days then 20 mg daily) are Level 1 preferred over Warfarin, achieving equivalent efficacy in preventing recurrent VTE while reducing major bleeding by 40% and intracranial hemorrhage by 65% (p<0.001) without requiring routine INR monitoring.
patient_plain_language: A blood clot forms inside the deep veins of your calf or thigh. It blocks blood from flowing smoothly back to your heart, causing painful swelling, warmth, and heaviness in one leg. The greatest danger is that a piece of the clot can break loose and travel to your lungs, causing a life-threatening pulmonary embolism.

symptoms.name: Lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly

name: Ruptured Baker's Popliteal Cyst (Pseudothrombophlebitis)
overview: Rupture of a popliteal (Baker's) cyst releases inflammatory synovial fluid into the gastrocnemius-soleus intermuscular plane, perfectly mimicking acute deep vein thrombosis (pseudothrombophlebitis). Lower extremity duplex ultrasound showing a non-occluded compressible popliteal vein and extravasated fluid in the calf muscle bellies rules out DVT, preventing unnecessary and dangerous anticoagulation.
patient_plain_language: A Baker's cyst is a fluid-filled sac behind your knee caused by arthritis or cartilage tears. If the sac pops, the fluid spills down into your calf muscle. It causes sudden, severe calf pain, swelling, and redness that looks and feels exactly like a dangerous blood clot (DVT). An ultrasound quickly proves the vein is open and the fluid is outside the vein.

name: Acute Pancreatitis (Atlanta Criteria / Lipase >3x ULN)
overview: The landmark WATERFALL multicenter randomized trial (n=249 patients) proved that MODERATE fluid resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's (1.5 mL/kg/h without bolus, or 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolemic) was superior to aggressive hydration (20 mL/kg bolus + 3 mL/kg/h), reducing fluid overload by 3-fold (20.5% vs 6.3%; p=0.004) without compromising clinical outcomes. Early oral feeding (within 24 hours) reduces hospital stay.
patient_plain_language: Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of your pancreas (most commonly caused by gallstones or heavy alcohol). Digestive enzymes that normally break down food in your intestines get activated prematurely inside the pancreas itself, literally starting to digest the gland from the inside out, causing severe boring stomach pain radiating to your back.

name: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning (Carboxyhemoglobinemia)

The antidote (Cyanokit) turns the poison directly into harmless Vitamin B12.

Beta-blockers or non-DHP calcium channel blockers remain foundational first-line therapy; vasodilators and pure inotropes (digoxin) are strictly contraindicated due to worsening outflow tract obstruction.
patient_plain_language: The muscular wall separating the left and right pumping chambers of your heart becomes excessively thick and overgrown due to a genetic trait. As the heart muscle squeezes, this thick wall bulges into the exit doorway, choking off blood flow to the body. Dehydration and hot showers make the blockage worse.

name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (Non-Ischemic Systolic Dysfunction)
overview: Quadruple guideline-directed medical therapy (ARNI Sacubitril/Valsartan + Evidence-based Beta-blocker + MRA Spironolactone + SGLT2 inhibitor Dapagliflozin/Empagliflozin) reduces 2-year all-cause mortality by 63% and promotes reverse ventricular remodeling (increasing LVEF from <35% to >45% in 38% of patients). patient_plain_language: Unlike HOCM where the heart muscle is overly thick, dilated cardiomyopathy causes the heart's main pumping chamber to stretch out, thin, and balloon like an over-inflated rubber glove. Because the stretched walls are weak, the heart cannot squeeze hard enough, causing fluid to back up into the lungs and legs.

name: Chronic Constrictive Pericarditis (Rigid Pericardial Shell)
overview: Right and left ventricular catheterization demonstrating ventricular interdependence (discordance of LV and RV systolic pressures during respiration) confirms constrictive physiology. Complete surgical pericardiectomy ('pericardial stripping') remains the only definitive curative therapy for chronic fibrotic constriction, restoring normal cardiac output in >80% of patients.
patient_plain_language: The sac surrounding your heart (pericardium) becomes stiff, thickened, and heavily calcified like an armor shell or eggshell. Because this rigid shell will not stretch, the heart cannot expand to fill with blood between beats, leading to massive fluid backup into the liver, stomach, and legs.

name: Cardiac Amyloidosis (ATTR Transthyretin Cardiomyopathy)
overview: The pivotal ATTR-ACT phase 3 trial (n=441) proved that Transthyretin stabilizer Tafamidis reduced all-cause mortality by 30% (p=0.026) and cardiovascular hospitalizations by 32% (p<0.001) in wild-type and hereditary ATTR cardiomyopathy. patient_plain_language: Misfolded proteins (amyloid fibrils) gradually deposit in between your heart muscle cells like cement or hardening glue. The heart walls become extremely stiff and thick, but unlike true muscle growth, the muscle fibers are replaced by dead protein, causing restrictive heart failure and conduction blocks.

Complicated Type B (refractory pain, malperfusion syndrome, rapid aortic expansion >44 mm) mandates Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair (TEVAR), which the INSTEAD-XL trial showed improves 5-year aorta-specific survival (86.9% vs 69.3%; p=0.04).
patient_plain_language: The main aorta tears downstream from the heart (after the left arm artery branch in your chest or abdomen). Unlike Type A, the tear is past the heart, so it usually does NOT need open-heart surgery. Instead, strict ICU blood pressure lowering and resting the artery wall allows it to heal, or a stent-graft (TEVAR) is placed if blood flow to organs is blocked.

name: Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome (Pre-Excited Atrial Fibrillation)
overview: Pre-excited Atrial Fibrillation conducts down an accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) at rates >250-300 bpm, risking ventricular fibrillation. AV-NODAL BLOCKING DRUGS (ADENOSINE, BETA-BLOCKERS, DILTIAZEM, VERAPAMIL, DIGOXIN) ARE STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED as they preferentially divert conduction down the accessory pathway, triggering fatal VF. Treatment is Procainamide IV or urgent electrical cardioversion.
patient_plain_language: You were born with an extra microscopic electrical wire (accessory pathway) connecting the upper and lower heart chambers. If you develop atrial fibrillation, impulses rush down this extra wire dangerously fast (over 250 beats a minute). Standard heart pills like beta-blockers and diltiazem are dangerous poisons here; Procainamide or catheter burning of the extra wire is required.

name: Brugada Syndrome (Type 1 Coved ST Elevation Channelopathy)
alternative_names: Brugada Syndrome (Type 1 Coved ST Elevation Channelopathy)
overview: Brugada syndrome (SCN5A sodium channel mutation) causes sudden nocturnal polymorphic VT / ventricular fibrillation in young individuals. Type 1 ECG pattern (coved ST elevation >=2 mm followed by negative T-wave in V1-V2) can be unmasked by fever or sodium channel blockers (Ajmaline, Flecainide). patient_plain_language: A genetic condition affecting the microscopic sodium gates in your heart cells. It causes a distinctive wave on your ECG and can trigger dangerous heart short-circuits, especially during a high fever or while sleeping at night. Taking fever-reducing pills immediately during an illness is life-saving, and an implantable defibrillator protects against sudden death.

name: Congenital Long QT Syndrome (LQTS - Torsades de Pointes)
alternative_names: Congenital Long QT Syndrome (LQTS - Torsades de Pointes)
overview: Congenital LQTS (LQT1 KCNQ1, LQT2 KCNH2, LQT3 SCN5A) delays cardiac repolarization, predisposing to early afterdepolarizations and polymorphic VT (Torsades de Pointes). Beta-blockers (Nadolol or Propranolol) are the mainstay of therapy, reducing cardiac events by >70% in LQT1 and LQT2. IV Magnesium Sulfate (2 g bolus) is first-line acute treatment for Torsades.
patient_plain_language: The electrical recharging phase of your heart muscle cells takes longer than normal. On an ECG, this appears as an extended QT interval. During times of stress, exercise (like swimming), or sudden loud alarms, this delay can cause the heart to wobble into a chaotic, twisty rhythm called Torsades de Pointes, leading to blackouts or cardiac arrest.

name: Sick Sinus Syndrome (Tachycardia-Bradycardia Syndrome)
overview: Intrinsic dysfunction of the sinoatrial node causes inappropriate sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, or alternating paroxysmal atrial tachyarrhythmias (tachy-brady syndrome). PERMANENT DUAL-CHAMBER PACEMAKER (DDDR) is the definitive class I therapy for symptomatic bradycardia, allowing safe initiation of AV-nodal blocking drugs to control the tachycardia component without worsening sinus pauses.
patient_plain_language: Your heart's natural spark plug (the sinus node) has worn out with age or fibrous scarring. It fires too slowly, skips beats, or pauses for several seconds, leaving you lightheaded or exhausted. Sometimes it alternates between racing too fast (atrial flutter/fibrillation) and suddenly stalling out. A dual-chamber pacemaker restores steady, reliable electrical beats.

name: Acute Fulminant Myocarditis (Inflammatory Cardiomyopathy)
overview: Acute viral or immune-mediated myocardial inflammation presenting with cardiogenic shock requires immediate advanced mechanical circulatory support (temporary Impella microaxial pump or VA-ECMO) to unload the LV and maintain perfusion. High-dose IV Methylprednisolone (1 g/day x 3 days) improves outcomes in giant cell myocarditis, eosinophilic myocarditis, and immune-checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) myocarditis.
patient_plain_language: An aggressive viral infection (or immunotherapy drug reaction) triggers your immune system to attack and inflame your heart muscle tissue. It can mimic a massive heart attack with high cardiac enzyme levels and chest pain, but the arteries are completely clear. Resting completely and letting the heart heal without strenuous exercise is critical.

name: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy (Stress-Induced Apical Ballooning)
overview: Triggered by acute severe emotional or physical stress (catecholamine storm), Takotsubo causes transient apical and mid-ventricular ballooning akinesia with hyperdynamic basal contraction, mimicking anterior STEMI. Beta-blockers or ACE inhibitors are used initially, but INOTROPES (DOBUTAMINE, NOREPINEPHRINE) ARE CONTRAINDICATED if dynamic LVOT obstruction occurs (present in ~10-15%). Complete LVEF recovery occurs in >90% within 4-8 weeks.
patient_plain_language: Also known as 'Broken Heart Syndrome', this condition happens when an overwhelming emotional shock or severe physical stress floods the heart with adrenaline. The tip of your heart temporarily paralyzes and balloons out into the shape of a Japanese octopus trap (takotsubo). Fortunately, in over 90% of cases, the heart completely recovers its strength within 1 to 2 months.

name: Atherosclerotic Renovascular Hypertension (Renal Artery Stenosis)
overview: The landmark CORAL (n=947) and ASTRAL (n=806) multicenter randomized trials proved that renal-artery stenting added to comprehensive medical therapy did NOT provide any significant benefit in blood pressure control, renal events, or cardiovascular outcomes compared to medical therapy alone. Renal stenting is strictly reserved for 'flash pulmonary edema' (Pickering syndrome) or refractory hypertension on >=4 drugs.
patient_plain_language: Cholesterol plaques narrow the main pipe supplying blood to one or both of your kidneys. The starved kidney mistakenly thinks your entire body has zero blood pressure, so it pumps out massive amounts of renin hormone, driving your body-wide blood pressure sky-high. In most patients, blood pressure pills work just as well as kidney artery stents without surgery.

name: Fibromuscular Dysplasia (Renal 'String-of-Beads' FMD)
overview: Unlike atherosclerotic stenosis, FMD is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory vascular disease affecting middle-aged women. Medial fibroplasia causes alternating webs and aneurysms ('string-of-beads' on angiography). PERCUTANEOUS TRANSLUMINAL RENAL ANGIOPLASTY (PTRA WITHOUT STENTING) is the curative intervention of choice, curing hypertension in 30-50% of patients and avoiding foreign metal stents.
patient_plain_language: A non-clotting disorder of blood vessel walls that most commonly affects young to middle-aged women. The muscular wall of the kidney or neck arteries develops fibrous ridges, making the artery look like a string of beads on X-ray. When it narrows the kidney artery, it causes severe high blood pressure that can often be completely cured with a simple balloon stretch (without needing a metal stent).

name: Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome / Aldosteronoma)
overview: Screening with Plasma Aldosterone Concentration to Plasma Renin Activity (PAC/PRA ratio >=20 with PAC >=15 ng/dL) detects primary aldosteronism. Unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's) is cured by LAPAROSCOPIC ADRENALECTOMY (curing HTN in 50% and improving control in 100%). Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is managed with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (Spironolactone or Eplerenone).
patient_plain_language: One or both of your adrenal glands (small caps on top of your kidneys) produce too much aldosterone hormone. This hormone tricks your kidneys into hoarding salt and water while dumping potassium down the toilet. It causes severe, stubborn high blood pressure and low potassium. If caused by a small benign lump in one gland, removing it surgically can cure the high blood pressure completely.

name: Acute Aortic Regurgitation (Flail Valve Leaflet / Endocarditis)
alternative_names: Acute Aortic Regurgitation (Flail Valve Leaflet / Endocarditis)
overview: Acute severe aortic regurgitation (caused by infective endocarditis or aortic dissection) results in sudden massive diastolic reflux into a non-compliant LV, causing catastrophic elevation in LVEDP, premature mitral valve closure, and pulmonary edema. URGENT SURGICAL AORTIC VALVE REPLACEMENT IS MANDATORY. Intra-aortic balloon pumps (IABP) and beta-blockers are ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED.
patient_plain_language: The one-way exit valve of your heart (aortic valve) suddenly blows open or gets destroyed by a severe bacterial infection. Instead of pumping blood out to your body, blood surges backward into the heart's main chamber during every single resting beat. The heart fills to bursting within minutes, causing sudden severe drowning breathlessness that requires emergency surgery.

name: Severe Calcific Aortic Stenosis (Low-Flow Low-Gradient vs High Gradient)
alternative_names: Severe Calcific Aortic Stenosis (Low-Flow Low-Gradient vs High Gradient)
overview: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis (aortic valve area <=1.0 cm2, mean gradient >=40 mmHg, or peak velocity >=4.0 m/s) carries a 50% 2-year mortality if untreated. Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) is non-inferior or superior to surgical replacement (SAVR) across all risk categories (PARTNER 3: 1-year death, stroke, or rehospitalization 8.5% TAVR vs 15.1% surgery; p=0.001). Low-dose Dobutamine stress echo differentiates true severe from pseudo-severe stenosis in low-flow states.
patient_plain_language: Over decades, calcium and bone-like crusts build up on your heart's main exit doorway (aortic valve), making it stiff and narrow like a rusty valve opened only a tiny crack. Your heart has to pump against enormous pressure to force blood out. Once symptoms like chest tightness, dizziness, or breathlessness appear, replacing the valve (often through a tiny catheter in the groin, called TAVR) restores normal lifespan.

name: Severe Mitral Regurgitation (Acute Papillary Rupture vs Chronic Degenerative)
alternative_names: Severe Mitral Regurgitation (Acute Papillary Rupture vs Chronic Degenerative)
overview: Acute severe MR (post-MI papillary muscle rupture) requires emergency surgery. In secondary MR with heart failure, the COAPT trial (n=614) proved that transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER with MitraClip) added to maximal GDMT reduced 24-month all-cause mortality from 46.1% to 29.1% (hazard ratio 0.62; p<0.001) and heart failure hospitalizations by 47% (p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: The two-door flap valve (mitral valve) that prevents blood from leaking backward into your lungs fails to seal tightly. In acute cases (such as after a heart attack when a supporting anchor cord snaps), it is a surgical emergency. In chronic cases, a tiny catheter clip (MitraClip) can be placed to clip the leaking flaps together in the center, dramatically reducing hospital visits and saving lives.

name: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS - Berlin Definition)
alternative_names: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS - Berlin Definition)
overview: The landmark ARDSNet trial established low tidal volume lung-protective ventilation (6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure <30 cmH2O), cutting mortality from 39.8% to 31.0% (p=0.007). In severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150), early prolonged prone positioning (>=16 hours/day; PROSEVA trial, n=466) reduced 28-day mortality from 32.8% to 16.0% (hazard ratio 0.39; p<0.001).
patient_plain_language: A severe, life-threatening lung inflammation that develops rapidly after pneumonia, sepsis, or severe trauma. The microscopic air sacs (alveoli) fill with inflammatory fluid and collapse, preventing oxygen from crossing into your blood. Patients need a breathing machine set to gentle low volumes and lying on their stomach (proning) to open healthy lung areas.

name: Cystic Fibrosis (CFTR Modulator Triplet Therapy)
overview: The transformative phase 3 trial of triple CFTR modulator therapy (Elexacaftor-Tezacaftor-Ivacaftor / Trikafta, n=403) produced unprecedented clinical breakthroughs: a 14.3 percentage-point increase in percent predicted FEV1 (p<0.001), 63% reduction in pulmonary exacerbations, and sweat chloride reduction of 41.8 mmol/L in patients with at least one F508del mutation.
patient_plain_language: A genetic condition affecting a microscopic salt channel (CFTR). name: Pulmonary Sarcoidosis (Non-Caseating Granulomatous Disease)
overview: Asymptomatic Stage I sarcoidosis (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy alone) undergoes spontaneous remission in >60-80% of cases and requires observation without steroids. Symptomatic Stage II-IV pulmonary sarcoidosis or dangerous extrapulmonary involvement (cardiac, neuro, ocular, or hypercalcemia) mandates Oral Prednisone (20-40 mg/day with slow taper). patient_plain_language: Your immune cells cluster together to form microscopic clumps of inflammation called granulomas, most often in the lymph nodes and tissue of your lungs. Many patients have a mild form that clears up entirely on its own. However, if it affects lung breathing, vision, or heart rhythm, steroid pills are used to calm the inflammation.

Removing the bird or feather bedding from your home is the only way to stop your lungs from developing permanent stiff scars.

name: Silicosis (Eggshell Calcification Pneumoconiosis)
overview: Inhalation of respirable crystalline silica (sandblasting, stone cutting, artificial stone countertops) causes irreversible macrophage lysis, fibrotic nodule formation, and progressive massive fibrosis (PMF). SILICOSIS CARRIES A 3-TO-30-FOLD INCREASED RISK OF ACTIVE TUBERCULOSIS (Silicotuberculosis). Routine annual screening with Tuberculin Skin Test (TST >=5 mm) or IGRA and prompt latent TB therapy (Rifampin or Isoniazid) is mandatory.
patient_plain_language: An occupational lung disease caused by inhaling fine silica dust from stone cutting, sandblasting, or manufacturing quartz countertops. The sharp mineral crystals cannot be cleared by your lungs, causing permanent nodules and hard scars. People with silicosis have a very high risk of contracting tuberculosis, so regular TB testing is essential.

overview: Asbestos fiber inhalation causes bilateral lower lobe predominant interstitial pulmonary fibrosis (asbestosis) and calcified parietal pleural plaques along the diaphragm and chest wall (pathognomonic hallmark). name: Pleural Empyema (Complicated Parapneumonic Infection)
overview: The landmark MIST-2 randomized trial (n=210) proved that combined intrapleural Tissue Plasminogen Activator (tPA 10 mg) and Recombinant Human DNase (5 mg) given twice daily for 3 days improved fluid drainage, reduced surgical referral by 77% (hazard ratio 0.23; p=0.003), and shortened hospital stay by 6.7 days versus placebo. patient_plain_language: A severe complication of pneumonia where the infection spills into the water space surrounding your lung (pleural cavity), creating a walled-off pocket of thick pus (empyema). name: Malignant Pleural Effusion (Metastatic Pleural Carcinomatosis)
overview: Malignant pleural effusion (MPE) causes recurrent dyspnea in advanced cancer. The AMPLE (n=146) and TIME2 (n=144) trials established that outpatient Indwelling Pleural Catheters (IPC / PleurX) achieve equivalent dyspnea relief while significantly reducing hospital days (10 days IPC vs 12 days talc pleurodesis; p<0.001) and re-intervention rates compared to chemical talc pleurodesis.
patient_plain_language: Cancer cells from the lung, breast, or other organs spread to the lining of your chest, causing fluid to continuously leak and crush the lung. Instead of staying in the hospital for days, doctors can place a tiny permanent soft catheter (IPC) under your skin so you or a nurse can drain the fluid at home with small vacuum bottles whenever breathlessness occurs.

name: Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH)
overview: CTEPH is the ONLY potentially curable form of pulmonary hypertension. PULMONARY ENDARTERECTOMY (PEA / open surgical removal of fibrotic clots) performed at an expert center cures hypertension and restores near-normal hemodynamics in >75% of patients. In inoperable CTEPH or residual post-PEA hypertension, soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator Riociguat (CHEST-1 trial, n=261) improves 6-minute walk distance (+46 meters; p<0.001) and pulmonary vascular resistance.
patient_plain_language: After a pulmonary embolism, old blood clots do not dissolve normally. Instead, they transform into tough, fibrotic yellow scars that permanently block your lung arteries, forcing your right heart to pump against crushing pressure. Unlike other forms of high lung pressure, this condition can be completely cured by expert surgeons who carefully peel the old scars out of the lung arteries.

Starting two medications at the exact same time works twice as well as taking one alone.

name: Bronchial Carcinoid Tumor (Neuroendocrine Bronchospasm)
overview: Typical and atypical bronchial neuroendocrine carcinoids arise from pulmonary Kulchitsky cells, presenting with recurrent pneumonia, hemoptysis, and pseudo-asthma wheezing. SURGICAL PARENCHYMAL-SPARING RESECTION (sleeve resection or lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection) is the curative gold standard (yielding >90% 10-year survival in typical carcinoids). Removing the small plug of tumor with keyhole surgery cures the disease in the vast majority of patients.

name: Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP - Steroid-Responsive)
overview: COP (formerly BOOP) is characterized by intra-alveolar fibromyxoid plugs (Masson bodies) and classic HRCT peripheral consolidations with the 'reverse halo' (atoll) sign. SYSTEMIC CORTICOSTEROIDS (Prednisone 0.75-1.0 mg/kg/day) achieve dramatic clinical and radiological resolution within 48-72 hours in >80% of patients. Relapses occur in 13-50% during steroid tapering, requiring slow withdrawal over 6-12 months.
patient_plain_language: Inflammatory plugs of connective tissue fill your microscopic air sacs, often appearing on X-rays like patches of stubborn bacterial pneumonia that never clear with antibiotics. Unlike permanent lung fibrosis, COP is remarkably steroid-responsive: taking Prednisone pills melts the inflammatory patches away within days, though the medicine must be tapered slowly to prevent relapse.
